fields.title: The Black Stair
fields.subtitle: The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, Book Two
fields.description: Wren, Tobin, Old Ash and Cinder have relit Emberwick's Ring and set out across the Greywaste for the Bright Mountain, with a grey rider on the road behind them. Then a swarm of mothwings drives them underground, into the Delver Deeps: a city built for sound, whose people have never seen light and think it a fairy tale. There they meet Mira, a blind girl who reads the world by echo and believes an old story carved on a hidden wall. When Captain Varrick comes down into the dark for the lamp, the only way out is the Black Stair, a thousand steps of total darkness, and Wren must do the hardest thing she has ever done: give the lamp away to someone else and trust him to carry it.
fields.about_html:
The Black Stair is the second book of The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, an adventure series by James DeGreef and Ochorus for readers aged nine to twelve. It follows straight on from Fire Against the Dark, but a new reader can begin here: the travellers are introduced again, and the story stands on its own.

This is a book about courage in the dark. Tobin, who has always been afraid of it, has to climb a thousand steps of it with hundreds of people trusting him. Wren, who has never trusted anyone, has to hand over the one thing she owns. And Mira, a girl who has never seen, believes in a light she cannot see because an old story told her it was coming. Like the book before it, it never preaches; it lets a story of faith, trust and a gift freely given speak for itself, for children to discover and for parents to talk about.

The book has fifteen chapters, about the length of a classic children's fantasy, each one a good evening's reading.

qa.question: Do I need to read Fire Against the Dark first?
qa.answer: It helps, because The Black Stair carries straight on from it, but the opening chapters introduce Wren, Tobin, Old Ash and Cinder again, so a new reader can begin here.

qa.question: What age is The Black Stair for?
qa.answer: Readers aged nine to twelve, and it reads aloud well to younger children from about seven. There is real danger in the dark, but nothing gory, and plenty of humour.

qa.question: Who is Mira?
qa.answer: A Delver girl who has been blind from birth and reads the world by the echo of clicks. She is quick, funny and brave, and she believes an old story about a Warm Man who promised that one day her people would see.

qa.question: What is the Black Stair?
qa.answer: A thousand steps of total darkness that climb from the Delver city of Deepholm to the surface. When Captain Varrick comes for the lamp, it is the only way out.

qa.question: What happens to the lamp in this book?
qa.answer: It still cannot be bought, stolen or earned, only given. On the Black Stair Wren has to truly give it to Tobin so that he can lead the Delvers up, the hardest act of trust she has ever made.

qa.question: Is it a Christian book?
qa.answer: Yes. Like the classic Christian fantasies, it tells its truths as story rather than sermon: faith in what cannot yet be seen, courage that trusts while it is afraid, and sight given as a gift. It never names God or quotes Scripture directly.

qa.question: How long is the book?
qa.answer: Fifteen chapters and about forty-eight thousand words, much the length of a classic children's fantasy.

fields.title: The Pale Road
fields.body_html:
If you had been a bird — and there were not many birds left in Gloamhaven, so you would have been a lonely one — and if you had flown out over the Greywaste on the fourth morning after the Ring of Emberwick was lit, you would have seen a great deal of nothing.

You would have seen grey grass, mile after mile of it, bending in a thin cold wind. You would have seen dead trees standing about in ones and twos, black and bare, with their branches held up like people who have just been told something dreadful. You would have seen a road running away north and a little east until it was lost in the mist. And over it all you would have seen the sun, Solenne, hanging in the sky as pale as a coin seen through dirty water, and giving about as much warmth as a coin does.

But if you had flown a little lower, you would have seen one thing more. On that long grey road, very small, there was a spot of gold.

It was moving. It went at about the pace of four travellers walking, one of whom was limping; and that is exactly what it was.

At the front went a girl of twelve, or near enough, small and wiry and sharp in the chin, with black hair that stuck out in tufts because she cut it herself with a knife. Her name was Wren Ashby, and until a few days ago she had been a chimney-sweep in the Low Quarter of Emberwick, owing money to everybody and owning nothing at all. She still owned very little: a coat too big for her, boots too small, a heel of bread in her pocket that she had not eaten and did not mean to, and a ribbon tied round her left wrist. And she had the lamp.

It was not much to look at. It was small enough to sit in two hands, made of brass dented in three places, with a little hook on top and a glass chimney that had a crack in it as fine as a hair. It had no oil and no place to put any. But inside it burned a flame no bigger than the tip of a finger, golden and white at the heart; and in the light of it, Wren’s ribbon was red. It was the only red thing for a hundred miles. Wren had learned the word only days ago, and she still looked at the ribbon when she thought nobody was watching.

Behind her came a tall, gangly boy of thirteen who seemed to be made mostly of elbows. He had untidy fair hair, ink on his fingers, spectacles that kept sliding down his nose, and a pack so full of tools that he clanked when he walked. This was Tobin Harrowgate, the son of the Warden of Emberwick. He had a brass compass in his hand, and he was looking at it instead of at the road, which was why he had already fallen over twice that morning.

Behind Tobin, slowest of all, came an old man so tall and so stooped that he looked like a question mark in a coat. His beard was long and white and singed brown at the edges; his coat was patched all over and had once been blue. He leaned on a long pole with a brass hook at the top, from which a little oil-lantern swung, and every second step he took was a careful one, because his left leg had been hurt in the battle for Emberwick and had not yet forgiven him for it. His name was Old Ash, and he was the last true Lamplighter in Gloamhaven.

And round the three of them, ahead and behind and sideways and back again, ran a small fox the grey of old ashes, whose tail-tip glowed with a living spark like a coal. Her name was Cinder. She could not talk, but she understood everything, and she had already stolen two oatcakes from Tobin’s pack before breakfast.

Far behind them, a ring of gold fire burned on the walls of Emberwick. Wren had lit it herself, at the top of the Great Beacon, by giving the lamp’s flame away. It had cost her everything she had; and when it was done she had found, to her great astonishment, that she had lost nothing at all. But that is the story of another book. This is the story of what happened next.

“It’s still pointing the same way,” said Tobin. “I did think it might wander. Compasses do, technically speaking, when they’ve been tampered with. But it’s quite steady. North and a bit east.” He looked up at the edge of the sky, where a faint pale point stood above the mist like the tip of a tooth. “Straight at the Bright Mountain.”

“You said that yesterday,” said Wren.

“Well, it’s still true.”

“Facts don’t stop being true just because you’ve heard them, Wren.”

“No,” said Wren, “but people stop listening.”

Old Ash, behind them, said “Hm,” which might have meant anything, and stopped.

At the side of the road, half sunk in the grey grass, stood a post of stone about as tall as Wren. Near the top a small niche had been cut into it, like a cupboard with no door, and the niche was empty. Below that, worn almost smooth, someone long ago had carved the shape of a flame inside a ring.

Old Ash limped over and laid his long hand on the stone, very gently, as you might lay your hand on the neck of an old horse. “Waystones. The Lamplighters set them a league apart all along this road, from Emberwick to the mountain. There was a light in every one of them once. You could walk the whole road by night and never be in the dark for longer than an hour.” He looked along the road, grey and empty both ways. “They called it the Pale Road, because it showed up pale in the dark, between the lights. Hm. It’s only pale in the daytime now.”

“What happened to the lights?” said Wren.

“What happens to all of them. Somebody stopped tending them.” He looked down at her, and then at the lamp. “Would you, child?”

Wren held the lamp a little tighter. She did not mean to. Her hands did it on their own, the way your hand closes on a coin in your pocket when someone in a crowd brushes against you.

“Would I what?”

“Give it one.”

She looked at the niche. It was full of dust and dead grass and the dry husk of a beetle. In an hour it would be behind them, burning away for nobody at all. It seemed, to a girl from Soot Lane, a terrible waste.

Then she remembered the top of the Beacon, and the little flame sliding off the lip of the lamp like a drop of honey, and her certainty that it was gone — and what had happened after.

“It hasn’t got a wick,” she said. “Or oil. Or anything.”

“It never needed them,” said Old Ash. “Neither does the lamp.”

Wren brushed out the beetle with her sleeve. Then, a little awkwardly, because she was still not used to doing it, she tipped the lamp towards the niche and said, under her breath so the others should not hear, “Here. It’s for you.”

A bead of gold ran off the brass and dropped onto the bare stone.

And it stayed there. It stood up straight on the bottom of the niche, on nothing at all — and then it grew. It grew until it filled the niche and spilled warm light down the face of the old stone, and the carved flame in its ring seemed to leap; and the warmth came out across the road and touched their faces like the first fire of winter.

Tobin made a noise like a kettle.

“But what’s it burning?” he said. “It has to be burning something. Fire’s a process, it needs fuel, that’s the whole point of—“

“Look at the grass,” said Old Ash.

All round the foot of the waystone, in a circle about as wide as a cartwheel, the grey grass was changing. It was the faintest wash of colour, like a drop of ink in a bucket of water. But it was there: a fresh, cool, living colour that none of them had a name for, and that made Wren think of the smell after rain.

“Green,” said Old Ash softly. “That’s green, that is. I’d nearly forgotten.”

Wren looked down at the lamp. She knew already what she would see, but she looked anyway, because she was still not quite sure she believed it. The flame was not smaller. If anything, it was brighter than before.

“What is given, grows,” said Old Ash. He did not say it as if he were teaching her. He said it as if he were reminding himself.

They walked on. Wren did not look back for nearly a mile, because she did not want the others to see her do it. When she did, the waystone was a tiny point of gold far behind them on the grey plain; and she found that it did not look like a waste. It looked as if somebody had left a door open for whoever came next.

They camped that night in the lee of a dead tree, because it was the only thing for miles that kept off any wind.

Tobin built the fire, with a great deal of explanation about draughts and kindling and the proper ratio of small sticks to large ones. Wren, who had been lighting fires in other people’s grates since she was five, let him get on with it and did not say a word, which was very nearly the kindest thing she had ever done. The dead wood burned with a thin, sour flame and a lot of smoke. Beside it the lamp, sitting on a flat stone, looked like a gold sovereign next to a heap of pennies.

Old Ash made tea.

I have told you before about Old Ash’s tea, and I am sorry to say that the Greywaste did not improve it. The water came from a muddy pool in a stream-bed, and Ash boiled it with the tea and, for reasons he did not explain, with a handful of grey leaves off a bush. It came out the colour of a puddle and smelled of wet dog.

“It tastes like somebody washed their socks in it,” said Wren. “Somebody with feet.”

“Hm,” said Old Ash, pleased, and drank his down in one go. Cinder sniffed at Wren’s cup, sneezed a small shower of sparks into it, and went off to see whether Tobin’s pack had any oatcakes left. It had not, by the end.

Then Ash leaned back against the tree and stretched his bad leg towards the fire.

“Out here there’s no Ring,” he said. “No wall. Nothing between us and whatever’s walking about in the dark but this fire and that lamp and our own eyes. So we keep watch. The lad takes the first, I take the middle, and you take the last, child, till the light comes.”

“Why do you get the middle?” said Wren, suspiciously. In her experience, whoever chose the jobs kept the best one.

“Because the middle is the worst. It’s when the dark is thickest. On the wall at home we called it the turning of the night.” Tobin had gone a little pale behind his spectacles. He turned his face to the fire so that nobody could see, and nobody did. “There’s a thing we used to say on the wall at the turning of the night,” Ash went on, “when you couldn’t see your own hand. The Lamplighters’ Psalm. It’s older than the Guild, older than the wall. I’ll say it once, and you can learn it or not, as you please.”

He did not sing it. He said it, slowly, in his dry old voice, looking into the fire:

“Though I walk through the gloaming, I will fear no dark, for the Flame is with me. It goes before me on the road; it keeps the watch while I am sleeping. The night is long, but it is not for ever. My light was lit by another’s hand, and no dark can take it from me. So I will walk in the Flame’s keeping, all my days, until morning comes.”

The fire hissed. Out on the plain the wind moved through the grass like a long breath let out.

“Rot,” said Wren, but not loudly. She was lying with her chin on her arms, saying the words over in her head. Until morning comes. It was too like the scrap of song she had left from her mother — Morning comes, morning comes — and she did not know what to do with the feeling it gave her, so she put it away.

Tobin was staring at Old Ash.

“I know that,” he said. “Not all of it. The first bit. Though I walk through the gloaming.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “My mother used to say it, when I couldn’t sleep. I thought she’d made it up.”

Old Ash looked at him for a long moment across the fire.

“Hm,” he said. “No. She didn’t make it up. But I expect she meant every word, lad. That’s the next best thing.”

Wren went to sleep the way she had every night since they left the Grey Gate: curled on the hard ground with her coat over her and one hand stretched out to rest on the lamp.

She did not hold it, exactly. She only kept her fingers against the brass, so that she would know if it moved. But the plain truth, which she did not tell herself at all, was that she had never owned anything that someone had not taken off her sooner or later, and she was not about to start trusting the world now, just because it had been kind to her once or twice. Not even Old Ash. Not even Tobin. She liked them both a good deal more than she would ever have said. That was not the same thing.

Tobin sat up against the dead tree and kept the first watch.

I will tell you about that watch, because Tobin never told anybody.

Beyond the little ring of firelight the dark began — not the dark of a city at night, with a lit window here and there, but the old dark, the kind that goes on in every direction with nothing in it at all. It came right up to the edge of the light and stopped there, and it seemed to Tobin that it was waiting. Every time a stick cracked in the fire, his heart jumped so hard it hurt.

He had helped save a city. He had stood on a dark stair beside Old Ash and held it against the Hollows. And he was just as frightened now as he had been at five years old, in his bed in the Warden’s Hall, the night after his mother died, when somebody had taken the candle away.

His hands began to shake. He sat on them. It did not help.

At last, very quietly, he reached into his pack and took out a little lamp of his own. It was nothing like Wren’s: a plain Guild-oil night-lamp with a pewter base and a glass shade painted with tiny stars. It had been his mother’s. He had slept with it burning beside his bed every night of his life, and he had brought it across the Greywaste wrapped in a spare shirt, and told nobody.

He lit it with a twist of grass from the fire and held it cupped against his chest. Its light was thin and yellow. There was not much oil left in it. Three nights, perhaps. Four, if he was careful.

It was a silly thing to want, with a fire, and a lamp with the real Flame in it not six feet away. He knew that. But Wren’s lamp was Wren’s. This one had been his mother’s, and it was the only thing in the whole of the dark that he had brought from home.

Though I walk through the gloaming, he whispered to it, I will fear no dark—

He could not remember what came next. He said the first line again instead, and then again, and after a while his hands stopped shaking.

On the other side of the fire, Wren half woke, as people who have slept rough most of their lives often do. She saw Tobin through the smoke, bent over a little light, and thought sleepily that he was reading his map again, and that he was the most hopeless swot in Gloamhaven. Then she went back to sleep with her hand on the lamp, and did not think of it again for a long time.

They had walked for perhaps an hour the next morning when Cinder stopped dead in the middle of the road.

Her ears went flat. Her tail went low, and the spark in it burned smaller and fiercer, like a coal when you blow on it. She was not looking ahead, towards the mountain. She was looking back.

Wren turned.

The Pale Road ran away behind them, grey on grey, to the edge of the mist. Far back she could see the waystone they had lit, still burning, a pinprick of gold. And on a low rise beyond it, against the dull sky, there was a rider.

He was too far off to have a face. He was only a shape: a man on a horse, both of them grey, sitting quite still and looking — Wren was sure of it — straight at them.

“It’s him,” said Tobin. His voice went up at the end. “Isn’t it? It’s Varrick.”

Nobody needed to answer. They had all seen that grey cloak before, at the top of the Great Beacon, with the fire roaring behind it.

“He’s been there since the gate,” said Wren. “Hasn’t he? The whole way.”

“Hm,” said Old Ash. He leaned on his pole and looked back for a long while, and Wren could not read his face at all. “He’s keeping his distance. I used to know what that lad was thinking before he thought it. I don’t any more.”

As they watched, the grey rider came slowly down off the rise to the road. He did not come towards them. He rode as far as the waystone, burning gold in the grey morning, and there he stopped.

From that distance it was impossible to tell what he was doing. He might have been waiting for them to go on. He might, Wren thought, with a cold feeling in her stomach, be about to put it out.

But he did not put it out. They watched for a long time, and all that time the little gold light burned on, and the grey rider sat beside it, quite still, as if he had forgotten where he was going.

Then Old Ash turned his back on him, planted his pole on the Pale Road, and said, “Come along.”

They went on towards the mountain. And I may as well tell you, since you will want to know, that whatever Captain Varrick did beside that waystone, he did it for a long time — for when Wren looked back again at noon, he was still there.

Out on the plain the wind moved through the grass like a long breath let out. “Rot,” said Wren, but not loudly. She was lying with her chin on her arms, saying the words over in her head. Until morning comes. It was too like the scrap of song she had left from her mother — Morning comes, morning comes — and she did not know what to do with the feeling it gave her, so she put it away. Tobin was staring at Old Ash. “I know that,” he said. “Not all of it. The first bit. Though I walk through the gloaming.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “My mother used to say it, when I couldn’t sleep. I thought she’d made it up.” Old Ash looked at him for a long moment across the fire. “Hm,” he said. “No. She didn’t make it up. But I expect she meant every word, lad. That’s the next best thing.” Wren went to sleep the way she had every night since they left the Grey Gate: curled on the hard ground with her coat over her and one hand stretched out to rest on the lamp. She did not hold it, exactly. She only kept her fingers against the brass, so that she would know if it moved. But the plain truth, which she did not tell herself at all, was that she had never owned anything that someone had not taken off her sooner or later, and she was not about to start trusting the world now, just because it had been kind to her once or twice. Not even Old Ash. Not even Tobin. She liked them both a good deal more than she would ever have said. That was not the same thing. Tobin sat up against the dead tree and kept the first watch. I will tell you about that watch, because Tobin never told anybody. Beyond the little ring of firelight the dark began — not the dark of a city at night, with a lit window here and there, but the old dark, the kind that goes on in every direction with nothing in it at all. It came right up to the edge of the light and stopped there, and it seemed to Tobin that it was waiting. Every time a stick cracked in the fire, his heart jumped so hard it hurt. He had helped save a city. He had stood on a dark stair beside Old Ash and held it against the Hollows. And he was just as frightened now as he had been at five years old, in his bed in the Warden’s Hall, the night after his mother died, when somebody had taken the candle away. His hands began to shake. He sat on them. It did not help. At last, very quietly, he reached into his pack and took out a little lamp of his own. It was nothing like Wren’s: a plain Guild-oil night-lamp with a pewter base and a glass shade painted with tiny stars. It had been his mother’s. He had slept with it burning beside his bed every night of his life, and he had brought it across the Greywaste wrapped in a spare shirt, and told nobody. He lit it with a twist of grass from the fire and held it cupped against his chest. Its light was thin and yellow. There was not much oil left in it. Three nights, perhaps. Four, if he was careful. It was a silly thing to want, with a fire, and a lamp with the real Flame in it not six feet away. He knew that. But Wren’s lamp was Wren’s. This one had been his mother’s, and it was the only thing in the whole of the dark that he had brought from home. Though I walk through the gloaming, he whispered to it, I will fear no dark— He could not remember what came next. He said the first line again instead, and then again, and after a while his hands stopped shaking. On the other side of the fire, Wren half woke, as people who have slept rough most of their lives often do. She saw Tobin through the smoke, bent over a little light, and thought sleepily that he was reading his map again, and that he was the most hopeless swot in Gloamhaven. Then she went back to sleep with her hand on the lamp, and did not think of it again for a long time. They had walked for perhaps an hour the next morning when Cinder stopped dead in the middle of the road. Her ears went flat. Her tail went low, and the spark in it burned smaller and fiercer, like a coal when you blow on it. She was not looking ahead, towards the mountain. She was looking back. Wren turned. The Pale Road ran away behind them, grey on grey, to the edge of the mist. Far back she could see the waystone they had lit, still burning, a pinprick of gold. And on a low rise beyond it, against the dull sky, there was a rider. He was too far off to have a face. He was only a shape: a man on a horse, both of them grey, sitting quite still and looking — Wren was sure of it — straight at them. “It’s him,” said Tobin. His voice went up at the end. “Isn’t it? It’s Varrick.” Nobody needed to answer. They had all seen that grey cloak before, at the top of the Great Beacon, with the fire roaring behind it. “He’s been there since the gate,” said Wren. “Hasn’t he? The whole way.” “Hm,” said Old Ash. He leaned on his pole and looked back for a long while, and Wren could not read his face at all. “He’s keeping his distance. I used to know what that lad was thinking before he thought it. I don’t any more.” As they watched, the grey rider came slowly down off the rise to the road. He did not come towards them. He rode as far as the waystone, burning gold in the grey morning, and there he stopped. From that distance it was impossible to tell what he was doing. He might have been waiting for them to go on. He might, Wren thought, with a cold feeling in her stomach, be about to put it out. But he did not put it out. They watched for a long time, and all that time the little gold light burned on, and the grey rider sat beside it, quite still, as if he had forgotten where he was going. Then Old Ash turned his back on him, planted his pole on the Pale Road, and said, “Come along.” They went on towards the mountain. And I may as well tell you, since you will want to know, that whatever Captain Varrick did beside that waystone, he did it for a long time — for when Wren looked back again at noon, he was still there.

fields.title: The Hollow Hunt
fields.body_html:
In the cities, Hollows drift. They come over a dark wall like fog over a sea-wall, and wander the streets, and touch whoever they happen to find. But out on the open Greywaste, where there are no walls and very few people, they do something else. They hunt.

Old Ash told them this on the fifth day, and Wren wished afterwards that he had told them sooner.

The waterskins were nearly empty by then. The muddy pools by the road had dried to cracked grey plates, and Tobin had begun licking his lips and looking at the sky as if he expected it to do something about it. So at noon Old Ash sat down on a waystone, unrolled his map across his knees, and frowned at it.

It was the map they had stolen back from the Guild vault in Emberwick: an old, soft, brown thing, much folded, drawn in faded ink by Lamplighters who had been dead a hundred years. The Pale Road ran across it in a dotted line, with a tiny flame drawn at every waystone. And off to the east, a thin wavering line went wandering down to a little circle with a word written beside it in a careful old hand.

“Hartsease Spring,” read Tobin, leaning over. “Oh, good. A spring’s fed from underground, so even in a dry season it ought to—“

“Ought to,” said Old Ash. “Hm. It was there a hundred years ago. We’ll follow the stream-bed down to it. It’ll be quicker than the road, and out of the wind.”

So they left the Pale Road and climbed down into the stream-bed.

It was a long, winding gully with steep banks of crumbling earth on either side, taller than Old Ash in places, and a floor of round grey stones that had not felt water in living memory. It was out of the wind, as Ash had promised, and out of everything else. You could see nothing from the bottom of it but the two banks and a strip of dull sky.

Wren did not like it. She had grown up on rooftops, where you can see everything coming. After an hour of stones and banks and sky she could bear it no longer.

“I’m going up,” she said. “I can see further from up there. I’ll see the spring before you do.”

“Stay close, child,” said Old Ash.

“I’ll be right along the top. You’ll hear me.” She tucked the lamp into the front of her coat and went up the bank like a cat up a curtain. In a moment her head appeared over the edge, black tufts against the grey. “See? Right here. Shouting distance.”

“You just want to look for him,” said Tobin.

Wren did not answer, which meant that he was right. She had looked back for the grey rider every hour since the waystone, and seen him every time, always far behind, as if he were tied to them by a very long string. In the gully she could not see him. That was worse than seeing him.

So she went along the top of the bank, keeping pace with the others below; and as the afternoon wore on, and she got further ahead and then further ahead again, and found a dead tree to climb and then a ridge to look over, shouting distance became a rather larger distance than it had been at the start. I do not say this to blame her. She was twelve, and she had been told what to do by grown-ups all her life, and very few of them had been worth listening to. It takes a while to learn the difference.

The dusk came down early that evening, the way it does on the Greywaste in autumn, when there is no gold in the sunset to keep it company. The grey of the day thickened into the grey of evening. Old Ash lit the little oil-lantern on the hook of his pole, and it threw a ring of thin yellow light on the stones round them.

Tobin looked up at the top of the bank. There was no Wren on it.

“She’s gone too far,” he said. “Hasn’t she? She said shouting distance. I don’t think this is shouting distance any more. Technically, I suppose it depends how loudly you shout—“

Cinder growled.

It was a low growl, so low that Tobin felt it in the stones under his boots before he heard it. The ember-fox had stopped in the middle of the stream-bed. Her back was up, and her tail-spark had gone small and white and fierce.

Then the cold came.

It came down the gully from behind them, the way water would have come if there had been any water: a creeping, flowing cold that ran along the floor of the stream-bed and up the banks. Tobin’s breath went white in front of his face. The round grey stones at his feet grew a fur of frost, all at once, as if somebody had breathed on them. And the silence came with it, thick and woolly.

“Hm,” said Old Ash, very quietly. “Lad. Stand behind me.”

Round the bend of the gully, out of the gloaming, came the Hollows.

There were six of them. Seven. They came the way Hollows always come, not walking but drifting, grey and faceless, like smoke poured into the shape of a person and left to set. They made no sound at all. They did not hurry. They came along the stream-bed in a line, and when Tobin turned his head, his heart turning over, he saw that more of them were coming round the bend ahead, so that the gully was stopped at both ends like a bottle with a cork in each.

“They hunt in packs out here,” said Old Ash, in the same quiet voice. He lifted his pole, so that the little lantern swung high and the ring of yellow light grew wider. “Like wolves used to. They drive you into a low place, and then they close in.” He did not take his eyes off them. “Tobin. Listen to me. Shout for her. Loud as you can.”

The Hollows had stopped at the edge of the lantern-light. It held them — just. It was only Guild oil, after all, and Guild oil can only hold a Hollow back; it cannot hurt one. They hung there at the edge of the yellow ring, grey on grey, and the frost crept in under the light towards Tobin’s boots.

“Tobin,” said Old Ash. “Shout.”

Tobin opened his mouth.

Nothing came out.

I want you to understand that he tried. He told his throat to shout Wren as loudly as it had ever shouted anything. But it was like a dream, the kind where something is coming and your legs will not move. His throat had shut like a fist. His hands hung at his sides and would not lift. He stood in the stream-bed with his mouth open and his spectacles fogging, and he could not do anything at all while the grey shapes leaned in towards him out of the dark.

One of them came round the edge of the light.

It slid along the bank where the lantern’s ring was thinnest, as smooth as oil on water, and it came at Tobin from the side. He saw it coming. He saw the grey blank where its face should have been, and one long grey arm lifting, reaching, and he could not move.

Old Ash stepped in front of him.

He did it without a word, and quicker than Tobin would have believed an old man with a bad leg could move. He swung his pole, and the lantern on its hook swept through the Hollow’s reaching arm, and the Hollow flinched back from the oil-light. But the arm swept low as it went, and it passed through Old Ash’s left leg, just below the knee — the bad leg, the hurt one — as easily as a hand passes through mist.

Old Ash made a sound Tobin had never heard him make. He staggered. His foot came down on a round stone and turned under him, and he fell hard on the stones of the stream-bed, and the lantern went skittering away across the frost, and its light rocked and dwindled.

And the leg — Tobin saw it in the swinging light — the leg had gone grey. Not the grey of his old breeches. A grey that was in the skin and the boot and the very shape of it, from the ankle to the knee, like a leg made of ash that a breath would blow away.

Then Cinder went for them.

She went with a screech like a gate in a gale, all teeth and fury and sparks, and her tail blazed white, and the nearest Hollow drew back from her. But she was one small fox, and her spark was one small spark, and the grey shapes were closing in from both ends of the gully, slow and silent and sure.

And somewhere above, on the top of the bank, there was a scrabble of boots, and a shower of earth, and a voice shouting, “Ash! Tobin!”

Wren came down the bank on her backside in a landslide of dirt and dead roots, and the lamp was already in her hands.

She did not think about it. There was no time to think. She came off the bottom of the bank onto her feet and held the lamp out in front of her, and it flared — white-gold, all at once, like a door flung open on a summer morning.

The Hollows shrieked.

It was the only sound they ever made: a high, thin, tearing scream, like wind through a broken window. The ones nearest the lamp twisted and shrank and fled, up the banks and over the top and away into the dusk, and the others went after them, from both ends of the gully at once, until there was nothing left but the frost melting on the stones and the smell of something burnt.

Wren stood there breathing hard. Then she saw Old Ash.

He had got himself up on one elbow. His face was grey too, now — not Hollow-grey, but the plain grey of pain — and his lips were pressed together so tight that they had gone white in his beard. The leg lay out on the stones in front of him, the colour of cold ashes.

Wren was on her knees beside him before she knew she had moved. She held out the lamp. She did not stop to remember the words, but they came anyway.

“Here,” she said. “It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

The flame leaned out of the lamp towards the old man like a flower towards a window. The warmth went down over the grey leg, and the colour came back into it — slowly, from the knee down, the way a stain spreads through cloth, until his breeches were brown and his boot was brown and his skin above the boot was an old man’s skin again. Old Ash let out a long breath.

“Thank you, child,” he said.

“Can you get up?”

He tried. He got as far as one knee, and then his face went very still and white, and he sat down again rather suddenly.

“Hm,” he said. “No. Not just now.” The knee was already swelling under his breeches. “The colour’s come back, but that’s not the same as mending. The Hollow had the warmth out of it, and the stones did the rest. Twice in one week. I’m getting careless in my old age.”

“It wasn’t you that was careless,” said Wren.

She stood up and turned round. Tobin was standing exactly where he had been standing all along. He had not moved. His hands were still at his sides, and his spectacles were still fogged, and his face was the colour of the frost.

“You just stood there,” said Wren.

Tobin opened his mouth. Nothing came out of it this time either.

“He told you to shout for me. I heard him — I heard him, I was halfway back already — and you never shouted. You just stood there with your mouth open like a fish on a slab, and he had to get in front of you, with his leg, because you were too scared to—“

“You went off!” Tobin’s voice came back all at once, cracked and much too loud. “You took the lamp and went off! He told you to stay close and you said shouting distance and then you went off over the hill to look for — for him, for Varrick, and you left us down here with nothing but an oil-lantern, and you knew—“

“Don’t you dare—“

“—you knew we had nothing! It’s not even a proper light! It’s not ours, the proper light, it’s only ever yours, you never let it out of your hand—“

“Because I can’t trust anybody with it!” Wren was shouting now, and she did not care. “Look what happens! You can’t even shout! Some Lamplighter you’d make. You’re scared of your own shadow, Tobin Harrowgate. You’re scared of the dark. You’re nothing but a nob’s boy with a bag full of spanners who should’ve stopped at home with his father—“

She stopped.

She had not meant to say that last part. She had not even known it was in her until it was out. It hung in the cold air of the gully between them like something broken that cannot be put back.

Tobin did not say anything. He took off his spectacles and wiped them on his coat, slowly, though they were not foggy any more. He put them back on. Then he turned round and went to pick up Old Ash’s lantern from where it lay among the stones, and he did not look at Wren again.

Old Ash had watched all of it from the ground. He said nothing either. He only looked at Wren for a long moment, the way he had looked at her once in the Leaning Tower when she had said that nothing in the world was free; and Wren found that she would rather he had shouted.

They could not go on that night, and they could not go far the next. Tobin and Wren got Old Ash between them to a place where the bank had fallen in and made a hollow out of the wind, without speaking a word to each other, which is not easy when you are lifting a tall old man. Tobin built a fire. Wren set the lamp beside Ash’s leg, where its warmth could reach the knee. Nobody made tea, which shows you how bad things were.

Wren took the first watch. She sat on a stone with her arms round her knees and her back to the others and glared out into the dark, daring something to come. Nothing did. She thought about what she had said, over and over, and every time she thought about it, it was worse. She had never said sorry to anyone in her life, not and meant it. She did not know how you began; so she glared at the dark instead, because it was easier.

Tobin lay on his side with his back to the fire, and did not sleep.

He did not take out his mother’s night-lamp; he thought he did not deserve it. He lay with his eyes open in the dark and heard Wren’s voice again and again — you’re scared of the dark — and the worst of it was not that she had said it. The worst of it was that it was true. Old Ash had told him on the Beacon stair that courage was being frightened and standing anyway; and today he had been frightened, and he had stood, all right. He had stood like a post. And an old man had been hurt for it.

Long after Wren had woken Old Ash for the middle watch, and curled up with her hand on the lamp, and gone to sleep, a voice spoke softly out of the hollow in the bank.

“Lad. Come here a minute. I know you’re awake.”

Tobin went and sat down beside him. In the firelight the old man’s face looked very tired, and he held himself carefully, as people do when moving hurts.

“I’m sorry,” said Tobin. It came out in a whisper. “It’s my fault. Your leg. She’s right. I’m a coward.”

“Hm,” said Old Ash. “No. You’re not.”

“I froze. You told me to shout, and I couldn’t even—“

“I know. I was there.” Ash shifted his leg, and winced. “Listen to me, Tobin, because I’ll only say this once tonight, and I want you to keep it. Fear is not the same as cowardice. They’re not even cousins. Fear is a thing that happens to you, like cold, or hunger. It comes up out of your belly and takes hold of your legs, and you don’t get a say in it. A hare freezes in the grass when the hawk goes over. Nobody calls the hare a coward.”

“I’m not a hare.”

“No. You’re a boy who was frightened. That’s no shame.” Old Ash looked into the fire. “Cowardice is something else. Cowardice is what you choose afterwards, when you’ve had time to think, and you’ve seen what the fear cost, and you decide to let it have its way next time too. That’s the only kind there is. And you haven’t made that choice, lad. Not yet. You won’t have to make it for a while.”

Tobin was quiet for a long time.

“And when I do have to?”

“Then you’ll be frightened again,” said Old Ash. “I expect you’ll always be frightened of the dark. Some people are. I’m not asking you not to be. I’m asking you to remember there’s more than one way to stand in it.” He paused. “And I stepped in front of you today because I’m old, and that’s what old men are for. Don’t you take that away from me by calling it your fault.”

Tobin wiped his nose on his sleeve. “Sir. You knew. About the dark. Before she said it.”

“I’ve known since the gate.” Ash’s beard moved; it might have been a smile. “That little lamp in your pack, with the stars on it. Light it, if it helps. There’s no shame in a light, lad. There never was.”

Tobin went back to his place. He did not light the night-lamp. But he lay with his hand on his pack, where he could feel the shape of it through the canvas, and after a while, for the first time that night, he slept.

Old Ash sat up alone through the turning of the night, with his leg stretched out to the lamp. He did not wake Wren for the last watch. He kept it himself, and it was a long one, and he spent most of it looking at his knee, and then at the long way still to go to the mountain, and then at his knee again.

And when the morning came, it did not come grey and cold, as every morning on the Greywaste had come before it. The wind had dropped away to nothing in the night. The air hung over the plain thick and warm and perfectly still, like the air in a shut room, and not one blade of the grey grass was moving.

Old Ash looked up at the heavy sky, and sniffed it, and did not like it at all.

She came off the bottom of the bank onto her feet and held the lamp out in front of her, and it flared — white-gold, all at once, like a door flung open on a summer morning. …it flared — white-gold, all at once, like a door flung open. The Hollows shrieked. It was the only sound they ever made: a high, thin, tearing scream, like wind through a broken window. The ones nearest the lamp twisted and shrank and fled, up the banks and over the top and away into the dusk, and the others went after them, from both ends of the gully at once, until there was nothing left but the frost melting on the stones and the smell of something burnt. Wren stood there breathing hard. Then she saw Old Ash. He had got himself up on one elbow. His face was grey too, now — not Hollow-grey, but the plain grey of pain — and his lips were pressed together so tight that they had gone white in his beard. The leg lay out on the stones in front of him, the colour of cold ashes. Wren was on her knees beside him before she knew she had moved. She held out the lamp. She did not stop to remember the words, but they came anyway. “Here,” she said. “It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.” The flame leaned out of the lamp towards the old man like a flower towards a window. The warmth went down over the grey leg, and the colour came back into it — slowly, from the knee down, the way a stain spreads through cloth, until his breeches were brown and his boot was brown and his skin above the boot was an old man’s skin again. Old Ash let out a long breath. “Thank you, child,” he said. “Can you get up?” He tried. He got as far as one knee, and then his face went very still and white, and he sat down again rather suddenly. “Hm,” he said. “No. Not just now.” The knee was already swelling under his breeches. “The colour’s come back, but that’s not the same as mending. The Hollow had the warmth out of it, and the stones did the rest. Twice in one week. I’m getting careless in my old age.” “It wasn’t you that was careless,” said Wren. She stood up and turned round. Tobin was standing exactly where he had been standing all along. He had not moved. His hands were still at his sides, and his spectacles were still fogged, and his face was the colour of the frost. “You just stood there,” said Wren. Tobin opened his mouth. Nothing came out of it this time either. “He told you to shout for me. I heard him — I heard him, I was halfway back already — and you never shouted. You just stood there with your mouth open like a fish on a slab, and he had to get in front of you, with his leg, because you were too scared to—“ “You went off!” Tobin’s voice came back all at once, cracked and much too loud. “You took the lamp and went off! He told you to stay close and you said shouting distance and then you went off over the hill to look for — for him, for Varrick, and you left us down here with nothing but an oil-lantern, and you knew—“ “Don’t you dare—“ “—you knew we had nothing! It’s not even a proper light! It’s not ours, the proper light, it’s only ever yours, you never let it out of your hand—“ “Because I can’t trust anybody with it!” Wren was shouting now, and she did not care. “Look what happens! You can’t even shout! Some Lamplighter you’d make. You’re scared of your own shadow, Tobin Harrowgate. You’re scared of the dark. You’re nothing but a nob’s boy with a bag full of spanners who should’ve stopped at home with his father—“ She stopped. She had not meant to say that last part. She had not even known it was in her until it was out. It hung in the cold air of the gully between them like something broken that cannot be put back. Tobin did not say anything. He took off his spectacles and wiped them on his coat, slowly, though they were not foggy any more. He put them back on. Then he turned round and went to pick up Old Ash’s lantern from where it lay among the stones, and he did not look at Wren again. Old Ash had watched all of it from the ground. He said nothing either. He only looked at Wren for a long moment, the way he had looked at her once in the Leaning Tower when she had said that nothing in the world was free; and Wren found that she would rather he had shouted. They could not go on that night, and they could not go far the next. Tobin and Wren got Old Ash between them to a place where the bank had fallen in and made a hollow out of the wind, without speaking a word to each other, which is not easy when you are lifting a tall old man. Tobin built a fire. Wren set the lamp beside Ash’s leg, where its warmth could reach the knee. Nobody made tea, which shows you how bad things were. Wren took the first watch. She sat on a stone with her arms round her knees and her back to the others and glared out into the dark, daring something to come. Nothing did. She thought about what she had said, over and over, and every time she thought about it, it was worse. She had never said sorry to anyone in her life, not and meant it. She did not know how you began; so she glared at the dark instead, because it was easier. Tobin lay on his side with his back to the fire, and did not sleep. He did not take out his mother’s night-lamp; he thought he did not deserve it. He lay with his eyes open in the dark and heard Wren’s voice again and again — you’re scared of the dark — and the worst of it was not that she had said it. The worst of it was that it was true. Old Ash had told him on the Beacon stair that courage was being frightened and standing anyway; and today he had been frightened, and he had stood, all right. He had stood like a post. And an old man had been hurt for it. Long after Wren had woken Old Ash for the middle watch, and curled up with her hand on the lamp, and gone to sleep, a voice spoke softly out of the hollow in the bank. “Lad. Come here a minute. I know you’re awake.” Tobin went and sat down beside him. In the firelight the old man’s face looked very tired, and he held himself carefully, as people do when moving hurts. “I’m sorry,” said Tobin. It came out in a whisper. “It’s my fault. Your leg. She’s right. I’m a coward.” “Hm,” said Old Ash. “No. You’re not.” “I froze. You told me to shout, and I couldn’t even—“ “I know. I was there.” Ash shifted his leg, and winced. “Listen to me, Tobin, because I’ll only say this once tonight, and I want you to keep it. Fear is not the same as cowardice. They’re not even cousins. Fear is a thing that happens to you, like cold, or hunger. It comes up out of your belly and takes hold of your legs, and you don’t get a say in it. A hare freezes in the grass when the hawk goes over. Nobody calls the hare a coward.” “I’m not a hare.” “No. You’re a boy who was frightened. That’s no shame.” Old Ash looked into the fire. “Cowardice is something else. Cowardice is what you choose afterwards, when you’ve had time to think, and you’ve seen what the fear cost, and you decide to let it have its way next time too. That’s the only kind there is. And you haven’t made that choice, lad. Not yet. You won’t have to make it for a while.” Tobin was quiet for a long time. “And when I do have to?” “Then you’ll be frightened again,” said Old Ash. “I expect you’ll always be frightened of the dark. Some people are. I’m not asking you not to be. I’m asking you to remember there’s more than one way to stand in it.” He paused. “And I stepped in front of you today because I’m old, and that’s what old men are for. Don’t you take that away from me by calling it your fault.” Tobin wiped his nose on his sleeve. “Sir. You knew. About the dark. Before she said it.” “I’ve known since the gate.” Ash’s beard moved; it might have been a smile. “That little lamp in your pack, with the stars on it. Light it, if it helps. There’s no shame in a light, lad. There never was.” Tobin went back to his place. He did not light the night-lamp. But he lay with his hand on his pack, where he could feel the shape of it through the canvas, and after a while, for the first time that night, he slept. Old Ash sat up alone through the turning of the night, with his leg stretched out to the lamp. He did not wake Wren for the last watch. He kept it himself, and it was a long one, and he spent most of it looking at his knee, and then at the long way still to go to the mountain, and then at his knee again. And when the morning came, it did not come grey and cold, as every morning on the Greywaste had come before it. The wind had dropped away to nothing in the night. The air hung over the plain thick and warm and perfectly still, like the air in a shut room, and not one blade of the grey grass was moving. Old Ash looked up at the heavy sky, and sniffed it, and did not like it at all.

fields.title: Mothwing Weather
fields.body_html:
By the middle of the morning it was as warm as a kitchen, and the Greywaste was holding its breath.

Not a blade of grass moved. Not a twig stirred on the dead trees. The air lay over the plain thick and heavy and close, like a blanket that has been left too long in front of the fire, and the pale sun hung in it without a single cloud to keep it company. After a week of wind and frost it ought to have been pleasant. It was not. It was the kind of warmth you get in a shut-up room where somebody has been ill.

“I don’t like it,” said Wren, who had not said anything to anybody since breakfast.

Nobody answered her. That was how it had been all morning.

Old Ash was sitting on a stone with his bad leg stuck out in front of him, and Tobin was kneeling in the grass a little way off, working at something with his knife and a coil of wire and his whole attention. He had been at it since first light. He had not looked at Wren once. Wren had not looked at him either, except all the time, out of the corner of her eye, which does not count.

At last Tobin stood up and brought the thing over to Old Ash.

It was a crutch. He had made it out of a forked branch from a dead tree, stripped and trimmed, with a crosspiece lashed into the fork with wire and padded thickly with cloth so that it would sit soft under an arm. Wren looked at the cloth and knew it. It was Tobin’s spare shirt — the one he kept something wrapped up in at the bottom of his pack, which she had never asked about.

“It ought to take about half your weight, sir,” said Tobin, not quite looking at anyone. “If you lean on it properly. The fork spreads the load, you see, and the wire’s brass, so it won’t rust, and I’ve cut it to the length of your — well, I measured you while you were asleep, actually. I hope you don’t mind.”

Old Ash took the crutch and turned it over in his long hands. Then he fitted it under his arm, and got up — slowly, but he got up — and stood leaning on it, with his pole in his other hand, looking down at the boy.

“Hm,” he said. “That’s a good piece of work, lad.”

Tobin went pink to the tips of his ears.

Wren turned away and pretended to be very interested in a dead tree. She did not know what was the matter with her. She felt hot and cross and miserable, all at once, and she wanted very badly to say something, and every time she opened her mouth the wrong words were waiting behind her teeth.

They went on slowly that day, because there was no other way to go. Old Ash swung along between the crutch and the pole, his jaw set, and at every hundred paces he stopped and breathed, and they stopped with him. Nobody complained. Cinder, who had decided that the crutch was a new kind of stick put there for her benefit, tried twice to carry it off while Ash was resting on it, and the second time Old Ash sneezed at her. This surprised her so much that she sat down in the road and stared at him, and did not try again.

Towards noon they found Hartsease Spring. It was not much of a spring any more: a dip in the ground with a ring of old stones round it and a few inches of brown water at the bottom. But it was water, and it was cold, and they filled the skins and drank until their stomachs sloshed. Even Cinder drank, lapping noisily with her tail stuck straight up behind her like a candle. Tobin drank three times, very politely, as if the spring might be offended if he stopped.

It was there, sitting on the stones of the spring with his leg up, that Old Ash looked round at the still, heavy air, and sniffed, and said what he had been thinking all morning.

“Mothwing weather.”

“What’s that?” said Wren — and then, because the question had come out of her before she could stop it, she went red.

“A warm, still dusk after a cold spell,” said Old Ash. “Very like this one. The mothwings sleep in the ground all the cold weeks, under the roots of the dead trees. And when a day like this comes, they wake up and come out, all together, and go looking for light.”

“Moths?” said Wren. “Moths? We had moths in Soot Lane. They ate Mott’s best jacket. Nobody was frightened of them except Mott.”

“Not that sort of moth.” Ash held out his hands, as wide apart as a dinner-plate. “Mothwings. Their wings are like old glass, the coloured sort, in a window with the light behind it. Only grey, of course, out here. Everything’s grey. And they’re gentle, child. They don’t bite. They don’t sting. They’ve never meant harm to a living thing.”

“Then what’s the trouble?”

“The trouble,” said Old Ash, “is that they love light more than anything in the world. More than food. More than their own lives. And there are thousands of them. When a swarm finds a light, it settles on it. One on top of another, and another on top of that, until the light’s under a heap of them as big as a haycart. And whoever is holding the light is under the heap as well.” He looked at Wren, and at the bulge in the front of her coat where the lamp was. “They’ll smother a lantern in a minute. They’ll smother a man in five. Not because they want to. Only because they can’t bear to be anywhere else.”

Nobody said anything for a while.

“Well,” said Tobin at last, in a small voice. “That’s a horrible way to be loved.”

Wren said nothing. But she put her hand flat on the front of her coat, over the lamp, and kept it there for the rest of the afternoon. And she found herself thinking, without at all wanting to, of the way she slept every night with her fingers pressed against the brass, as if letting go of it for one moment might lose it for ever.

They did not see any mothwings all that afternoon, and Wren began to think that Old Ash had been making a fuss about nothing. But as the sun sank down the sky, pale and swollen in the heavy air, the stillness grew stiller, and the warmth grew warmer, and the grey grass round their feet seemed to be waiting for something.

They stopped for the night beside a stand of dead trees on a low rise. Tobin was gathering sticks. Old Ash was easing himself down onto the ground with his crutch. Wren had taken the lamp out of her coat and set it on a stone, the way she always did, to warm the place up before the fire was going.

And something came out of the dusk on soft, slow wings, and landed beside it.

It was a moth. That is to say, it was shaped like a moth: a plump, furry body as long as Wren’s hand, two feathery feelers, and wings. But the wings were as big as the pages of a book laid open, and they were not dusty and brown like the wings of a Soot Lane moth. They were made — or seemed to be made — of a hundred tiny panes, each one set in a thin dark line like the lead in a window. Out in the dusk they had been grey. But the moth had come down within a hand’s breadth of the lamp, and in that light, as Wren watched, the little panes began to change.

They went faintly gold, first. Then one or two of them, near the edges, went a soft, deep colour like the inside of a shell. Then a pane went the colour of Wren’s ribbon, and another the cool fresh colour of the grass round the waystone, and one, right at the tip of the wing, went a colour Wren had never seen and did not have even the beginning of a name for, a clear bright colour like a far-off sky.

The moth sat beside the lamp with its great wings spread out, quite still, as if it were warming them. It looked as though it had come home.

“Oh,” said Tobin.

He had come up beside Wren without her noticing, with an armful of sticks, and he was staring at the moth with his mouth open.

“It’s like the window in the Guild Hall,” he whispered. “The big round one, over the stairs. My mother used to take me to look at it when I was small. There’s a story in it, in pieces of glass. Only you couldn’t really see the story, because all the glass had gone grey.” He swallowed. “I never knew it was meant to look like that.”

Wren looked at him sideways. In the lamplight his face was turned towards the moth, and his spectacles had two tiny coloured wings in each lens.

Now, she thought. Say it now. Tobin, what I said in the gully—

She opened her mouth.

And Cinder whined.

It was not a growl. It was a long, high, frightened whine, which Wren had never heard her make before. The ember-fox was standing at the top of the rise with her nose pointed out across the plain to the east, and every hair on her body was standing on end.

Wren looked where she was looking.

The plain was rising.

That is what it looked like, at first. The whole grey Greywaste to the east, as far as she could see, seemed to be lifting up off the ground in the dusk, the way dust lifts off a carpet when you beat it. Then it was not the plain. It was something coming up out of the plain — out of the grass, out of the roots of the dead trees, out of the ground itself — thousands and thousands of somethings, rising together into the still warm air in a vast, soft, rolling cloud. And there was a sound coming with it. It was the softest sound Wren had ever heard. It was like rain on a roof a long way off. It was the sound of wings.

The cloud turned in the sky, slowly, like a flock of starlings turning. And then it began to come towards them.

“Hide it,” said Old Ash. His voice cracked like a whip. “Hide it, child. Every scrap of light. Now.”

Wren snatched up the lamp and stuffed it into the front of her coat, and the lone moth beside it rose up in a flurry and went blundering after it, battering softly at her chest. She did up the coat over the lamp, all the way to her chin, and wrapped her arms round herself on top of that, and held on.

The light went out of the world.

Old Ash had pinched out his own little lantern on the hook of his pole. Tobin had kicked dirt over the beginnings of the fire. And Cinder — Wren saw it in the last of the dusk — Cinder curled her tail right round under her belly and lay on it, and buried the spark deep in her fur, until there was nothing to see of it but the faintest red prickle, like a coal at the very bottom of a dead grate.

Then the swarm came over them, and there was no more dusk at all.

It was like being caught in a snowstorm, if the snow were soft and warm and as big as books. The wings were everywhere. They brushed against Wren’s face and her hands and her hair; they whispered past her ears; they filled the air so thickly that the sky disappeared. It was not frightening at first. It was almost beautiful — the softness, and the hush, and the great slow beating all around. And then they began to land.

They landed on Wren.

She had hidden the light. But she could not hide the warmth. The lamp was burning against her ribs, warm as a loaf from the oven, and the mothwings could feel it through her coat the way you can feel a fire through a door. One settled on her shoulder. Then another on her back. Then three more, then ten, soft and heavy and clinging, crawling over each other to get closer, until she could feel the weight of them on her like a wet blanket, and then like two, and then like a pile of them.

“Ash,” she said. A mothwing brushed across her mouth, and she spat out a mouthful of dust and fur. “Ash—“

“I know, child. I know.” The old man’s voice came out of the dark close by, and it was calm, but it was the calm of somebody working very hard at it. “We can’t stay. They’ll bury her. We have to run, and keep running, until they lose the warmth. Cinder! Cinder — lead us.”

Wren heard a small sharp yip from somewhere ahead in the dark.

“Follow the fox,” said Old Ash. “Hold on to each other. Don’t let go, whatever you do. Lad — give me your shoulder.”

Wren put out her hand behind her, into the dark, into the soft blind storm of wings. She did not know what she was reaching for. She only knew that she could not run alone into a darkness she could not see.

A hand caught hers. It was a long, thin hand, with ink-stained fingers, and it was shaking. But it held on.

Neither of them said anything. There was no time to say anything, and anyway they would both have got a mouthful of mothwing. But Wren held on to that hand as tightly as she had ever held anything — tighter, almost, than she held the lamp — and Tobin held on to her, and on his other side he took Old Ash’s weight on his shoulder, and Old Ash swung along on his crutch, and somewhere ahead of them Cinder yipped and yipped again; and the four of them ran.

I do not know if you have ever run in the pitch dark across open ground. I hope you never have to. You cannot see your feet. You cannot see the ground. Every step is a step off the edge of the world, and you take it anyway, because the thing behind you is worse.

They ran through the grass, with the mothwings crawling over Wren’s back and shoulders and clinging to her hair, falling away and settling again. They ran stumbling over tussocks and through dry ditches and once, painfully, into a dead tree, which Tobin apologised to. They ran with Cinder’s yip always just ahead, pulling them on through the dark like a thread. Old Ash’s breath was coming in long harsh gasps. Tobin was making a little sound every time he put his foot down, half a word, over and over, and it took Wren a long time to understand that it was gloaming — gloaming — gloaming.

And slowly — so slowly that at first she thought she was imagining it — the weight on her back grew lighter.

They were losing her. Out here in the dark, running, with the warmth of the lamp wrapped tight inside her coat and her arms wrapped tight round that, the mothwings were losing her. One by one they let go and fluttered off, confused, into the night. The great soft roar of wings began to fall away behind.

“It’s working,” panted Tobin. “Ash — sir — it’s working, they’re—“

Cinder yipped. It was a different yip — short and sharp, a warning — and it came from much too close, and from somewhere below them.

And the ground was not there.

It did not crack, or tip, or give any warning at all. One moment there was grass under Wren’s feet, and the next there was a soft, dreadful tearing sound, like old cloth ripping, and the grass went down from under her, and she went down with it. She felt Tobin’s hand jerk in hers as he fell too. She heard Old Ash cry out. Then they were all falling — not straight down, but down and down a long, steep, rushing slope of loose stones that rolled and clattered and poured along with them, like sliding down the inside of a chimney full of gravel. Something struck her knee. Something struck her elbow. Stones were roaring all round her. She held on to the lamp with one arm and kept hold of Tobin with the other, and she did not let go of either, not once, all the way down.

It was a long way down.

At last the slope grew less steep, and the stones slowed, and she slid to a stop on her back in a heap of rubble, with the breath knocked out of her and dust in her mouth. The clattering went on for a while, further and further below, as the last loose stones went bouncing away into the depths. Then it stopped too.

Tobin’s hand was not in hers any more. She had not felt it go.

Wren lay quite still and opened her eyes as wide as they would go.

It made no difference at all. She had been inside more chimneys than anyone in Emberwick, and she had never known a dark like this. There was not a crack of grey anywhere — not above, where the hole they had fallen through must be, not anywhere. It was as if the whole world had been put out like a candle. The air was cold, and smelled of stone and water, and it was so quiet that she could hear the blood going in her own ears.

Somewhere above her, very faint, a single pebble trickled down the slope and was still.

And then, out of the dark, from somewhere she could not tell — near or far, above or below — there came a small, dry, careful sound.

Click.
