That is to say, it was shaped like a moth: a plump, furry body as long as Wren’s hand, two feathery feelers, and wings. But the wings were as big as the pages of a book laid open, and they were not dusty and brown like the wings of a Soot Lane moth. They were made — or seemed to be made — of a hundred tiny panes, each one set in a thin dark line like the lead in a window. Out in the dusk they had been grey. But the moth had come down within a hand’s breadth of the lamp, and in that light, as Wren watched, the little panes began to change. They went faintly gold, first. Then one or two of them, near the edges, went a soft, deep colour like the inside of a shell. Then a pane went the colour of Wren’s ribbon, and another the cool fresh colour of the grass round the waystone, and one, right at the tip of the wing, went a colour Wren had never seen and did not have even the beginning of a name for, a clear bright colour like a far-off sky. The moth sat beside the lamp with its great wings spread out, quite still, as if it were warming them. It looked as though it had come home. “Oh,” said Tobin. He had come up beside Wren without her noticing, with an armful of sticks, and he was staring at the moth with his mouth open. “It’s like the window in the Guild Hall,” he whispered. “The big round one, over the stairs. My mother used to take me to look at it when I was small. There’s a story in it, in pieces of glass. Only you couldn’t really see the story, because all the glass had gone grey.” He swallowed. “I never knew it was meant to look like that.” Wren looked at him sideways. In the lamplight his face was turned towards the moth, and his spectacles had two tiny coloured wings in each lens. Now, she thought. Say it now. Tobin, what I said in the gully— She opened her mouth. And Cinder whined. It was not a growl. It was a long, high, frightened whine, which Wren had never heard her make before. The ember-fox was standing at the top of the rise with her nose pointed out across the plain to the east, and every hair on her body was standing on end. Wren looked where she was looking. The plain was rising. That is what it looked like, at first. The whole grey Greywaste to the east, as far as she could see, seemed to be lifting up off the ground in the dusk, the way dust lifts off a carpet when you beat it. Then it was not the plain. It was something coming up out of the plain — out of the grass, out of the roots of the dead trees, out of the ground itself — thousands and thousands of somethings, rising together into the still warm air in a vast, soft, rolling cloud. And there was a sound coming with it. It was the softest sound Wren had ever heard. It was like rain on a roof a long way off. It was the sound of wings. The cloud turned in the sky, slowly, like a flock of starlings turning. And then it began to come towards them. “Hide it,” said Old Ash. His voice cracked like a whip. “Hide it, child. Every scrap of light. Now.” “Hide it, child. Every scrap of light. Now.” Wren snatched up the lamp and stuffed it into the front of her coat, and the lone moth beside it rose up in a flurry and went blundering after it, battering softly at her chest. She did up the coat over the lamp, all the way to her chin, and wrapped her arms round herself on top of that, and held on. The light went out of the world. Old Ash had pinched out his own little lantern on the hook of his pole. Tobin had kicked dirt over the beginnings of the fire. And Cinder — Wren saw it in the last of the dusk — Cinder curled her tail right round under her belly and lay on it, and buried the spark deep in her fur, until there was nothing to see of it but the faintest red prickle, like a coal at the very bottom of a dead grate. Then the swarm came over them, and there was no more dusk at all. It was like being caught in a snowstorm, if the snow were soft and warm and as big as books. The wings were everywhere. They brushed against Wren’s face and her hands and her hair; they whispered past her ears; they filled the air so thickly that the sky disappeared. It was not frightening at first. It was almost beautiful — the softness, and the hush, and the great slow beating all around. And then they began to land. They landed on Wren. She had hidden the light. But she could not hide the warmth. The lamp was burning against her ribs, warm as a loaf from the oven, and the mothwings could feel it through her coat the way you can feel a fire through a door. One settled on her shoulder. Then another on her back. Then three more, then ten, soft and heavy and clinging, crawling over each other to get closer, until she could feel the weight of them on her like a wet blanket, and then like two, and then like a pile of them. “Ash,” she said. A mothwing brushed across her mouth, and she spat out a mouthful of dust and fur. “Ash—“ “I know, child. I know.” The old man’s voice came out of the dark close by, and it was calm, but it was the calm of somebody working very hard at it. “We can’t stay. They’ll bury her. We have to run, and keep running, until they lose the warmth. Cinder! Cinder — lead us.” Wren heard a small sharp yip from somewhere ahead in the dark. “Follow the fox,” said Old Ash. “Hold on to each other. Don’t let go, whatever you do. Lad — give me your shoulder.” Wren put out her hand behind her, into the dark, into the soft blind storm of wings. She did not know what she was reaching for. She only knew that she could not run alone into a darkness she could not see. A hand caught hers. It was a long, thin hand, with ink-stained fingers, and it was shaking. But it held on. Neither of them said anything. There was no time to say anything, and anyway they would both have got a mouthful of mothwing. But Wren held on to that hand as tightly as she had ever held anything — tighter, almost, than she held the lamp — and Tobin held on to her, and on his other side he took Old Ash’s weight on his shoulder, and Old Ash swung along on his crutch, and somewhere ahead of them Cinder yipped and yipped again; and the four of them ran. I do not know if you have ever run in the pitch dark across open ground. I hope you never have to. You cannot see your feet. You cannot see the ground. Every step is a step off the edge of the world, and you take it anyway, because the thing behind you is worse. They ran through the grass, with the mothwings crawling over Wren’s back and shoulders and clinging to her hair, falling away and settling again. They ran stumbling over tussocks and through dry ditches and once, painfully, into a dead tree, which Tobin apologised to. They ran with Cinder’s yip always just ahead, pulling them on through the dark like a thread. Old Ash’s breath was coming in long harsh gasps. Tobin was making a little sound every time he put his foot down, half a word, over and over, and it took Wren a long time to understand that it was gloaming — gloaming — gloaming. And slowly — so slowly that at first she thought she was imagining it — the weight on her back grew lighter. They were losing her. Out here in the dark, running, with the warmth of the lamp wrapped tight inside her coat and her arms wrapped tight round that, the mothwings were losing her. One by one they let go and fluttered off, confused, into the night. The great soft roar of wings began to fall away behind. “It’s working,” panted Tobin. “Ash — sir — it’s working, they’re—“ Cinder yipped. It was a different yip — short and sharp, a warning — and it came from much too close, and from somewhere below them. And the ground was not there. It did not crack, or tip, or give any warning at all. One moment there was grass under Wren’s feet, and the next there was a soft, dreadful tearing sound, like old cloth ripping, and the grass went down from under her, and she went down with it. She felt Tobin’s hand jerk in hers as he fell too. She heard Old Ash cry out. Then they were all falling — not straight down, but down and down a long, steep, rushing slope of loose stones that rolled and clattered and poured along with them, like sliding down the inside of a chimney full of gravel. Something struck her knee. Something struck her elbow. Stones were roaring all round her. She held on to the lamp with one arm and kept hold of Tobin with the other, and she did not let go of either, not once, all the way down. It was a long way down. At last the slope grew less steep, and the stones slowed, and she slid to a stop on her back in a heap of rubble, with the breath knocked out of her and dust in her mouth. The clattering went on for a while, further and further below, as the last loose stones went bouncing away into the depths. Then it stopped too. Tobin’s hand was not in hers any more. She had not felt it go. Wren lay quite still and opened her eyes as wide as they would go. It made no difference at all. She had been inside more chimneys than anyone in Emberwick, and she had never known a dark like this. There was not a crack of grey anywhere — not above, where the hole they had fallen through must be, not anywhere. It was as if the whole world had been put out like a candle. The air was cold, and smelled of stone and water, and it was so quiet that she could hear the blood going in her own ears. Somewhere above her, very faint, a single pebble trickled down the slope and was still. And then, out of the dark, from somewhere she could not tell — near or far, above or below — there came a small, dry, careful sound. Click.

fields.title: Down Among the Delvers
fields.body_html:
There are two kinds of dark in the world. There is the ordinary kind, which you find in a cupboard or under the bedclothes; wait in it a while and shapes come creeping back — the edge of a door, the gleam of a cup. And there is the other kind, which is found only deep under the earth, where no light has fallen since the world was made. Your eyes never grow used to that kind. It is like having your eyes shut and open at the same time.

Wren lay at the bottom of the long slope of stones in the second kind of dark and tried to work out which way was up.

Everything hurt a little and nothing hurt a lot, which she decided was good. And the lamp — she clutched at her coat — the lamp was still there, a hard warm lump against her ribs, wrapped tight where she had stuffed it when the mothwings came. Not a thread of light got out. She had done that so well that now she could not see her own hand.

“Tobin?” she said. Her voice came back from somewhere high up, smaller. “Ash?”

Stones slithered to her left. “I’m — here. I think.” Tobin’s voice was thin and shaking. “I’ve lost my spectacles. No — they’re on my face. They just aren’t doing anything.”

“Ash?”

A long pause. Then, from below and to the right, slow and dry as ever but with something tight underneath it: “Here, child. Hm. Still in one piece. Mostly.” A breath sucked in through teeth. “The leg has opinions.”

Then a cold nose pushed into Wren’s ear, and a small warm weight pressed against her side and stayed there. Cinder had her tail curled under her, the spark buried deep in her fur as she had hidden it in the swarm, and only the faintest red prickle showed where it lay. It lit nothing, not even Cinder.

Wren sat up. “Right,” she said, because somebody had to say something. “I’m getting the lamp out.”

Her fingers were on the top of her coat when Old Ash said, very quietly, “Wait.”

“Wait for what? We can’t see a—“

“Listen.”

She listened: pebbles trickling, water dripping somewhere far off, Tobin’s breath going much too fast. Then it came again — the sound she had half hoped she had imagined.

Click.

It came from somewhere above them on the slope: a small, dry, neat sound, like a fingernail tapped on a slate. Then another, from the right. Click. Click-click. Then from behind, and from the left, and from — Wren’s skin crept — almost beside her, so close she could have reached out and touched whatever was making it.

“Wh-what is it?” breathed Tobin. “Beetles? Some cave beetles, actually, make a noise with their—“

“Hush, lad.”

The clicks moved. That was the worst of it. They were not scattered about like crickets in a hedge; they were going somewhere. They came down the slope in a long, careful ring, and did not knock loose a single stone. Wren knew how hard that was. The hair stood up on her neck. Whatever was coming was better at the dark than she was.

She slid her hand into her boot, where she kept her knife.

“Keep the lamp hidden, child,” said Ash, very low. “We don’t know what it will do to them. Or what they’ll do about it.”

The clicking stopped. Then a voice spoke out of the dark — a man’s voice, low and soft and oddly musical, as if each word had been turned on a lathe before it was let out.

“Four,” it said. “Three large. One small, with fur. One breathes like a bellows. One is hurt — I hear the leg. And one—“ a pause, and a sniff — “one is warm.”

“Warm?” said a woman’s voice, sharp.

“Warm like a fever. Can you not feel it? From here.”

A murmur went round the ring. Wren caught the words sick, and the Roof.

“We’re not sick,” she said loudly. “We fell. Down a hole. Out of the sky, I suppose, as far as you lot are concerned. And we’re not stopping, so you can just show us the way out and—“

“It speaks,” said the man’s voice, with interest. “And rudely.”

“I’ll show you rude—“

Then a great many things happened very fast. A net dropped over Wren’s head and shoulders, soft and heavy and smelling of mushrooms. Cinder snarled and sneezed, and a shower of sparks went up, and for half a heartbeat they lit — a shoulder, pale as candle-wax, a white braid, an open hand — and then dark again. Somebody yelped. Tobin cried out. Ash said, “Peace! Peace, we mean no harm—“ and then grunted with pain.

Hands found Wren’s wrists in the dark — quick, cool, sure hands that seemed to know exactly where her wrists were before they touched them — and then let go at once, as if she had burned them.

“Ai! Hot as a hearth-stone. Don’t touch her. Net her and leave her be.”

Wren kicked at nothing, and missed, and kicked again, and was sat on, firmly, by someone who smelled of moss.

“Enough, child,” came Ash’s voice. “There are twenty of them, and they can see us, and we cannot see them.”

“They can’t see anything! It’s pitch black!”

“Hm,” said Old Ash. “Are you quite sure?”

They were not, as it turned out, killed. They were not even hurt, apart from Wren’s pride, which had been sat on. Somebody worked the knife out of her fingers, and her hands were tied in front of her with a soft cord by someone who took great care not to touch her skin. Then the voices went off to argue in low, singing murmurs, and somebody new sat down beside her on the stones.

“I’m set to guard you,” said a voice. “Please don’t run. You’re very bad at running. I’ve been listening.”

It was a girl’s voice, about Wren’s age, clear and precise, every word set down like a cup on a saucer — with something under the neatness that sounded very like a person trying not to laugh.

“I’m the best runner in Soot Lane,” said Wren.

“Soot Lane must be full of light, then. You run like someone who’s used to knowing where the ground is before her feet get there.” A pause. “Down here the ground doesn’t tell you. You have to ask it.”

Click. Wren jumped. It had come from right in front of her nose.

“Sorry,” said the girl. “I was looking at you.”

“Looking at me?”

“Hearing you. It’s nearly the same word, in the old speech.” Click. Click. The sound moved round her, curious as a cat. “You’re smaller than your voice. Your voice is twice your size.” There was a small rustle, as if the girl had drawn her knees up. “I’m Mira. Mira of the Low Hum, granddaughter of Hessa. Clear echo to you.” She waited. Then she added, helpfully, “That’s when you say And a true return. It’s rude not to.”

Wren said nothing at all, which was ruder still.

“Oh, well,” said Mira. “Never mind. What’s your name? I can’t keep calling you the warm one inside my head. It makes you sound like soup.”

In spite of everything — the dark, the cord, Ash’s breath hissing somewhere off to the right — Wren felt the corner of her mouth twitch. “Wren,” she said. “Wren Ashby.”

“Wren.” The girl tried it the way you might try a sweet. “A small quick sound. It suits you. What does it mean?”

“It’s a bird.”

“What’s a bird?”

“It’s — a little brown thing. It flies.”

“What’s brown?”

“It’s a colour.”

“Ah,” said Mira wisely. “One of those. And this warm thing in your coat. Is that a bird too?”

Wren’s arms tightened round her middle before she could stop them. “It’s a lamp.”

“What’s a lamp?”

“It makes light.”

There was a short silence, and then Mira laughed. It was not an unkind laugh. It was quick and surprised and delighted, the laugh of someone who has been told that the person in front of her keeps a dragon in her pocket.

“Light,” she said. “You carry light about in your coat. Like in the nursery stories. Like the Burning that comes up the Black Stair for children who won’t go to sleep.”

“It’s not a story. It’s real. It lets you see.”

“I can see.”

“Not properly—“ Wren stopped, because she had heard what she was saying, and it sounded stupid even to her. “I mean — it lets you see things that are far away. Without touching them. Without clicking at them. You just look, and there they are, all at once, every one of them.”

“How horrible,” said Mira, interested. “All at once? How do you know which one to listen to first?”

Wren did not know. She sat in the dark with her mouth open, which at least nobody could see.

“What does it feel like?” said Mira, more quietly. “Your light. When it’s on you.”

Wren thought of the garret in Soot Lane, and Mrs Fenn on her step saying her children’s names. “Like when somebody says your name,” she said slowly, “and they’re glad it’s you.”

There was a long pause. The clicks had stopped.

“Show me,” said Mira.

“You can’t see it.”

“Show me anyway.”

Wren looked — out of habit — towards where Ash had been. She could not see him, of course; and he did not say anything. So she worked her tied hands up to the front of her coat, and fumbled it open, and drew the lamp out into the dark.

Light poured out of it like water out of a broken jar. After that blackness Wren had to screw her eyes shut, and when she opened them she saw — all at once, every one of them — the people who had caught her.

There were about twenty, standing in a ring on the fallen stones, and they were pale: not grey, like the greyed, but pale like the inside of a shell, like a candle that has never been lit. Their hair was white, even on the young ones, and worn in many small braids. They carried long staves and coils of net, and their feet were bare. Their eyes were open, large and pale as pearls; and not one of those eyes turned towards the lamp. Not one. Instead every face in the ring had flinched sideways, the way your face flinches from an oven door, and every hand had come up, palm out, as though to keep off a heat.

“Cover it,” said the man with the lathe-turned voice — Dask, Wren learned afterwards he was called; tall and bony, with a white beard braided into two points. “Cover it, girl. It’s spreading.”

But the girl beside Wren had not flinched. She was thin and sharp-elbowed and a little taller than Wren, with a pointed face and a great many braids, and in every braid were threaded small round beads of polished stone that ticked softly against one another when she moved. She had put out both her hands towards the lamp — not palm out, to keep it off, but palm up, the way you hold your hands out to be given something.

“Oh,” said Mira, very softly. “Oh. It’s like standing next to someone who’s laughing.”

Her eyes, the pale grey of a morning mist, rested a little to one side of the lamp, quite calm, not searching for anything. But her face was turned straight into the warmth, and she looked so astonished and so pleased that Wren, who did not usually notice faces unless they meant trouble, noticed hers and did not forget it.

Then Wren noticed something else. One of the stone beads in Mira’s hair, just above her ear, had caught the light, and it was not pale any longer. It had gone the same deep, glad colour as the ribbon on Wren’s own wrist. The bead beside it was a colour she had no name for at all: a cool, bright colour, like the smell of cut grass.

“Mira,” said Dask. “Away from it.”

“It isn’t hurting me.”

“It will. Fevers start pleasant. Away.” He turned his pale face towards Wren, and she understood with a jolt that he knew exactly where she was, and exactly how tall. “Cover it, Roof-girl, or I will cover it for you, and I would rather not touch the thing.”

Wren looked at Old Ash. He lay among the stones with his leg out at an angle she did not like, his face grey with pain. But he caught her eye, and nodded once.

“Do as they ask, child,” he said. “We’re guests.”

“We’re prisoners.”

“Guests who happen to be tied up. It happens to the best of us. Hm. Mostly to the best of us.”

So Wren wrapped the lamp in her coat again; and the dark came down like a lid; and the last thing she saw before it closed was Mira’s face, still turned towards where the warmth had been, smiling.

They made a litter for Ash out of two staves and a net. Four of the Delvers — that was what they called themselves, Mira said: Delvers, of Deepholm — lifted him onto it as gently as a basket of eggs, and when he gasped they stopped and waited without being asked. Cinder rode on his chest with her chin on his beard.

Dask ruled that the warm thing should stay with the warm girl. “She’s sick with it already,” he said. “No sense spreading it.” So Wren walked at the back of the line with the lamp bundled against her and a Delver holding the far end of her cord at the full stretch of his arm, as though she were a dog with something catching.

Then they set off into the second kind of dark, and kept going.

I should like to tell you that Wren was brave about that march. She was brave about most things. But she had never in her life been led anywhere she could not see, and it turned out she did not like it at all. The floor rose and fell without warning. Once she walked straight into a point of rock hanging from the roof, and sat down hard.

“Low rock,” said Mira’s voice, from up the line.

“Thanks for the warning,” said Wren, holding her forehead.

“I gave it. You were listening to your own feet.”

But it was not Wren whom Mira was walking beside. Wren could tell that, from the voices. It was Tobin.

He had not said a word since the net. But Wren could hear his breathing a few places ahead, quick and high and shallow. She knew that breathing. She had heard it in the dry stream-bed, just before the Hollows came, when he had frozen and Ash had stepped in front of him; and she had said things afterwards she was still not sorry for, quite. She could not think what to say now. So she said nothing, and listened to him breathe.

Then she heard Mira say, quietly, “May I?”

“M-may you what?”

“Put my hand on your sleeve. Only your sleeve. You’re breathing like a bird in a box.”

There was a silence. Then Tobin said, in a very small voice, “Yes. Please. Thank you. I’m — I’m not very good in the dark. I’m not — actually, I’m terrible in it. I always have been. I’m sorry.”

“Why are you sorry? You’ve never been here before. The dark’s only where everything is, before you’ve been introduced to it.” Mira’s voice was perfectly matter-of-fact. “Shall I introduce you? Listen. There’s water on your left, running fast, quite small — you could step over it. Hear it?”

“Y-yes.”

“The roof’s coming down in front. Not yet. Soon. Your voice will sound close when it does — say something.”

“Something,” said Tobin. Then, a few steps on, “Something. Oh. It — it went flat.”

“It did. Duck.”

He ducked. Wren, behind, did not, and caught her ear on the rock, and said a word that Mrs Fenn would not have liked.

They went on like that for a long time. Mira told him the dark the way you might tell somebody a road: here a wide place, where his footsteps went out and didn’t come back; here a stretch of stone worn smooth as soap by bare feet over hundreds of years. And Tobin — Wren could hear it happening — Tobin began to listen. His breathing slowed. After a while he began to ask questions. Then he began to count.

“Four hundred and twelve,” he said at last, sounding almost like himself. “Paces, since the slope. I’m trying to keep a map. In my head. If I know the distance and the turnings—“

“Four hundred and fourteen,” said Mira. “You don’t count your stumbles. Your stumbles are steps too, you know. They still get you somewhere.”

Tobin laughed. It was a small, shaky laugh, but it was a real one; and Wren, trudging behind with a lump on her forehead, felt something she did not much like. It was as if she had been carrying something heavy for a long way and had just watched somebody else pick up the other end of it without being asked — and she did not know whether she was glad or cross.

“Is your friend always so loud?” Mira called back. “He thinks very loudly.”

“He’s not my friend,” said Wren. “He’s just — Tobin.”

“Ah,” said Mira. “One of those.”

It was after what felt like hours that the air changed.

Wren felt it first on her face: a breath of moving air, cool and damp and enormous. Then her footsteps changed. All the march they had slapped back at her off close walls. Now they went away from her, out and out, and came back so faint and so late that they seemed to belong to somebody else.

The line stopped. Somebody up ahead hummed one long, low note — and from far off in front and below, as if the whole dark had been waiting for it, another note answered.

Then another. Then a dozen. Then more than Wren could count, high and low and between, until the black air in front of her was humming like the inside of a bell: a sound so big and so deep that she felt it in her teeth and in the soles of her feet. Under it, water was falling — not one stream but hundreds, splashing and trickling and tumbling, each one at its own pitch, so that they made a kind of tune together that never quite repeated. And under that, there were voices. A great many voices, talking and calling and laughing, children shrieking somewhere, a hammer ringing on stone, the creak of rope; and through all of it, everywhere, like rain on a roof, the soft dry sound of a thousand tongues going click.

Mira’s voice came out of the dark, close beside Wren’s ear. She must have dropped back down the line without a sound.

“There,” she said, and Wren could hear that she was smiling. “That’s Deepholm. Hush now, Roof-girl, and listen. You’ll never hear it for the first time again.”

And Wren, who had never in her life stood still to listen to anything that was not a threat, stood still in the dark with her hands tied and the lamp warm against her heart, and listened.

One small, with fur. One breathes like a bellows. One is hurt — I hear the leg. And one—“ a pause, and a sniff — “one is warm.” “Warm?” said a woman’s voice, sharp. “Warm like a fever. Can you not feel it? From here.” A murmur went round the ring. Wren caught the words sick, and the Roof. “We’re not sick,” she said loudly. “We fell. Down a hole. Out of the sky, I suppose, as far as you lot are concerned. And we’re not stopping, so you can just show us the way out and—“ “It speaks,” said the man’s voice, with interest. “And rudely.” “I’ll show you rude—“ Then a great many things happened very fast. A net dropped over Wren’s head and shoulders, soft and heavy and smelling of mushrooms. Cinder snarled and sneezed, and a shower of sparks went up, and for half a heartbeat they lit — a shoulder, pale as candle-wax, a white braid, an open hand — and then dark again. Somebody yelped. Tobin cried out. Ash said, “Peace! Peace, we mean no harm—“ and then grunted with pain. Hands found Wren’s wrists in the dark — quick, cool, sure hands that seemed to know exactly where her wrists were before they touched them — and then let go at once, as if she had burned them. “Ai! Hot as a hearth-stone. Don’t touch her. Net her and leave her be.” Wren kicked at nothing, and missed, and kicked again, and was sat on, firmly, by someone who smelled of moss. “Enough, child,” came Ash’s voice. “There are twenty of them, and they can see us, and we cannot see them.” “They can’t see anything! It’s pitch black!” “Hm,” said Old Ash. “Are you quite sure?” They were not, as it turned out, killed. They were not even hurt, apart from Wren’s pride, which had been sat on. Somebody worked the knife out of her fingers, and her hands were tied in front of her with a soft cord by someone who took great care not to touch her skin. Then the voices went off to argue in low, singing murmurs, and somebody new sat down beside her on the stones. “I’m set to guard you,” said a voice. “Please don’t run. You’re very bad at running. I’ve been listening.” It was a girl’s voice, about Wren’s age, clear and precise, every word set down like a cup on a saucer — with something under the neatness that sounded very like a person trying not to laugh. “I’m the best runner in Soot Lane,” said Wren. “Soot Lane must be full of light, then. You run like someone who’s used to knowing where the ground is before her feet get there.” A pause. “Down here the ground doesn’t tell you. You have to ask it.” Click. Wren jumped. It had come from right in front of her nose. “Sorry,” said the girl. “I was looking at you.” “Looking at me?” “Hearing you. It’s nearly the same word, in the old speech.” Click. Click. The sound moved round her, curious as a cat. “You’re smaller than your voice. Your voice is twice your size.” There was a small rustle, as if the girl had drawn her knees up. “I’m Mira. Mira of the Low Hum, granddaughter of Hessa. Clear echo to you.” She waited. Then she added, helpfully, “That’s when you say And a true return. It’s rude not to.” Wren said nothing at all, which was ruder still. “Oh, well,” said Mira. “Never mind. What’s your name? I can’t keep calling you the warm one inside my head. It makes you sound like soup.” In spite of everything — the dark, the cord, Ash’s breath hissing somewhere off to the right — Wren felt the corner of her mouth twitch. “Wren,” she said. “Wren Ashby.” “Wren.” The girl tried it the way you might try a sweet. “A small quick sound. It suits you. What does it mean?” “It’s a bird.” “What’s a bird?” “It’s — a little brown thing. It flies.” “What’s brown?” “It’s a colour.” “Ah,” said Mira wisely. “One of those. And this warm thing in your coat. Is that a bird too?” Wren’s arms tightened round her middle before she could stop them. “It’s a lamp.” “What’s a lamp?” “It makes light.” There was a short silence, and then Mira laughed. It was not an unkind laugh. It was quick and surprised and delighted, the laugh of someone who has been told that the person in front of her keeps a dragon in her pocket. “Light,” she said. “You carry light about in your coat. Like in the nursery stories. Like the Burning that comes up the Black Stair for children who won’t go to sleep.” “It’s not a story. It’s real. It lets you see.” “I can see.” “Not properly—“ Wren stopped, because she had heard what she was saying, and it sounded stupid even to her. “I mean — it lets you see things that are far away. Without touching them. Without clicking at them. You just look, and there they are, all at once, every one of them.” “How horrible,” said Mira, interested. “All at once? How do you know which one to listen to first?” Wren did not know. She sat in the dark with her mouth open, which at least nobody could see. “What does it feel like?” said Mira, more quietly. “Your light. When it’s on you.” Wren thought of the garret in Soot Lane, and Mrs Fenn on her step saying her children’s names. “Like when somebody says your name,” she said slowly, “and they’re glad it’s you.” There was a long pause. The clicks had stopped. “Show me,” said Mira. “You can’t see it.” “Show me anyway.” Wren looked — out of habit — towards where Ash had been. She could not see him, of course; and he did not say anything. So she worked her tied hands up to the front of her coat, and fumbled it open, and drew the lamp out into the dark. Light poured out of it like water out of a broken jar. After that blackness Wren had to screw her eyes shut, and when she opened them she saw — all at once, every one of them — the people who had caught her. There were about twenty, standing in a ring on the fallen stones, and they were pale: not grey, like the greyed, but pale like the inside of a shell, like a candle that has never been lit. Their hair was white, even on the young ones, and worn in many small braids. They carried long staves and coils of net, and their feet were bare. Their eyes were open, large and pale as pearls; and not one of those eyes turned towards the lamp. Not one. Instead every face in the ring had flinched sideways, the way your face flinches from an oven door, and every hand had come up, palm out, as though to keep off a heat. “Cover it,” said the man with the lathe-turned voice — Dask, Wren learned afterwards he was called; tall and bony, with a white beard braided into two points. “Cover it, girl. It’s spreading.” But the girl beside Wren had not flinched. She was thin and sharp-elbowed and a little taller than Wren, with a pointed face and a great many braids, and in every braid were threaded small round beads of polished stone that ticked softly against one another when she moved. She had put out both her hands towards the lamp — not palm out, to keep it off, but palm up, the way you hold your hands out to be given something. “It’s like standing next to someone who’s laughing.” “Oh,” said Mira, very softly. “Oh. It’s like standing next to someone who’s laughing.” Her eyes, the pale grey of a morning mist, rested a little to one side of the lamp, quite calm, not searching for anything. But her face was turned straight into the warmth, and she looked so astonished and so pleased that Wren, who did not usually notice faces unless they meant trouble, noticed hers and did not forget it. Then Wren noticed something else. One of the stone beads in Mira’s hair, just above her ear, had caught the light, and it was not pale any longer. It had gone the same deep, glad colour as the ribbon on Wren’s own wrist. The bead beside it was a colour she had no name for at all: a cool, bright colour, like the smell of cut grass. “Mira,” said Dask. “Away from it.” “It isn’t hurting me.” “It will. Fevers start pleasant. Away.” He turned his pale face towards Wren, and she understood with a jolt that he knew exactly where she was, and exactly how tall. “Cover it, Roof-girl, or I will cover it for you, and I would rather not touch the thing.” Wren looked at Old Ash. He lay among the stones with his leg out at an angle she did not like, his face grey with pain. But he caught her eye, and nodded once. “Do as they ask, child,” he said. “We’re guests.” “We’re prisoners.” “Guests who happen to be tied up. It happens to the best of us. Hm. Mostly to the best of us.” So Wren wrapped the lamp in her coat again; and the dark came down like a lid; and the last thing she saw before it closed was Mira’s face, still turned towards where the warmth had been, smiling. They made a litter for Ash out of two staves and a net. Four of the Delvers — that was what they called themselves, Mira said: Delvers, of Deepholm — lifted him onto it as gently as a basket of eggs, and when he gasped they stopped and waited without being asked. Cinder rode on his chest with her chin on his beard. Dask ruled that the warm thing should stay with the warm girl. “She’s sick with it already,” he said. “No sense spreading it.” So Wren walked at the back of the line with the lamp bundled against her and a Delver holding the far end of her cord at the full stretch of his arm, as though she were a dog with something catching. Then they set off into the second kind of dark, and kept going. I should like to tell you that Wren was brave about that march. She was brave about most things. But she had never in her life been led anywhere she could not see, and it turned out she did not like it at all. The floor rose and fell without warning. Once she walked straight into a point of rock hanging from the roof, and sat down hard. “Low rock,” said Mira’s voice, from up the line. “Thanks for the warning,” said Wren, holding her forehead. “I gave it. You were listening to your own feet.” But it was not Wren whom Mira was walking beside. Wren could tell that, from the voices. It was Tobin. He had not said a word since the net. But Wren could hear his breathing a few places ahead, quick and high and shallow. She knew that breathing. She had heard it in the dry stream-bed, just before the Hollows came, when he had frozen and Ash had stepped in front of him; and she had said things afterwards she was still not sorry for, quite. She could not think what to say now. So she said nothing, and listened to him breathe. Then she heard Mira say, quietly, “May I?” “M-may you what?” “Put my hand on your sleeve. Only your sleeve. You’re breathing like a bird in a box.” There was a silence. Then Tobin said, in a very small voice, “Yes. Please. Thank you. I’m — I’m not very good in the dark. I’m not — actually, I’m terrible in it. I always have been. I’m sorry.” “Why are you sorry? You’ve never been here before. The dark’s only where everything is, before you’ve been introduced to it.” Mira’s voice was perfectly matter-of-fact. “Shall I introduce you? Listen. There’s water on your left, running fast, quite small — you could step over it. Hear it?” “Y-yes.” “The roof’s coming down in front. Not yet. Soon. Your voice will sound close when it does — say something.” “Something,” said Tobin. Then, a few steps on, “Something. Oh. It — it went flat.” “It did. Duck.” He ducked. Wren, behind, did not, and caught her ear on the rock, and said a word that Mrs Fenn would not have liked. They went on like that for a long time. Mira told him the dark the way you might tell somebody a road: here a wide place, where his footsteps went out and didn’t come back; here a stretch of stone worn smooth as soap by bare feet over hundreds of years. And Tobin — Wren could hear it happening — Tobin began to listen. His breathing slowed. After a while he began to ask questions. Then he began to count. “Four hundred and twelve,” he said at last, sounding almost like himself. “Paces, since the slope. I’m trying to keep a map. In my head. If I know the distance and the turnings—“ “Four hundred and fourteen,” said Mira. “You don’t count your stumbles. Your stumbles are steps too, you know. They still get you somewhere.” Tobin laughed. It was a small, shaky laugh, but it was a real one; and Wren, trudging behind with a lump on her forehead, felt something she did not much like. It was as if she had been carrying something heavy for a long way and had just watched somebody else pick up the other end of it without being asked — and she did not know whether she was glad or cross. “Is your friend always so loud?” Mira called back. “He thinks very loudly.” “He’s not my friend,” said Wren. “He’s just — Tobin.” “Ah,” said Mira. “One of those.” It was after what felt like hours that the air changed. Wren felt it first on her face: a breath of moving air, cool and damp and enormous. Then her footsteps changed. All the march they had slapped back at her off close walls. Now they went away from her, out and out, and came back so faint and so late that they seemed to belong to somebody else. The line stopped. Somebody up ahead hummed one long, low note — and from far off in front and below, as if the whole dark had been waiting for it, another note answered. Then another. Then a dozen. Then more than Wren could count, high and low and between, until the black air in front of her was humming like the inside of a bell: a sound so big and so deep that she felt it in her teeth and in the soles of her feet. Under it, water was falling — not one stream but hundreds, splashing and trickling and tumbling, each one at its own pitch, so that they made a kind of tune together that never quite repeated. And under that, there were voices. A great many voices, talking and calling and laughing, children shrieking somewhere, a hammer ringing on stone, the creak of rope; and through all of it, everywhere, like rain on a roof, the soft dry sound of a thousand tongues going click. Mira’s voice came out of the dark, close beside Wren’s ear. She must have dropped back down the line without a sound. “There,” she said, and Wren could hear that she was smiling. “That’s Deepholm. Hush now, Roof-girl, and listen. You’ll never hear it for the first time again.” And Wren, who had never in her life stood still to listen to anything that was not a threat, stood still in the dark with her hands tied and the lamp warm against her heart, and listened.

fields.title: The City of Echoes
fields.body_html:
The first thing Wren learned about Deepholm was that it had been built by people who did not care in the least what anything looked like, and cared enormously how it sounded.

She learned it on the bridge.

There was no warning. One moment there was stone under her feet; the next there was something that swayed, and creaked, and gave a little when she trod on it, and from somewhere a very long way below came the hiss of running water. Wren stopped dead.

“Rope bridge,” said Mira, behind her. “Keep walking. Stopping is the worst thing you can do on a bridge. It makes the bridge think you’re unhappy.”

“I am unhappy.”

“Yes, but the bridge doesn’t need to know.”

Wren walked, with her teeth clenched, and every step the bridge sang under her — a low, twanging note that went up as she reached the middle and down again towards the far side, so that she could tell, without seeing anything, exactly how far she had come. When she was nearly across she understood that this was on purpose. Somebody had strung the bridge so that it would tell you where you were.

After the bridge there was a ramp, and after the ramp a long ledge with a wall on one side and on the other nothing at all but the great humming dark, and all along it were doorways — Wren could hear them as they passed, each one breathing out a different sound: a mutter of voices, a child’s laugh, a pot bubbling, somebody snoring like a saw. Before some of the doors hung curtains of thin stone slips threaded on cords, and when anyone brushed past they rang softly, like teacups shaken in a basket.

“Chime-doors,” said Mira. “So you know who’s coming in. Everyone in Deepholm has a door-note. You hum it at the curtain, and then the people inside know it’s you, and not a stranger, and not a thief.”

“You have thieves?” said Wren, cheering up slightly.

“Not really,” said Mira. “But it’s polite to hum anyway.”

The Delvers brought them at last to a round room cut into the cliff of the ledge, set down Ash’s litter on something soft, and went away — all but Mira, who unpicked the cord from Wren’s wrists with quick light fingers.

“There,” she said. “Don’t run. There are three bridges between you and anywhere at all, and you can’t hear a single one of them properly. You’d fall off and then Dask would say I’d guarded you badly, and he’d be right.”

Wren rubbed her wrists. Then she pulled the lamp out of her coat.

She had been wanting to do it for so long that her hands shook a little. The light filled the round room in one warm breath, and there were Tobin, blinking and filthy and pushing his spectacles up his nose with both hands as if to make sure they were real; and Old Ash on a heap of woven mats, grey in the face, with Cinder curled on his good knee and her tail-spark beginning to glow again; and Mira, sitting cross-legged in the doorway with her face turned up into the warmth like a cat on a sunny step.

Then Wren went to the door and held the lamp out, as high as she could reach, and looked at Deepholm.

I wish I could show it to you as she saw it. But I cannot, because she saw so little of it, and that was the most astonishing thing of all.

The lamp’s light went out from the doorway in a gold ring, perhaps thirty paces each way, and then it simply stopped, the way a voice stops in a large room. Above that ring there was no roof that she could see. Beyond it there was no far wall. There was only darkness — not empty darkness, but darkness so full of sound that it seemed to move, the way a crowd moves even when you cannot see the faces in it.

And within the ring, everything was carved.

Every surface. The ledge they stood on was cut into long, shallow ridges like ripples in sand, which Mira said were roads: three ridges meant a bridge ahead, two meant steps, and a single smooth groove down the middle meant this way home. The wall above the doorways was carved in great sweeping spirals, so deep you could have put your arm in them to the elbow, and when the hum of the city passed across them they softened it, and gentled it, and sent it on. A little channel of water ran along the foot of the wall in a stone gutter, and every few paces the gutter had been shaped into a small lip, or a step, or a cup, so that the water fell and splashed and tinkled at a dozen different pitches as it went: a whole tune, played by one thin stream, over and over, all day long. Across the gap in front of them, just at the edge of the light, stood a column of pale stone, fluted like the pipes of an organ and taller than six men; and it hummed. Wren could feel it in the lamp’s brass.

“Singing-stone,” said Mira. “One of the Hour-Stones. The water strikes it at every turn. That’s the low hum it’s making now, so it’s nearly the low turn, which means supper.” She tilted her head. “Why are you so quiet? Your breathing’s gone all round and soft.”

“It’s—“ Wren hunted for the word and could not find one. “It’s beautiful.”

“Is it?” Mira sounded pleased, and a little puzzled. “How can you tell? You haven’t even touched it.”

There was something else, too, that Wren did not mention, because she did not know how. The walls were not the dull grey of the Greywaste. Close to the lamp, in the carved spirals, there were veins running through the stone — fine threads and ribbons of colour that came out as the light touched them and faded as it moved away. One was the colour of her ribbon. One was the cut-grass colour of Mira’s bead. One was a colour like nothing she had words for, deep and still, like the hush in a room after somebody has sung. Nobody in Deepholm had ever seen them. They had been there in the dark all along, waiting, the way the red had been in her ribbon.

A Delver came along the ledge carrying a basket on her head. As she drew near the doorway she slowed, and flinched, and put up one hand towards the warmth; then she went past on the far edge of the ledge, as close to the drop as she could go, clicking anxiously.

“She thinks I’m catching,” said Wren.

“Everyone does,” said Mira comfortably. “Don’t mind it. Most people here have never been warmer than a bowl of soup.”

Mother Hessa came at the low turn, while the great column was still humming.

They heard her before anything else: a door-note at the chime-curtain, round and low and pleasant, like a pigeon on a roof — and then she simply kept humming, all the way in, and all the time afterwards, as though she had forgotten how to stop. She was a short, broad, quick old woman with a face as creased as a walnut and white braids wound round and round her head like a loaf, and she carried a basket that clinked, and she smelled strongly of pepper.

“Gran,” said Mira. “These are the Roof-folk.”

“So I hear. So does the whole of the Low Hum.” Mother Hessa set down her basket, turned her face towards the lamp, flinched, frowned, and turned it firmly away again. “Which is the leg?”

“Mine,” said Old Ash, from the mats. “Good evening, madam. Hm. It is very kind of you to—“

“Hush. I’m listening.” She knelt beside him and laid her hands flat on his leg, below the knee, and was silent. It was a strange sort of silence — very busy, Wren thought, the way a person is silent when they are reading. Her fingers moved an inch, and pressed, and moved again. Ash hissed through his teeth.

“An old hurt,” said Hessa at last, “and a new hurt on top of it, and a long fall on top of that, and a stubborn old man on top of the whole heap, walking on it when he should have been lying down.” She sniffed. “You’re lucky it’s not broken. It’s thinking about it.”

“I’ll ask it to think again,” said Ash.

“You’ll lie still for ten days, is what you’ll do, or I’ll sit on you.” She began pulling things out of her basket: a pot of grey moss paste that made Cinder sneeze sparks all over the mats; strips of soft woven cloth; two long splints of a pale, light, springy stuff that Tobin said afterwards must be some kind of cave-reed. “And if you so much as think about standing up, I’ll hear you thinking it.”

Wren felt a small, mean flicker of satisfaction. Nobody had ever told Old Ash what to do before. He was taking it like a lamb.

Then Mother Hessa stood up, dusted off her knees, turned round, and laid a cold wet cloth across Wren’s forehead.

“What’s that for?”

“Warm-sickness,” said Hessa. “You’re burning up, child. I could feel it from the door. Keep that on and drink this.” She pushed a cup into Wren’s hands. It was full of something pale and thin that smelled of mint and mushrooms.

“I’m not sick! It’s the lamp! It’s—“

“Yes, yes,” said Hessa kindly, in the voice of somebody who has heard a great many fevered people say a great many strange things. “Drink up.”

Behind her, Ash made a noise into his beard that might have been a cough. It was not a cough.

Wren drank, because it was easier than arguing, and it was not bad — a good deal better than Ash’s tea, which was not saying much. And while she drank, Mother Hessa went on humming as she packed up her basket: an old, slow, swinging tune, round and round, like somebody rocking a cradle.

Wren lowered the cup.

She knew that tune. She did not know how she knew it — she had never been within a hundred miles of this place — but she did. It went down where hers went down and turned where hers turned, and for a moment her heart did something odd and painful, like a foot missing a step on a dark stair.

“That song,” she said. “What is it?”

“Mm?” said Hessa. “Oh — an old hush-song. Every grandmother in the Deeps knows it. Mira, take these Roof-folk to the Long Table, or they’ll eat my mats.” And she was gone through the chimes, still humming, before Wren could ask anything else; and the tune went away along the ledge, getting smaller, until the water in the gutter covered it.

The Long Table was the great eating-hall of the Low Hum, and Wren never saw it at all.

“You’ll have to cover the warm thing,” Mira said. “There’ll be hundreds of people. They’ll all think they’ve caught something and nobody will eat, and then there’ll be leftovers, and nobody in Deepholm knows what to do with leftovers.”

So Wren wrapped the lamp away again, and Mira took Tobin’s sleeve and Wren took the back of Tobin’s coat, and they went out into the dark like a very small and very unhappy procession.

Wren was unhappy all the way there — bumping, stumbling, catching her shins on everything in Deepholm that could be caught on — but Tobin, in front of her, was not. Tobin was talking.

“The bridge,” he was saying. “The way the note changes as you cross — it must be the tension in the ropes, they’ve tuned the lengths so the pitch tells you your position, that’s — that’s actually brilliant. And the spirals on the walls, those are baffles, they’re absorbing the echo so the city isn’t deafening, and the water channels — Mira, does the water drive the Hour-Stones directly, or is there some kind of escapement, a—“

“I don’t know what an escapement is,” said Mira. “The water fills a stone cup. When the cup’s full it tips, and strikes the stone. Then it empties and starts again.”

“That’s an escapement!”

“Then that’s what it is. You don’t need to shout. I’m holding your sleeve. Low rock.”

He ducked without slowing down. “And the — what were they — the ridges on the floor—“

“Touch-roads. Your feet are on one now. Can you feel it? Two ridges. Steps coming.”

“I can feel it. I can actually feel it. Mira, this is the most—“ He stopped so suddenly that Wren walked into the back of him. “Oh,” he said, in a different voice. “Oh. I’ve forgotten to be frightened.”

“Have you?” said Mira. “I wondered when you would.”

Wren said nothing. But she held on to the back of his coat a little less tightly after that, and more as if she were walking with him than being towed.

They heard the Long Table from a long way off: a hall full of voices and the scrape of bowls, with a waterfall at one end that filled the whole place with a deep, soft roar, like a giant breathing in his sleep. There were children chasing each other under the benches, clicking and shrieking. And as Wren came in, groping for the edge of the bench, she knocked over somebody’s cup, trod on somebody’s foot, and sat down, very hard, in somebody else’s lap.

A shout of laughter went down the table.

“Why do the Roof-folk walk like that?” said a young voice in delight, from the other side of the board. “Like they’re carrying soup on their heads?”

“Tavi,” said a woman’s voice reprovingly.

“But they do! Listen to them! Bump, bump, ow! Didn’t anyone ever teach them to click?”

“They come from a place that’s all light, Tavi,” said Mira, with great dignity, helping Wren off a stranger’s knee. “They’ve never needed to. It’s like a fish that’s never learned to walk. You don’t laugh at a fish.”

“I would,” said Tavi. “If a fish walked into me.”

He came round the table, quick and bold as a sparrow, and before Wren could stop him he had put both small hands on her face — her forehead, her nose, her sharp chin — as lightly as moths. Then he did the same to Tobin, and jumped back with a squeak.

“This one’s got glass on his face!”

“They’re called spectacles,” said Tobin, a little stiffly.

“What do they do?”

“They help me to — well — see.”

“Does that help?” said Tavi doubtfully, and was hauled away by his collar by a grown-up who said something low about your father and the Speaker’s son, of all people.

Then the bowls came.

That was the part Wren remembered afterwards, longer than the bridges or the carvings or even the hush-song. They came down the table from hand to hand, out of the dark: a warm bowl of something thick and savoury with mushrooms in it, and a round of flat, chewy, faintly sweet bread, and a cup of water so cold it tasted of stone. Somebody put a bowl into her hands. Somebody else put bread on top of it. Nobody asked for anything. Nobody counted. Nobody said that’s yours or that’s mine, or who’s paying for the strangers? The bowls simply came, and people ate, and when somebody’s bowl was empty somebody else’s hands filled it.

Wren found that she had already slipped half her bread into her pocket — quickly, without thinking, the way she had done at every meal in her life, in case there was no next one. She sat with her hand over it in the dark and felt her face go hot.

“What do I owe?” she said, under her breath, to the woman on her left. “For the food. What’s the — what does it cost?”

The woman stopped eating. “Owe?” she said. She sounded genuinely puzzled, as though Wren had asked her what colour Tuesday was.

“She means,” said Mira, from Wren’s other side, “who does the bread belong to.” And then, to Wren, gently: “It doesn’t belong to anybody. The deep grows the mushrooms. The deep gives the water. All we do is carry it from one pair of hands to the next. What the deep gives, the deep shares. That’s all. It’s the first thing anybody learns here — before walking, nearly.”

Wren sat very still.

Then, slowly, she took the bread out of her pocket. There was a child next to her on the bench — she could hear him, small and snuffling and bored, kicking his heels — and she found his hand in the dark and put the bread into it. He took it without a word, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. In Deepholm, I suppose, it was.

She did not say anything about it, and neither did Mira. But a little later, when Wren put her hand to her coat, she could feel through all the folds that the lamp had grown warmer.

Further down the table, a small child was wailing that it was not tired, and would not go to sleep, and would not, and would not.

“Hush now,” said its mother, in a cheerful sing-song, “or the Burning will come up the Black Stair and eat your ears. Hot, hot, hot! Nibble, nibble!” And the child shrieked with laughter, and so did the children round it, and the mother laughed too.

“They think light is a bogeyman,” Tobin whispered, close to Wren’s ear. He sounded shaken. “Like a goblin, or the — the sort of thing you make up to frighten babies.”

Wren put her hand flat against the warm place over her heart, and said nothing.

Then a voice spoke from the head of the table, and the whole hall went still.

It was not a loud voice. It did not need to be. It was so deep and so slow that it seemed to come up through the stone bench into her bones, and every other sound — the bowls, the children, even the waterfall, somehow — drew back from it a little, the way a crowd draws back for somebody it is used to obeying.

“I hear,” said the voice, “that the Roof-folk who fell through the Waste are eating at the Long Table. And I hear that one of them carries a warm thing that makes our people sick.”

Nobody answered. Down the table, someone set a bowl down very carefully, so that it would make no sound at all.

“At the high turn,” said the voice, “they will come before the Elders. They will bring the warm thing with them. And we will hear what they are.”

There was a creak of a bench, and slow footsteps going away, and the clatter of the hall came back, but quieter than before.

Mira’s hand found Wren’s sleeve under the table. Her voice was the lowest Wren had heard it yet.

“That was Speaker Gorrim,” she said. “Tavi’s father. He’s head of the Elders, and he’s not unkind, and he’s not a fool. But he doesn’t believe in stories, Wren. Not one. Whatever you do tomorrow—“ her fingers tightened — “don’t tell him it’s light.”
fields.body_text: The first thing Wren learned about Deepholm was that it had been built by people who did not care in the least what anything looked like, and cared enormously how it sounded. She learned it on the bridge. There was no warning. One moment there was stone under her feet; the next there was something that swayed, and creaked, and gave a little when she trod on it, and from somewhere a very long way below came the hiss of running water. Wren stopped dead. “Rope bridge,” said Mira, behind her. “Keep walking. Stopping is the worst thing you can do on a bridge. It makes the bridge think you’re unhappy.” “I am unhappy.” “Yes, but the bridge doesn’t need to know.” Wren walked, with her teeth clenched, and every step the bridge sang under her — a low, twanging note that went up as she reached the middle and down again towards the far side, so that she could tell, without seeing anything, exactly how far she had come. When she was nearly across she understood that this was on purpose. Somebody had strung the bridge so that it would tell you where you were. After the bridge there was a ramp, and after the ramp a long ledge with a wall on one side and on the other nothing at all but the great humming dark, and all along it were doorways — Wren could hear them as they passed, each one breathing out a different sound: a mutter of voices, a child’s laugh, a pot bubbling, somebody snoring like a saw. Before some of the doors hung curtains of thin stone slips threaded on cords, and when anyone brushed past they rang softly, like teacups shaken in a basket. “Chime-doors,” said Mira. “So you know who’s coming in. Everyone in Deepholm has a door-note. You hum it at the curtain, and then the people inside know it’s you, and not a stranger, and not a thief.” “You have thieves?” said Wren, cheering up slightly. “Not really,” said Mira. “But it’s polite to hum anyway.” The Delvers brought them at last to a round room cut into the cliff of the ledge, set down Ash’s litter on something soft, and went away — all but Mira, who unpicked the cord from Wren’s wrists with quick light fingers. “There,” she said. “Don’t run. There are three bridges between you and anywhere at all, and you can’t hear a single one of them properly. You’d fall off and then Dask would say I’d guarded you badly, and he’d be right.” Wren rubbed her wrists. Then she pulled the lamp out of her coat. She had been wanting to do it for so long that her hands shook a little. The light filled the round room in one warm breath, and there were Tobin, blinking and filthy and pushing his spectacles up his nose with both hands as if to make sure they were real; and Old Ash on a heap of woven mats, grey in the face, with Cinder curled on his good knee and her tail-spark beginning to glow again; and Mira, sitting cross-legged in the doorway with her face turned up into the warmth like a cat on a sunny step. Then Wren went to the door and held the lamp out, as high as she could reach, and looked at Deepholm. I wish I could show it to you as she saw it. But I cannot, because she saw so little of it, and that was the most astonishing thing of all. The lamp’s light went out from the doorway in a gold ring, perhaps thirty paces each way, and then it simply stopped, the way a voice stops in a large room. Above that ring there was no roof that she could see. Beyond it there was no far wall. There was only darkness — not empty darkness, but darkness so full of sound that it seemed to move, the way a crowd moves even when you cannot see the faces in it. And within the ring, everything was carved. Every surface. The ledge they stood on was cut into long, shallow ridges like ripples in sand, which Mira said were roads: three ridges meant a bridge ahead, two meant steps, and a single smooth groove down the middle meant this way home. The wall above the doorways was carved in great sweeping spirals, so deep you could have put your arm in them to the elbow, and when the hum of the city passed across them they softened it, and gentled it, and sent it on. A little channel of water ran along the foot of the wall in a stone gutter, and every few paces the gutter had been shaped into a small lip, or a step, or a cup, so that the water fell and splashed and tinkled at a dozen different pitches as it went: a whole tune, played by one thin stream, over and over, all day long. Across the gap in front of them, just at the edge of the light, stood a column of pale stone, fluted like the pipes of an organ and taller than six men; and it hummed. Wren could feel it in the lamp’s brass. Above that ring there was no roof that she could see. “Singing-stone,” said Mira. “One of the Hour-Stones. The water strikes it at every turn. That’s the low hum it’s making now, so it’s nearly the low turn, which means supper.” She tilted her head. “Why are you so quiet? Your breathing’s gone all round and soft.” “It’s—“ Wren hunted for the word and could not find one. “It’s beautiful.” “Is it?” Mira sounded pleased, and a little puzzled. “How can you tell? You haven’t even touched it.” There was something else, too, that Wren did not mention, because she did not know how. The walls were not the dull grey of the Greywaste. Close to the lamp, in the carved spirals, there were veins running through the stone — fine threads and ribbons of colour that came out as the light touched them and faded as it moved away. One was the colour of her ribbon. One was the cut-grass colour of Mira’s bead. One was a colour like nothing she had words for, deep and still, like the hush in a room after somebody has sung. Nobody in Deepholm had ever seen them. They had been there in the dark all along, waiting, the way the red had been in her ribbon. A Delver came along the ledge carrying a basket on her head. As she drew near the doorway she slowed, and flinched, and put up one hand towards the warmth; then she went past on the far edge of the ledge, as close to the drop as she could go, clicking anxiously. “She thinks I’m catching,” said Wren. “Everyone does,” said Mira comfortably. “Don’t mind it. Most people here have never been warmer than a bowl of soup.” Mother Hessa came at the low turn, while the great column was still humming. They heard her before anything else: a door-note at the chime-curtain, round and low and pleasant, like a pigeon on a roof — and then she simply kept humming, all the way in, and all the time afterwards, as though she had forgotten how to stop. She was a short, broad, quick old woman with a face as creased as a walnut and white braids wound round and round her head like a loaf, and she carried a basket that clinked, and she smelled strongly of pepper. “Gran,” said Mira. “These are the Roof-folk.” “So I hear. So does the whole of the Low Hum.” Mother Hessa set down her basket, turned her face towards the lamp, flinched, frowned, and turned it firmly away again. “Which is the leg?” “Mine,” said Old Ash, from the mats. “Good evening, madam. Hm. It is very kind of you to—“ “Hush. I’m listening.” She knelt beside him and laid her hands flat on his leg, below the knee, and was silent. It was a strange sort of silence — very busy, Wren thought, the way a person is silent when they are reading. Her fingers moved an inch, and pressed, and moved again. Ash hissed through his teeth. “An old hurt,” said Hessa at last, “and a new hurt on top of it, and a long fall on top of that, and a stubborn old man on top of the whole heap, walking on it when he should have been lying down.” She sniffed. “You’re lucky it’s not broken. It’s thinking about it.” “I’ll ask it to think again,” said Ash. “You’ll lie still for ten days, is what you’ll do, or I’ll sit on you.” She began pulling things out of her basket: a pot of grey moss paste that made Cinder sneeze sparks all over the mats; strips of soft woven cloth; two long splints of a pale, light, springy stuff that Tobin said afterwards must be some kind of cave-reed. “And if you so much as think about standing up, I’ll hear you thinking it.” Wren felt a small, mean flicker of satisfaction. Nobody had ever told Old Ash what to do before. He was taking it like a lamb. Then Mother Hessa stood up, dusted off her knees, turned round, and laid a cold wet cloth across Wren’s forehead. “What’s that for?” “Warm-sickness,” said Hessa. “You’re burning up, child. I could feel it from the door. Keep that on and drink this.” She pushed a cup into Wren’s hands. It was full of something pale and thin that smelled of mint and mushrooms. “I’m not sick! It’s the lamp! It’s—“ “Yes, yes,” said Hessa kindly, in the voice of somebody who has heard a great many fevered people say a great many strange things. “Drink up.” Behind her, Ash made a noise into his beard that might have been a cough. It was not a cough. Wren drank, because it was easier than arguing, and it was not bad — a good deal better than Ash’s tea, which was not saying much. And while she drank, Mother Hessa went on humming as she packed up her basket: an old, slow, swinging tune, round and round, like somebody rocking a cradle. Wren lowered the cup. She knew that tune. She did not know how she knew it — she had never been within a hundred miles of this place — but she did. It went down where hers went down and turned where hers turned, and for a moment her heart did something odd and painful, like a foot missing a step on a dark stair. “That song,” she said. “What is it?” “Mm?” said Hessa. “Oh — an old hush-song. Every grandmother in the Deeps knows it. Mira, take these Roof-folk to the Long Table, or they’ll eat my mats.” And she was gone through the chimes, still humming, before Wren could ask anything else; and the tune went away along the ledge, getting smaller, until the water in the gutter covered it. The Long Table was the great eating-hall of the Low Hum, and Wren never saw it at all. “You’ll have to cover the warm thing,” Mira said. “There’ll be hundreds of people. They’ll all think they’ve caught something and nobody will eat, and then there’ll be leftovers, and nobody in Deepholm knows what to do with leftovers.” So Wren wrapped the lamp away again, and Mira took Tobin’s sleeve and Wren took the back of Tobin’s coat, and they went out into the dark like a very small and very unhappy procession. Wren was unhappy all the way there — bumping, stumbling, catching her shins on everything in Deepholm that could be caught on — but Tobin, in front of her, was not. Tobin was talking. “The bridge,” he was saying. “The way the note changes as you cross — it must be the tension in the ropes, they’ve tuned the lengths so the pitch tells you your position, that’s — that’s actually brilliant. And the spirals on the walls, those are baffles, they’re absorbing the echo so the city isn’t deafening, and the water channels — Mira, does the water drive the Hour-Stones directly, or is there some kind of escapement, a—“ “I don’t know what an escapement is,” said Mira. “The water fills a stone cup. When the cup’s full it tips, and strikes the stone. Then it empties and starts again.” “That’s an escapement!” “Then that’s what it is. You don’t need to shout. I’m holding your sleeve. Low rock.” He ducked without slowing down. “And the — what were they — the ridges on the floor—“ “Touch-roads. Your feet are on one now. Can you feel it? Two ridges. Steps coming.” “I can feel it. I can actually feel it. Mira, this is the most—“ He stopped so suddenly that Wren walked into the back of him. “Oh,” he said, in a different voice. “Oh. I’ve forgotten to be frightened.” “Have you?” said Mira. “I wondered when you would.” Wren said nothing. But she held on to the back of his coat a little less tightly after that, and more as if she were walking with him than being towed. They heard the Long Table from a long way off: a hall full of voices and the scrape of bowls, with a waterfall at one end that filled the whole place with a deep, soft roar, like a giant breathing in his sleep. There were children chasing each other under the benches, clicking and shrieking. And as Wren came in, groping for the edge of the bench, she knocked over somebody’s cup, trod on somebody’s foot, and sat down, very hard, in somebody else’s lap. A shout of laughter went down the table. “Why do the Roof-folk walk like that?” said a young voice in delight, from the other side of the board. “Like they’re carrying soup on their heads?” “Tavi,” said a woman’s voice reprovingly. “But they do! Listen to them! Bump, bump, ow! Didn’t anyone ever teach them to click?” “They come from a place that’s all light, Tavi,” said Mira, with great dignity, helping Wren off a stranger’s knee. “They’ve never needed to. It’s like a fish that’s never learned to walk. You don’t laugh at a fish.” “I would,” said Tavi. “If a fish walked into me.” He came round the table, quick and bold as a sparrow, and before Wren could stop him he had put both small hands on her face — her forehead, her nose, her sharp chin — as lightly as moths. Then he did the same to Tobin, and jumped back with a squeak. “This one’s got glass on his face!” “They’re called spectacles,” said Tobin, a little stiffly. “What do they do?” “They help me to — well — see.” “Does that help?” said Tavi doubtfully, and was hauled away by his collar by a grown-up who said something low about your father and the Speaker’s son, of all people. Then the bowls came. That was the part Wren remembered afterwards, longer than the bridges or the carvings or even the hush-song. They came down the table from hand to hand, out of the dark: a warm bowl of something thick and savoury with mushrooms in it, and a round of flat, chewy, faintly sweet bread, and a cup of water so cold it tasted of stone. Somebody put a bowl into her hands. Somebody else put bread on top of it. Nobody asked for anything. Nobody counted. Nobody said that’s yours or that’s mine, or who’s paying for the strangers? The bowls simply came, and people ate, and when somebody’s bowl was empty somebody else’s hands filled it. Wren found that she had already slipped half her bread into her pocket — quickly, without thinking, the way she had done at every meal in her life, in case there was no next one. She sat with her hand over it in the dark and felt her face go hot. “What do I owe?” she said, under her breath, to the woman on her left. “For the food. What’s the — what does it cost?” The woman stopped eating. “Owe?” she said. She sounded genuinely puzzled, as though Wren had asked her what colour Tuesday was. “She means,” said Mira, from Wren’s other side, “who does the bread belong to.” And then, to Wren, gently: “It doesn’t belong to anybody. The deep grows the mushrooms. The deep gives the water. All we do is carry it from one pair of hands to the next. What the deep gives, the deep shares. That’s all. It’s the first thing anybody learns here — before walking, nearly.” Wren sat very still. Then, slowly, she took the bread out of her pocket. There was a child next to her on the bench — she could hear him, small and snuffling and bored, kicking his heels — and she found his hand in the dark and put the bread into it. He took it without a word, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. In Deepholm, I suppose, it was. She did not say anything about it, and neither did Mira. But a little later, when Wren put her hand to her coat, she could feel through all the folds that the lamp had grown warmer. Further down the table, a small child was wailing that it was not tired, and would not go to sleep, and would not, and would not. “Hush now,” said its mother, in a cheerful sing-song, “or the Burning will come up the Black Stair and eat your ears. Hot, hot, hot! Nibble, nibble!” And the child shrieked with laughter, and so did the children round it, and the mother laughed too. “They think light is a bogeyman,” Tobin whispered, close to Wren’s ear. He sounded shaken. “Like a goblin, or the — the sort of thing you make up to frighten babies.” Wren put her hand flat against the warm place over her heart, and said nothing. Then a voice spoke from the head of the table, and the whole hall went still. It was not a loud voice. It did not need to be.
