And I hear that one of them carries a warm thing that makes our people sick.” Nobody answered. Down the table, someone set a bowl down very carefully, so that it would make no sound at all. “At the high turn,” said the voice, “they will come before the Elders. They will bring the warm thing with them. And we will hear what they are.” There was a creak of a bench, and slow footsteps going away, and the clatter of the hall came back, but quieter than before. Mira’s hand found Wren’s sleeve under the table. Her voice was the lowest Wren had heard it yet. “That was Speaker Gorrim,” she said. “Tavi’s father. He’s head of the Elders, and he’s not unkind, and he’s not a fool. But he doesn’t believe in stories, Wren. Not one. Whatever you do tomorrow—“ her fingers tightened — “don’t tell him it’s light.”

fields.title: The Elders’ Judgment
fields.body_html:
The high turn of the Hour-Stones is the loudest sound in Deepholm. Wren had not known that. She was asleep on Mother Hessa’s mats, with the lamp in the crook of her arm and Cinder across her feet, when every singing-stone in the city struck at once; and she sat bolt upright with her heart going like a hammer, quite sure that the roof of the world had fallen in.

It was only morning, or what passes for morning in a place that has never had one. The great note went rolling away down the cavern until it was only a shiver in the stone; and in the quiet afterwards, Wren heard the chime-curtain ring, and Dask’s lathe-turned voice saying, “The Elders will hear you now.”

The Hall of Answers was shaped like the inside of a shell.

Wren could tell that much before she uncovered the lamp, from the way the sound behaved. Every little noise they made — the scuff of her boots, Tobin’s cough, the creak of Ash’s litter — went curling away round a great smooth wall and came back from the other side, softened and multiplied, like a whisper passed from mouth to mouth. Hundreds of people were in that hall; she could hear them breathing and clicking under their breath. But not one of them spoke.

“Uncover the warm thing,” said the deep slow voice from the night before. “Let us all feel what it is.”

Wren drew out the lamp.

The hall leapt out of the dark around her. It was round and very high, and the walls went up in tiers of carved stone benches, ring above ring, like the inside of a great curled seashell, and every bench was packed with pale, white-braided Delvers. All of them flinched as the warmth reached them. A murmur ran round the tiers and came back doubled.

At the centre of the floor, where the company stood, was a single flat round stone, polished smooth by centuries of feet. “The Answering Stone,” Mira had told them on the way. “Whatever’s said on it, every seat in the hall hears. You can’t mumble on the Answering Stone. Tobin, you’ll hate it.”

Facing it, on a ledge of carved rock, sat seven Elders. And in the middle of the seven sat Speaker Gorrim.

He was the biggest Delver Wren had seen: broad as a door, with a white beard plaited past his belt, and great slow hands resting on his knees. His face was heavy and lined and very still, like a cliff that has been rained on for a thousand years. When the warmth of the lamp reached the Elders’ ledge, the other six turned their faces aside. Gorrim did not. He set his jaw against it, the way a man sets his shoulder to a door, and kept his blind pale eyes straight on the place where Wren was standing.

Down on the lowest bench, beside Mother Hessa, Mira sat with her hands folded in her lap and her chin up. Further along, a small boy was bouncing — Tavi, wriggling with excitement, with a grown-up’s hand clamped on his shoulder to keep him on the bench.

“Elder Ruen,” said Gorrim. “Speak the matter.”

A thin old woman at the end of the ledge rose. Her voice was dry and quick, like twigs snapping.

“Four Roof-folk came down through the Waste at the edge of the Low Hum,” she said. “Three, and a beast. One is hurt. One carries a thing that burns without fire, and makes all who come near it hot and strange. Two of the patrol are sick with it still. They say—“ she paused, as if the word tasted odd — “that it is light.”

A ripple of laughter went round the tiers: not cruel, quite, but the laughter of grown-ups when a child says something silly at table.

“Who speaks for the Roof-folk?” said Gorrim.

“I do,” said Old Ash.

He had made the Delvers prop him up on his litter, and his beard was combed, and his long hands were folded on his blanket; and in spite of the splints and the greyness of his face he looked, Wren thought, more like a king than anybody she had ever seen.

“My name is Ash,” he said. “Once I was Master Lamplighter of Emberwick, a city on the Roof, as you call it, far to the south. These are my companions. We are travelling to the Bright Mountain, and we fell into your country by accident, and we are sorry for the trouble we have brought you. We will go as soon as you show us the way.” He bowed his head, as far as the litter would let him. “And we are grateful for your bread.”

“Courteous,” said Gorrim. “Hrrm.” It was a low rumble, like a boulder settling, and nothing like Ash’s dry little hm. “And what is this thing your girl carries, Master Lamplighter, that makes my people sick?”

“It is a lamp,” said Ash. “There is a Flame in it, which was given to her. It makes no one sick. It is warm, because it is a Flame, and it gives light, because that is what a Flame is for.”

“Light.” Gorrim said the word slowly, turning it over. “My grandmother told me of light, when I was smaller than my son. Go not up the Black Stair, little one, she said, for at the top there is the Burning, and it will eat your eyes. Every child in Deepholm is told so. It is a good tale. It keeps children off the Stair, which is a thousand steps and kills those who climb it carelessly.” He leaned forward a little. “But I am not a child, Master Lamplighter. And I have never yet met a grown man who believed it.”

“If I m-may,” said Tobin.

Wren shut her eyes. She could not help it.

“Light,” said Tobin, stepping onto the Answering Stone, where his voice came back at him from every side so that he jumped, “is — technically — it’s what comes off a flame, and when it hits things it bounces off them into your eyes, and that’s how you — how you see them.”

“Into our eyes,” said Gorrim.

“Well — yes.”

“And yet here is your light, if you call it so, burning before the whole of Deepholm. And not one eye in this hall has seen anything at all.”

“That’s — that’s because—“ Tobin’s face had gone red; Wren could see it plainly, which made it worse. “Because your eyes have never — I mean, possibly, in the dark, over generations, they—“

“Are you telling the Elders,” said Elder Ruen sharply, “that there is something wrong with our eyes?”

“No! No, I — not wrong, exactly, just — different—“

The laughter came again, louder, and went round the shell of the hall and came back louder still. Tobin stepped off the Answering Stone with his ears scarlet, and stood behind Ash’s litter, and did not say anything else.

So Wren did the only thing she could think of. She walked onto the Stone herself and held the lamp out towards the Elders’ ledge in both hands.

She did not argue. She had heard what arguing got you. She only stood there and held it out — not like a weapon, and not like a thing for sale, but the way she had held it out on the bakery step in Soot Lane — and said, “Here. Feel it. It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

And the lamp blazed.

It went up gold and white, so bright that Tobin cried out and Ash closed his eyes and smiled. The light ran up the tiers of the hall to the very top, and every carved spiral in the walls lit up with those threads of hidden colour, rose and green and gold, all the way round, like a necklace being lifted out of a box. The warmth went with it, and rolled up over the benches like a wave; and the whole of Deepholm, all those hundreds of people who had never been warm in their lives, gasped at once.

Some of them cried out in fear. A baby began to wail. But some of them — Wren saw it, and would remember it — some of them, here and there among the tiers, an old man, a girl, a woman holding a child, did not flinch away. They sat quite still with their faces turned into the warmth and their mouths a little open, as though they were listening to something a very long way off.

Gorrim rose to his feet.

“Enough,” he said; and the word went into the stone and came out of every wall. “Cover it.”

Wren did not move.

“Cover it, Roof-girl.”

She covered it. The hall fell back into blackness, and in the blackness she heard hundreds of people breathing hard, and a woman sobbing, and the baby still wailing; and Gorrim’s voice went on, slow and heavy as a cartwheel.

“A trick,” he said. “A hot stone in a box, such as any of our own smiths could make, if they wished to frighten fools. They carry a fever-stone in their coats, these Roof-folk, to make us sick and afraid — and then tell us nursery tales to explain it.” He paused. “Hear me, Deepholm. I do not say they mean us harm. Perhaps they believe their own tale. Perhaps the old man has carried his hot stone so long that he has forgotten it is only a stone. But hear this also.”

The hall was absolutely silent.

“Above us is the Waste. And on the Waste, of late, walk the cold ones. You have heard them. Our patrols have heard them, through the Roof, at the edges — the grey ones, the silent ones, who pass over and leave the moss dead behind them. And now these four come down through the Roof, out of the very place where the cold ones walk, with a fever in a box and a story in their mouths.” His voice did not rise. It only grew heavier. “I am Speaker of Deepholm. I will not risk my people on a story.”

“Speaker.”

It was Mira.

Wren heard her stand up on the lowest bench — heard the soft tick of the beads in her hair — and heard Mother Hessa whisper, “Mira—“

“Speaker,” said Mira, very clearly, “I was set to guard them. Let the guard speak.” She did not wait to be given leave. “I’ve walked beside them from the Waste to the Low Hum. I’ve held my hands to the warm thing. It isn’t a sickness, Speaker, I know sickness, I’m Hessa’s granddaughter. It doesn’t feel like a fever. It feels like — like standing next to someone who’s laughing. And the old stories don’t only talk about the Burning. The oldest ones say—“

“Enough.”

Gorrim did not say it loudly. He did not need to, on that ledge, in that hall. The word came down on Mira like a stone lid on a well.

“You are a child,” he said, “and you were set to guard, not to speak. Hessa. Take your granddaughter home.”

There was a short silence. Then Wren heard Mira sit down. But in the dark, from where she sat, came one small, clear sound, so quiet that nobody who was not listening for it would have noticed.

Click.

Wren did not know what it meant. She found out later that in Deepholm, one click alone, said soft and straight at somebody, means I’m here.

The Elders gave their verdict in a way Wren had never heard before, and hoped never to hear again.

They hummed. Each of the seven, one after another, sang a single long note into the dark, and the notes went round the shell of the hall and met each other. Where they agreed, Mira told her afterwards, they made one sound, round and whole. Where an Elder disagreed, the note would sit against the others and jar, like two bells that do not belong together. Wren listened hard. Five notes came together, deep and sure. Then a sixth. And the seventh — she was nearly certain — wavered, and rubbed against the rest, and then gave way and fell in with them, and was lost.

“It is heard,” said Gorrim. “At the next high turn, the Roof-folk will be taken to the Silent Pit, and lowered into it, with their warm thing and their beast. Let what they carry be carried where it can harm no one.”

There was a sound all round the tiers, like a great sigh going round. It was not a cheer. Wren found out afterwards why. The Silent Pit, Mira told her, was a shaft at the far end of the Deeps so wide and so deep that a stone dropped into it made no sound when it landed — or if it did, the sound never came back. For a Delver there is nothing worse. In the Pit you cannot click and hear an answer. You cannot hear a wall, or a floor, or a friend. You cannot hear where you are. Those who go down into the Silent Pit do not come up again; and the Delvers do not sing songs about them afterwards, because there is nothing to sing.

“Father,” came Tavi’s voice, high and anxious, from the far side of the hall. “Father, can I feel the warm thing first? Just once? Before it goes in the—“

“Be silent, Tavi.”

They were put in a hush-room for the night: a small square cell cut into the rock, with a door of heavy stone slabs on a rope, and two Delvers sitting outside it: a large one called Pell, and a smaller one called Oddny.

“Mira,” she said.

Mira waited. She was good at waiting; Wren had noticed that about her. At last she said, quite kindly, “You breathe very loudly when you’re being proud. Did you know?”

fields.title: Mira’s Secret
fields.body_html:
Pell snored in two notes, and Oddny hummed.

That was the first thing Mira taught Wren, in a breath of a whisper, with her mouth so close to Wren’s ear that it tickled. All Delvers hum when they sleep, a low, contented sound like a pot simmering at the back of a stove; and Pell, who was large, added a snore on top of it, one note going in and a lower one coming out. So long as the two guards were making their noises, they were asleep. If either noise stopped, they were not.

“And then,” breathed Mira, “we are in a great deal of trouble. Come.”

Wren had never in her life crept anywhere behind somebody else. She was the one who knew the roofs and the flues; other people crept behind her. But she did as she was told. She scooped the lamp up off the floor of the hush-room and did up every button of her coat over it. She left Tobin on his blanket with his spectacles folded on his chest like a dead beetle, and Old Ash lying straight and still on his litter with his bad leg packed in Hessa’s moss-paste, his eyes open on the roof, saying nothing at all, and Cinder curled on Tobin’s collar. Cinder opened one eye as Wren passed. Then she shut it again, as if to say that she had seen nothing and would swear to it.

Mira stepped over the guards’ feet without a sound. Wren stepped over them with a great deal of care and almost no sound, and the humming and the two-note snore went on, and grew fainter behind them, and then there was only the drip of water and the soft pad of Mira’s bare feet, and the dark.

Mira did not walk like someone in the dark. She walked like someone in her own kitchen. Every few steps she made a small sound with her tongue against the roof of her mouth — tck — and listened, with her head a little on one side, and then went on, turning left, ducking under something Wren could not see, stepping long over something else. Wren held on to the back of her tunic and followed.

“How do you do that?” whispered Wren.

“I ask the stone where it is,” said Mira. Tck. “And it answers. Everything answers, if you ask it properly. Your head is about to — duck.”

Wren ducked. Something cold and rough brushed the top of her hair.

“Your people never listen,” said Mira, and Wren could hear that she was smiling. “You walk about the Deeps like falling rocks.”

“We’ve got eyes,” said Wren, a little stung.

“So I have heard,” said Mira politely. “They do not seem to be much use to you.”

At last Mira stopped, so suddenly that Wren walked into her.

“Here,” she said. And then, in a different voice, quieter and more careful: “No one else knows about this place. Not Gran. Especially not the Elders. I found it when I was six, and I have never brought anyone. Not once.” She paused. “You must promise not to laugh.”

“Why would I laugh?”

“Because everyone does,” said Mira simply.

“I promise,” said Wren.

Mira knelt and felt along the bottom of the wall. There was a scrape of stone on stone. Cool air breathed out at them from a gap no higher than a dog-kennel, and Mira wriggled into it like an eel. Wren went after her on her elbows, the way she had gone through a hundred flues, and came out into a space she could not see at all — only feel, from the way her breathing came back to her, that it was small and round and very still.

“Now,” whispered Mira. “Now you may have your warm thing out. The stone is too thick for anyone to feel it.”

Wren undid her buttons and took out the lamp.

I want to tell you about the Story-Wall properly, because it was one of the most beautiful things Wren ever saw. But I must tell you first that it was not made to be seen at all. It was made for hands.

The chamber was round, like the inside of an egg, and not much bigger than Wren’s garret in Soot Lane. One whole side of it was a single sweep of pale stone, smooth as a cheek, running from the floor to high over their heads. And every inch of it was carved. There were Delvers, no taller than Wren’s hand, with their long fingers and their heads tipped to one side, listening. There were tunnels, and the terraces of Deepholm, and rope bridges hanging like cobwebs. And all through it, between the pictures, ran rows of tiny ridges and dots and grooves, which must be writing, though it was like no writing Wren had ever seen on a shop sign.

In the light of the little lamp every carving threw a small soft shadow beside it, and the whole wall seemed to rise up out of itself and stand there, alive. The people who had made it had never once looked at it. They had only known it was true to fingers.

Mira went to the left-hand end of the wall, where the carving began low down, and knelt, and laid her fingertips on the first row of marks. The stone was worn smooth there, Wren saw, as though a great many fingers had rested on that place over a great many years — and then, for a long time, only one small pair.

“It is called the Wall of the Warm Man,” said Mira. “It is older than Deepholm. I know it by heart. But I like to read it anyway. It is different, reading.”

Wren sat down cross-legged on the cold floor, with the lamp in her lap. Mira’s fingers began to move along the stone.

“In the long dark, before the songs were counted, a Man came down the Stair.”

Wren looked where the fingers went, and saw a long stair spiralling down out of the top of the wall, and a figure coming down it. All round him, on every side, the carvers had cut ring after ring in the stone, like the rings that spread on water when you drop a pebble in.

“He was warm,” read Mira. “Where he walked, the stone was warm after him.”

“Those rings,” said Wren softly. “Round him. What are they?”

“That is how we carve a sound,” said Mira. “A loud one — a song, or a bell. That is what a thing feels like to the fingers when it fills a room.” She tipped her head. “But he was not making a sound. The old carvers felt something coming off him that filled the Deeps, and they did not know how else to show it. So they carved it like a song.”

Wren looked at the rings spreading round the little stone man, and then down at the lamp, and at its light spreading out across the floor and her own knees in a soft gold ring. She did not say anything.

“He did not click, and he did not stumble. He walked as one who knows the way.

“He sat with the Delvers and ate their bread, and learned their songs, and sang them a new one.

“He laid his hands on the eyes of the children, and said: Here is a thing you have never heard of, and you will not believe it. There is a light. You cannot hear it, and you cannot hold it, but it is warm, and it is coming.”

Mira’s fingers had come to the middle of the wall. Wren lifted the lamp and leaned closer.

The Warm Man was carved larger here, kneeling. Before him a small Delver child stood with its face turned up. One of the Man’s hands rested on the child’s eyes, very gently. The other was held out a little to the side, and in it was something small, round-bellied, with a narrow chimney and a little hook on top.

Wren’s heart gave one hard knock against her ribs.

It was only a shape in the stone. It could have been a jug, or a bell, or a bird-cage. The carvers had never seen a lamp in their lives; how could they have carved one? And yet in the very middle of that little shape someone had set a bead of pale crystal no bigger than a pea, polished by years and years of fingers. As Wren leaned close, the light went into the crystal and caught there; and for the first time in longer than anyone in Deepholm could have told you, the little bead in the Warm Man’s hand shone gold.

“What is it?” said Mira sharply. “Your breath has gone strange.”

“Nothing,” said Wren. “Go on. Read the rest.”

Mira laid her fingers on the last lines, under the kneeling Man.

“Do not be afraid of the dark. It is not as deep as it sounds.

“One day you shall see. One day, all of you shall see.

“Then he went up the Stair, and the stone was warm behind him for a hundred years. Keep the stone warm, for he will come again.”

She took her fingers off the wall and folded her hands in her lap, and the little round chamber was very quiet.

“The children used to be told it, long ago,” said Mira at last, in a brisk, careless voice that was not quite brisk enough. “But the Elders said it was only a story to frighten children, because what is more frightening than a thing you cannot hear or touch? And it made the little ones restless, always asking when he was coming back. So they stopped telling it, and somebody walled up this room. All that is left of him now is the Burning that comes up the Black Stair to eat naughty children’s ears. They forgot the Man, and kept only the warm, and made it frightening.” She shrugged. “Then I found the gap. I was looking for a lost spoon.”

“Did you find the spoon?”

“No,” said Mira. “I found this. I told everyone about the Warm Man, when I was small. They laughed, and then they were sorry for me, which was worse. Speaker Gorrim told Gran I was a dreamy child who would grow out of it.” She lifted her chin. “I have not grown out of it.”

“But you’ve never seen it,” said Wren. “Light. You don’t know what it is. How can you believe in something you’ve never seen?”

Mira was quiet for a moment. Then she said, “How do you believe in the far side of a tunnel?”

“What?”

“When you are in a tunnel, and it goes on and on, and you cannot hear the end of it yet. You don’t sit down and say, there is no far side, because I have not got there. You feel the air moving on your face. And the air is coming from somewhere. So you keep walking.” She turned her face towards Wren. “I have felt the air on my face all my life. That is all. Something is coming from somewhere.”

Wren had nothing to say to that. She was a girl who believed in exactly what she could hold in her two hands, and not a crumb more. You could not eat a promise. You could not sell a story. And here was this girl, who had never seen anything at all, who had sat alone in the dark for six years with her fingers on a wall, believing.

Then Mira said, in a small voice with no mischief in it whatever, “Wren. Your warm thing. Is it — is that what the Wall means? Is that the light?”

I am sorry to say that Wren did not answer at once. A lifetime in Soot Lane is not undone in a week; and a small sharp voice at the back of her head said: careful. It’s yours. It’s the only thing that’s ever been yours.

And then another thought came, and pushed the first one out of the way, the way Cinder pushed her way into a warm lap. It cannot be bought, stolen or earned. Only given.

“I don’t know what your Wall means,” said Wren slowly. “But there’s an old man back in that cave who’d tell you there was a man once, who walked about with a lamp, lighting people’s lamps for nothing. And this is his lamp. Ash says.” She looked at the gold bead shining in the stone hand. “I don’t know if it’s the same man. I don’t know anything. But—“

She stopped. And then, before the small sharp voice could say anything else, she leaned forward, took Mira’s hand, turned it palm upwards, and put the lamp into it.

“Here,” she said gruffly. “You hold it. I’m giving it you to hold.”

Mira went absolutely still.

Wren had a quick cold flash of fright. She thought of Grubb in Crookback Market, yelping and shaking his burned fingers.

But Mira did not flinch. Her long pale fingers closed round the dented brass slowly, carefully, the way you might close your hands round a bird that has flown in at the window. The little flame stood up calm and golden in its cracked glass, and its light lay on Mira’s face — her thin, clever face, which had never once in its life been lit by anything — and turned it, very faintly, the colour of a peach.

“Oh,” said Mira. Just oh, very quietly, the way you say it when you step into warm water.

“It isn’t sickness,” she whispered. “They said it was sickness. It’s like when Gran sings the long song for the new babies, and you feel it here.” She pressed one hand flat against her chest. “But in my hands.” She held the lamp up close to her face and tipped her head as though she were listening to it. “It answers. I can’t hear it, but it answers.”

There was a lump in Wren’s throat the size of a walnut, and she did not care for it at all. “You can’t see it, though. Can you? Not even a bit.”

“No,” said Mira. “Not even a bit.” And then she smiled — a wide, sudden, delighted smile. “I can’t see your lamp, Wren. But I can feel that it’s true.”

“What is red?”

“It’s—“ Wren had only known the word herself for a little while; it still felt new in her mouth. “You know when you come in out of the cold, and you hold your hands near a fire, and they go all prickly, and it hurts a bit, but it’s a nice hurt? It’s like that. But for your eyes.”

Mira considered this for a long time.

“I think,” she said at last, “that red must be a very good colour.”

“It’s the best one,” said Wren. “So far.”

It was very soft, the way you hum to yourself when you are happy and do not know anyone can hear. And Wren felt every hair on her arms stand straight up.

“— and the dark shall not keep us.”

Then she went back to humming, and the tune wandered on without words.

“What was that?” It came out much too loud, and bounced round the chamber. “What did you say? Sing it again!”

Mira jumped. “It is only the Wall-song, the one the Warm Man taught — the Waking Song, the grandmothers call it. fields.title: The Whispering Galleries
fields.body_html:
Have you ever tried to be perfectly silent? Not just quiet, but silent: no cough, no sniff, no creak of a shoe? It is much harder than it sounds. Most people manage it for about a minute. Wren and her friends had to manage it for most of a night.

It began badly, because Tobin woke up talking.

Wren had crept back into the hush-room and put her hand on his shoulder, and he sat bolt upright on his blanket and said, quite loudly, “Actually, I’ve been thinking about the drainage—“

Wren clapped her hand over his mouth. Outside the door, Pell’s snoring stopped.

Nobody moved. Tobin’s eyes went very wide over the top of Wren’s fingers. In the dark Wren could hear her own heart, and Mira’s breathing, quick and light by the door, and nothing at all from Pell. One breath. Two. Three.

Then there was a great snort, and a scratching sound, like a large Delver scratching his ear; and the two-note snore began again, exactly where it had left off.

Wren took her hand away from Tobin’s mouth very slowly. She put her lips against his ear and breathed, “Not one word. Not one.” Tobin nodded so hard his spectacles fell off into his lap.

Old Ash, it turned out, was already awake. When Wren leaned over him he only raised one white eyebrow, as if to ask whether she had enjoyed her evening. Cinder had already moved from Tobin’s collar to the old man’s chest, and sat there with her tail-spark glowing a low, eager red.

Mira had brought a sledge.

It was the kind the Delvers used for hauling cut stone: a flat bed of dark wood, low to the ground, on two long runners rubbed with fat until they shone. When Mira pushed it with one finger, it slid across the floor of the hush-room without a whisper. Tobin looked at it the way other boys look at a cake. Wren could see the explanation building up inside him like steam under a pot-lid, and she gave him a look, and he swallowed it.

Between them they got Old Ash off his litter and onto the sledge. His bad leg would not bend, and his face went grey and tight about the mouth; but he did not make a sound. They laid his long brass-hooked pole along beside him. Cinder settled on his chest like a small grey hearthrug.

Then Mira did something Wren did not expect. She took Wren’s wrist, turned it over, and tapped once on the inside of it with two fingers. Then twice. Then three times, quick and hard. She did the same to Tobin, and then, gravely, to Old Ash, who watched her with great interest.

Wren worked it out. One: go. Two: stop. Three— Mira tapped three again, hard, and pressed Wren’s arm down towards the floor. Three: hide.

Wren nodded. Then, because Mira could not see a nod, she tapped once on Mira’s wrist. Mira smiled in the dark.

They went out past the guards. Tobin and Wren took the rope at the front of the sledge, and Mira walked ahead, and Old Ash slid along behind them on the greased runners as smoothly as a boat on still water. Pell’s feet were stretched right across the passage. They had to lift the front of the sledge over them, inch by inch, with Ash’s weight on it, while Pell snored and Oddny hummed and Tobin’s arms shook. Halfway over, Oddny’s humming caught and wobbled. Everyone froze, the sledge held up in the air between them.

Oddny smacked twice, and said, very distinctly, “Mushrooms.” Then the humming went on.

They set the sledge down on the far side of his feet, and went on into the dark, and none of them dared to breathe out until the humming and the snoring were a long way behind.

The Whispering Galleries began at the end of a passage that no one in Deepholm had any reason to walk down. There was an old stone doorway, carved with rings, and beyond it the floor sloped gently away into a tunnel that was not like any tunnel Wren had seen.

Mira stopped at the doorway and put her mouth right against Wren’s ear for the last time.

“No one walks the Galleries,” she breathed. “Your fever-thing may come out now. But from here — nothing.”

Wren took out the lamp.

The tunnel was round, and smooth, and ribbed all along its length with long, curving ridges, like the roof of a mouth. It curled away ahead of them in a slow spiral, and the ribs curled with it. In the lamplight the stone was pale and polished as old ivory. Tobin’s mouth fell open. He lifted both hands and made a shape in the air — and Wren knew, as clearly as if he had shouted it, that he had understood exactly how it worked and was going to burst if he could not tell somebody.

She shook her head at him. He shut his mouth and nodded, and looked, for a moment, close to tears.

Then they stepped inside, and they heard Deepholm.

It came out of the walls all round them, faint and clear, the way the sea comes out of a shell held to your ear. Four hundred Delvers humming in their sleep, a soft low murmur like bees in a summer hedge. The slow drip of the water-gates, closed for the hush. Somewhere a baby fussing, and a mother’s voice hushing it. Somewhere, a long way off, someone laughing at a joke Wren would never hear. All of it carried down the Galleries to them, clear and small and near, as though the whole of Deepholm were a doll’s house and they had put their ears to its walls.

Wren stood very still with the lamp in her hands. Then she understood what it meant. If they could hear a baby fussing a mile away, then a mile away, if they made one sound, somebody could hear them.

Mira tapped her wrist once. Go.

They went.

I will not tell you every step of that journey; there were thousands, and all of them slow and silent. But I will tell you how they found the way, because it took two of them together.

The Galleries were not one tunnel but many, curling and crossing and splitting like the roots of a tree. At every place where two of them met, someone long ago had cut a mark into the wall at the height of a Delver’s hand — a little cluster of grooves and dots — and Mira would stop, and lay her fingers on it, and read it, and tap once on Wren’s wrist and turn. Usually she did not need to. But at home Mira found her way by clicking, and she could not click here. One tck in the Galleries would have rung out like a dropped pan. So she walked with one hand always on the wall, and Wren saw, after a while, that she was not quite as sure of herself as she pretended.

At the fifth crossing, Mira laid her fingers on the wall and stopped.

She moved her hand along. She moved it up, and down, and along again. Wren held the lamp close. There had been a mark there once; you could see where. But a sheet of stone had cracked away from the wall, long ago, and taken the mark with it, and there was nothing left under Mira’s fingers but a smooth broken face. Three tunnels led on from the crossing. Mira turned her head one way, and then the other, and Wren saw her lips press tight together.

And then Tobin did something clever.

He had been walking all this while with his lips moving, counting, and his ink-stained fingers twitching at his sides as if they were drawing. He had been making a map of Deepholm in his head ever since they arrived; he could no more help it than Cinder could help stealing biscuits. Now he set down the sledge-rope, very gently. He took hold of a loose thread at the cuff of his coat, and pulled, and pulled, until he had a length of it as long as his finger. He held it up in front of the first tunnel. It hung straight down. He held it in front of the second. It hung straight down.

He held it in front of the third, and the thread stirred, and lifted, and leaned — very slightly, but quite certainly — into the tunnel, as if something in there were breathing it in.

Tobin turned round with his face blazing, and pointed up, and then pointed at the tunnel, and then made a winding motion with his finger, round and round and up. Air. Going up. The Stair.

Mira could not see any of that. So Tobin, after a moment of flapping, took her hand, and put her fingers very lightly on the end of the thread, so that she could feel it lean.

Mira turned towards Tobin with an expression Wren had not seen on her face before. It was the look one craftsman gives another. She found his wrist and tapped once, firmly: yes. Then she patted his arm in a way that was not any signal at all, and only meant well done.

Tobin went pink to the ears. He picked up the sledge-rope again and pulled with a will, and somewhere about the next crossing Wren noticed that his hands had stopped shaking. He had forgotten to be frightened. He had been far too busy.

It was at the eighth crossing that Wren nearly ruined everything.

There were two ways on. Mira read the mark and tapped Wren’s wrist once and turned to the right. But Wren had stopped. She was standing at the mouth of the left-hand tunnel with her face lifted, because she could feel air on it — cool, steady air, flowing up past her. She knew that kind of air. She had spent her whole life in chimneys, and she knew a draught going up the way a sailor knows the wind. Up meant out. Up meant the Stair.

She pulled on Mira’s sleeve and pointed left, hard, forgetting for a moment that Mira could not see her point.

Mira found her hand and tapped twice. Stop. No.

Wren tapped once. Yes. This way.

Mira tapped twice again, harder, and then again, and her blind face was turned towards Wren, and it was not cross. It was asking.

Every bone in Wren’s body told her she was right. She was always the one who knew the way. She had never followed anybody anywhere, not since she was four years old. Following was how you got caught. Following was how you got sold.

Then she thought of the Story-Wall, and the girl who had sat alone in the dark believing in something she could not see.

Trust her, thought Wren. It was the strangest thought she had ever had. It was like stepping off a roof in the dark.

She tapped Mira’s wrist once, and turned right.

Not long afterwards, their tunnel curled round and ran for a little way beside another one, with only a wide crack between them, and Wren held up the lamp and looked through the crack. It was the left-hand tunnel. It ran for twenty paces more and then simply stopped, at the lip of a hole. A great round black shaft went straight down out of the floor, into nothing. Out of it came a slow, cool breath of air, rising steadily up past the edge. It was the draught she had felt.

There was no sound from that shaft. None at all. The lamp-light went down into it and did not come back.

Wren did not need anyone to tell her what it was. Her stomach turned over. She looked at Mira’s back, walking steadily ahead with one hand on the wall, and she did not say anything — she could not, of course — but she reached out and touched Mira’s shoulder, just once, lightly. Mira did not turn round. But she put her own hand up, and laid it over Wren’s for a moment, and then went on.

They nearly came to grief three more times before the end.

The first time was Cinder. The sledge had stirred up a little puff of old dust from the floor, and Cinder put her nose into it, and Wren saw the fox’s whiskers twitch, and her eyes begin to cross, and her mouth begin to open. Wren lunged across the sledge and pinched Cinder’s nose shut between finger and thumb. Cinder’s eyes bulged. Her whole body jerked once, silently. And two small, indignant puffs of golden sparks shot out of her ears and floated gently down onto Old Ash’s beard, where he patted them out without a word. Cinder glared at Wren for a full minute afterwards. Wren had never been so glad to be glared at.

The second time was Tobin’s spectacles, which slid off his nose as he bent to ease the sledge over a ridge. Wren caught them one inch above the stone floor, and Tobin looked at her with such enormous gratitude that she nearly laughed out loud, which would have been worse than the spectacles.

The third time was the patrol.

Mira heard it first. She stopped dead, and her hand shot out and found Wren’s wrist, and tapped three times — hard, quick, frightened. Hide.

Then Wren heard it too. It was coming along a cross-tunnel ahead of them, from the direction of the city: a soft tck... tck... tck-tck, very quiet, and the pad of bare feet. Several pairs. And the Galleries carried it to them so clearly that it seemed to be happening right beside Wren’s ear.

A Delver night-patrol. And a Delver clicked, and the click came back off whatever was there — stone, or sledge, or a girl holding her breath — and then he knew.

Wren pushed the lamp deep inside her coat and did up the buttons over it, and the dark fell down on them like a sack. She felt Tobin’s arm go rigid beside her. Mira was pulling at them — pulling them sideways, towards the wall — and then Wren’s shoulder sank into something soft and cold and damp. Moss. A deep pad of it, hanging down over a hollow in the wall like a curtain. Mira pushed them all into it, one after another, and dragged the sledge in after them with Old Ash on it, and pulled the moss closed.

Even her own breathing sounded muffled, as if someone had wrapped her head in a quilt. In here, a click would not come back.

The patrol came on. Tck. Tck-tck. They were right outside. They were level with the moss. She could feel the lamp burning warm against her ribs, and she pressed her arms over it as tightly as she could, and she thought: they can’t see it. They can’t see it. But they can feel warm.

One set of feet stopped.

There was a long pause. Wren could hear a Delver breathing, slow and deep, on the other side of the moss, a hand’s breadth from her face. Beside her, Tobin was shaking all over. On the sledge, Old Ash had taken his own sleeve between his teeth.

“Warm,” whispered the Delver.

And the Galleries took the word and carried it away. Wren heard it go — warm... warm... warm... — running off down the curling tunnels in every direction, growing fainter and fainter, out towards the sleeping city and beyond it, until it seemed that the whole of the Deeps was whispering it.

“Hush, Doran,” whispered another voice, sharp and cross. “You’ll wake the Elders. It’s only the hot spring under the sixth gallery. It always does that.”

...the Elders... the Elders... only the hot spring...

A grunt. The feet moved on. Tck. Tck-tck. Fainter, and fainter, and gone.

They stayed in the moss a long time after that. When at last Mira pulled the curtain back and Wren took out the lamp, she saw that Old Ash’s face was the colour of tallow, and wet, and that there were teeth-marks in his sleeve. But he caught her eye and gave her a small, crooked smile, and raised one finger to his lips, as if to say that she was doing very well.

The Galleries ended without warning. The ribbed tunnel curled round one last time and simply opened out, and they were standing on a ledge at the edge of a great black emptiness, with cold air moving on their faces.

Wren lifted the lamp.

A chasm lay in front of them, so wide that the lamplight barely reached its far side, and so deep that it did not reach the bottom at all. Across it, swaying very slightly, hung a rope bridge: a narrow walk of pale stone slats threaded on rope, with two rope rails at the height of Wren’s hands. And on the far side, at the end of the bridge, the rock rose up sheer; and cut into the foot of it was a doorway. Beyond the doorway, a stair went up. It turned almost at once, and was gone into the blackness, round and up and round and up.

“There,” whispered Mira. It was the first word any of them had spoken in hours, and it was so soft that even here, out of the Galleries, it hardly stirred the air. “That is the Cleft. And that is the Black Stair. A thousand steps, and nothing at the top but the open Waste.” She let out a long, shaky breath. “We are out. You may speak now. Softly.”

Tobin opened his mouth. Everything he had not said for the whole night came out of it at once, in a rapid, ecstatic whisper.

“The ribs,” he whispered. “Did you see the ribs? They’re reflectors, and the spiral means the sound doesn’t spread, it travels, it’s a speaking-tube miles long, and the moss, it’s a damper — Mira, who worked out the curve? It would take Guild engineers a century to—“

“Tobin,” whispered Wren.

“Yes?”

“Shut up.”

“Yes,” said Tobin happily. “Sorry. Yes.”

Mira laughed without a sound, her shoulders shaking. And Wren stood on the ledge at the edge of the Cleft with the lamp warm in her hands, and the bridge in front of her, and the Stair beyond it going up towards the open sky, and thought that she had never in her whole life been so tired, or so proud of anybody, or so nearly free.

That was when the ground moved.

It was not much, at first. A shiver under their feet, as though something very large, very far off, had turned over in its sleep. A trickle of grit pattered down from the roof of the Galleries behind them. The rope bridge swung, and creaked.

Then it came again — a long, deep, grinding shudder that went right up through the soles of Wren’s boots and into her teeth. Dust poured down from the dark overhead. Cinder leapt off Old Ash’s chest with every hair on end. Tobin grabbed the sledge-rope.

And from the mouth of the Galleries behind them, carried out to them along a mile of curling stone, came a sound like a great door breaking.

Then, one by one, all the faint far sounds of sleeping Deepholm — the humming, and the snores, and the murmur of a thousand dreaming voices — began to stop.

That was when the ground moved. It was not much, at first. A shiver under their feet, as though something very large, very far off, had turned over in its sleep. A trickle of grit pattered down from the roof of the Galleries behind them. The rope bridge swung, and creaked. Then it came again — a long, deep, grinding shudder that went right up through the soles of Wren’s boots and into her teeth. Dust poured down from the dark overhead. Cinder leapt off Old Ash’s chest with every hair on end. Tobin grabbed the sledge-rope. And from the mouth of the Galleries behind them, carried out to them along a mile of curling stone, came a sound like a great door breaking. Then, one by one, all the faint far sounds of sleeping Deepholm — the humming, and the snores, and the murmur of a thousand dreaming voices — began to stop.

fields.title: Varrick in the Deeps
fields.body_html:
The humming went first.

It did not stop all at once. That would almost have been better. It went out the way lamps go out along a street when the oil runs short: here, and then there, and then two together, and then a whole stretch at once. Four hundred sleepy voices had been murmuring out of the mouth of the Galleries, soft as bees; and now there were nine hundred, and now there were six, and now Wren could pick out single voices among them, the way you can count the last few stars before a cloud covers them.

Then, somewhere far off, an Hour-Stone that had been silent all through the hush rang out once, wild and wrong, as if something had struck it in passing. The note hung in the Galleries for a long time. Nobody answered it.

Mira stood on the ledge at the edge of the Cleft with her face turned towards the Galleries and her hands pressed flat against her chest.

“The songs,” she whispered. “Someone is stopping the songs.”

Cinder was growling. She stood stiff-legged on the stones with every hair along her back on end and her tail-spark flaring white, staring into the dark mouth of the tunnel they had just come out of; and Wren, who had learned in Emberwick what that growl meant, felt the cold come creeping over her skin before there was any cold to feel.

Then a voice came out of the Galleries.

It came from a mile away, and it was as clear as if the speaker stood at Wren’s shoulder. It was smooth and pleasant and quite unhurried, and it did not shout. It did not need to. The Galleries carried it for him, into every curling tunnel and every sleeping house in Deepholm.

“Good evening,” said the voice. “Please don’t be alarmed. I am looking for a lamp.”

Wren knew that voice. She had last heard it on top of the Great Beacon, in the wind, offering her the world.

Old Ash, lying on the sledge, closed his eyes. “Hm,” he said, very quietly. That was all. But Wren saw his long hand tighten on the pole beside him until the knuckles went white.

“Varrick,” whispered Tobin. “How can he — we came down a hole, we fell, there’s no road, how could he possibly—“

“He followed us,” said Wren. Her mouth had gone dry. “He’s been following us all the way. Ever since the Grey Gate.”

The first Delvers came running out of the Galleries a few minutes later.

They came clicking — frantic, rattling clicks, all at once, so that the tunnel-mouth was full of a sound like hail on a roof — and they came stumbling and crowding, with no care at all now for silence. Mothers with babies tied on their backs. Old men leaning on younger ones. Children clinging to anybody’s hand. They poured out onto the ledge, and stopped short at the edge of the Cleft, swaying, clicking at the drop.

Mother Hessa came among them, with a basket on her arm as if she had grabbed the first thing she could find, and a small child holding each corner of her apron. She was not humming.

“Gran!” Mira caught at her sleeve. “What is it? What’s happened?”

“Grey men.” Hessa’s brisk voice was shaking. “They came down the hole these Roof-folk fell through. Cold came with them, child. Such cold. And things with them that are not men at all. Your clicks go through them.” She shuddered. “Anyone they touch stops singing. They just — stop. They sit down where they are and they don’t know their own songs.” She drew a breath. “They took Gorrim’s boy.”

“Tavi?” Mira’s face went white. “Not Tavi—“

“He ran towards them. You know how he is. He thought it was a game.” Hessa’s voice cracked. “He’s sitting in the Great Echo-Hall, and he’s quiet. Tavi. Quiet. The Speaker’s carrying him out, but the Speaker is slow, and the grey men are behind him. The Elders have sent everyone to the Black Stair. Burning or no Burning, it’s the only way out.”

Wren looked at the stream of Delvers pressing out onto the ledge, and at the narrow, swaying bridge, and at the endless black Stair beyond it. There were hundreds of them. There would be more. And they could not see the bridge. They would have to feel their way across it, one by one.

“Who’s Tavi?” she said to Mira, low.

“He’s nine. He’s—“ Mira swallowed. “He follows me everywhere. He thinks I’m the cleverest person in Deepholm. He’s always asking me to tell him about the Warm Man, though his father says not to. He wanted to feel your warm thing. He asked, in front of everyone.” She tried to smile, and could not. “He’s a nuisance.”

Wren thought of a small freckled face with two teeth missing. She thought of a thin voice saying Wren, you’re the betht. She thought of that same face gone grey, sitting on a cold step, not knowing her name.

She did not say anything. She found that she could not.

“Child,” said Old Ash.

He had pushed himself up on one elbow on the sledge. His face was grey with pain, but his eyes were quite steady, and he looked at her the way he had looked at her across his table in the Leaning Tower, as though he could see straight through to the back of her head.

“The bridge is there,” he said. “And the Stair. You could be across it before the first of them. You could be halfway up before Varrick reaches this ledge. He wants the lamp, not these people.” He paused. “And these people, I’ll remind you, were going to lower you into a pit at the high turn.”

“What about you?” said Wren.

“I can’t climb a thousand steps, child. You know that. I’ll do very well here.”

“Rot,” said Wren.

But she went to the bridge.

She did not quite know why. Her feet took her. She stepped out onto the first slat, and it swayed under her, and the cold air of the Cleft came up past her from the dark below. Ahead of her, at the far end, the doorway of the Black Stair stood open, and beyond it the steps went round and up into the dark. A thousand steps. And at the top, the Greywaste, and the wind, and the pale sun, and the long road to the Bright Mountain. Nobody would blame her. There was nobody to blame her. Everything costs, said the small sharp voice at the back of her head, and this has nothing to do with you, and you have paid enough.

She took a second step. The bridge creaked.

Behind her, on the ledge, a child was crying — a thin, frightened wail, on and on. And over it, she heard Mira’s voice. Mira was not running. Mira was standing at the mouth of the Galleries with one hand on the wall, calling out names into the dark, one after another, tck, tck, finding the lost ones by their echoes and sending them on towards the bridge. She was not going to cross. Wren could hear it in her voice. She was going to stand there and call until the cold came.

Wren stood on the bridge with the lamp in her hands.

I should like to tell you that she made up her mind in a noble flash, like a knight in a story. She did not. She stood there for what felt like a very long time, and she was very frightened, and she was also extremely cross.

“Rot,” said Wren, out loud, to the Cleft. “Rot and blast.”

And she turned round, and went back.

“Tobin,” she said, when she reached the ledge. “Get them over. All of them. One at a time, holding the rails. You’re good at — at organising things. Tell them where to put their feet.”

Tobin stared at her. “Where are you going?”

“In there.” She pointed at the Galleries with her chin. “To fetch the slow ones.”

“Wren, you can’t, that’s — that’s exactly where he is—“

“I know where he is.” She looked at Mira, who had turned towards her voice. “Coming?”

Mira was already at her side. Cinder was already ahead of them both.

They went back into the Galleries with the lamp held high, and they did not trouble to be quiet now. The ribbed walls went streaming past, pale as ivory. And the Delvers coming towards them out of the dark — stumbling, clicking, lost — stopped as they passed, and turned their blind faces towards the lamp.

“Warm,” one of them said, an old woman with her hands out in front of her. “Oh — it’s warm.”

And Wren saw something she had not expected. The Delvers did not flinch from it. Not now. Behind them was the cold, the dreadful creeping cold that stopped songs; and here in front of them, coming the other way, was a warmth like a hearth. They could not see the light. They did not need to. They turned towards the warmth the way cold hands turn towards a stove, and they followed it.

“This way,” said Wren. “Keep close. Follow the warm. Mira, tell them.”

Mira told them. She told them, quick and low, and they gathered behind Wren in a long, stumbling line, holding one another’s sleeves. Wren led them back round the curling Galleries towards the Cleft, and then went back again for more, and then again. She lost count of how many times.

On the fourth time, they met Speaker Gorrim.

He was coming slowly along the Gallery towards them, the great proud Speaker, alone. His Elder’s robe was torn. In his arms he carried a boy of about nine, long-limbed and pale, with his head lolling against his father’s shoulder. The boy’s eyes were open. He was not crying. He was not doing anything at all.

Gorrim stopped. He clicked, once, and Wren knew he had found her.

“You,” he said. “Roof-girl.” His deep slow voice was rough. “This is your doing. You and your fever. You brought them down on us.”

“Probably,” said Wren. “Come on.”

She held out the lamp towards the boy. She did not quite know why. But Gorrim swung away from it, sharp, and turned his shoulder between it and his son.

“Keep your sickness away from my child,” he said. “Haven’t you done enough?”

There was no time to argue. Because at that moment Cinder, who had been padding ahead, stopped dead in the middle of the Gallery and set her four feet and snarled. And the cold came round the curve of the tunnel.

It came like water coming under a door. It came along the floor first, so that Wren felt it through her boots, and then up her legs and into her stomach, and her breath smoked in front of her face. Mira clicked, fast — tck-tck-tck — towards the bend, and then again, and her face went blank with fear.

“There’s nothing there,” she whispered. “Wren, there’s nothing there. My clicks go straight through. But it’s so cold—“

Wren held up the lamp.

They were there.

They filled the curve of the Gallery from wall to wall: grey shapes, tall and thin and faceless, like smoke poured into the outline of a person. They did not walk. They drifted. Where they had passed, the pale ivory stone of the walls had gone a dull dead grey, as if the colour had been licked off it. And behind them, ringing on the stone, came the tramp of boots.

The Hollows shrank from the lamp. They always did. They bent away from it like grass in a wind, and hung there at the edge of its light, and waited.

“Back,” said Wren. Her voice came out much smaller than she wanted. “Everybody back. Slowly. Speaker — back.”

And for once in his life, Speaker Gorrim did what somebody else told him.

They went back along the Galleries step by step, Wren last of all, walking backwards, with the lamp held up in front of her like a shield. The Hollows came after them as fast as they went, and no faster: a grey wall of cold, always at the very edge of the gold. Behind the Hollows, Wren could see the Knights now. Grey armour, grey faces, empty eyes, marching in step. And at their head, walking easily, his grey cloak swinging, came a tall pale man who was not hurrying at all.

They came out onto the ledge at the edge of the Cleft.

Tobin had done well. Wren saw that at once, with a quick hot rush of pride. He had them lined up along the ledge, the Delvers, each one holding the sleeve of the one in front, and he was standing at the head of the bridge, his spectacles crooked, calling softly — “Left hand on the rail. Good. Next step. Mind the gap, it’s wider, that’s it” — and they were going over, one by one, and on the far side Mother Hessa was gathering them in at the foot of the Black Stair. Dozens were across. But there were so many still waiting. And not one of them had started up the Stair.

Wren backed up until she stood beside Old Ash’s sledge, in front of all of them, with the lamp held up. Mira stood on one side of her, and Cinder on the other. Behind her, Gorrim set his son down gently on the stones.

Captain Varrick stepped out of the mouth of the Galleries, and stopped, just at the edge of the light, and smiled at her.

He had not changed since the night of the Beacon. Tall, pale, grey-eyed, in grey armour that made no noise, with a grey cloak hanging from his shoulders. His Knights stood behind him in the tunnel-mouth like a row of grey statues. The Hollows hung behind them in the dark. Varrick drew off his gloves, one finger at a time, and Wren saw him rub his thumb, without seeming to notice, across the palm of his right hand.

“Good evening, Wren Ashby,” he said. “You have led me a long way. Across the Waste. Through the mothwings. Down a hole in the world.” He looked round at the ledge, at the crowding Delvers, at the swaying bridge, with polite interest. “And here you are, holding the door for the very people who meant to drop you down a well. I confess I find that hard to understand.”

“Nobody asked you to understand it,” said Wren.

“Quite right.” He inclined his head. “Let me be plain, as I was before. I can’t take your lamp. You know that. It must be given. I am not here to take anything. I am here to make an offer.”

“I’ve heard your offers.”

“Not this one.” He nodded towards the bridge, and the Delvers feeling their way across it, and the dark mouth of the Stair beyond. “A thousand steps. In the dark. The old ones. The little ones. And my Hollows, I should tell you, do not tire, and do not make a sound. These people find their way by echoes. They will never hear them coming.” He let that sit a moment. “Or. You could give me the lamp. And I will take my Knights back up the way I came, and my Hollows with them, and not one more voice in Deepholm will stop. You have my word.”

He smiled at her, quite kindly.

“Give me the lamp, child, and I leave them their songs.”

The ledge was silent. Even the crying child had stopped. Wren felt every blind face on the ledge turn towards her, listening. She felt Mira’s hand find her sleeve and hold on.

And the worst of it — I must tell you this, because it is true — was that a part of her wanted to. Not for herself. For Tavi, lying on the stones. For the old woman who had held out her hands and said warm. Just hand it over, said a voice in her that sounded almost kind. Just once, give it up, and let it be over, and let them sing.

Then there was a scraping sound behind her.

Old Ash was getting up.

He did it the slow, dreadful way, with his pole planted on the stones and both hands on it, hauling himself up off the sledge onto his one good leg. His face was the colour of ash. Tobin started forward to help, and Ash waved him off without looking. He stood, at last, swaying, leaning on the brass-hooked pole, very tall in the gold light, his singed white beard on his chest. He looked across the ledge at Captain Varrick.

“Lad,” he said.

Only that.

And Varrick went still.

It lasted one heartbeat. Wren saw it, and she was always sure afterwards that she had seen it, just as she had on the top of the Beacon. His left hand had closed over his right palm, over the old scar, and was holding it. And his grey eyes, looking at the old man leaning on his pole, were not quite grey.

“You used to sing the night-song on the wall,” said Old Ash, low. “Louder than any of us. Out of tune, every time.” He drew a breath. “Do you remember the words, lad? Because I do.”

Varrick’s hand fell from his palm.

“That was somebody else, old man,” he said. His voice was as smooth as ever, but it had come a moment late. “You buried him a long time ago.”

“No,” said Old Ash. “I never did. I’ve been waiting.”

For an instant something moved in Varrick’s face, and was gone. Then he turned his back on the old man, as if he had not spoken, and looked at Wren again, and his voice was oiled iron.

“I am a patient man,” he said. “I will wait, as well. My Knights will hold this ledge. Your bridge is narrow and your Stair is long, and the old man cannot climb a single step of it. Think it over, Wren Ashby. When you are ready to be sensible, I shall be here.”

He stepped back into the mouth of the Galleries. The Knights closed in front of him, shoulder to shoulder, grey and silent. And beyond them, at the very edge of the light, the cold came creeping, and waited.

Wren stood on the ledge with the lamp in her hands.

She looked at the bridge, swaying, with its long, slow line of blind Delvers feeling their way across. She looked at the Black Stair beyond it — a thousand steps in total dark, where the Hollows would come without a sound, and nobody who climbed it would ever hear them. Whoever went up those stairs would need the light. And whoever stayed on this ledge, with the Knights at the tunnel-mouth and Old Ash who could not climb, would need it too.

There was only one lamp. And there was only one of her.

Slowly, without wanting to, she turned her head; and she looked at Tobin.
