Captain Varrick stepped out of the mouth of the Galleries, and stopped, just at the edge of the light, and smiled at her. “Give me the lamp, child, and I leave them their songs.” He had not changed since the night of the Beacon. Tall, pale, grey-eyed, in grey armour that made no noise, with a grey cloak hanging from his shoulders. His Knights stood behind him in the tunnel-mouth like a row of grey statues. The Hollows hung behind them in the dark. Varrick drew off his gloves, one finger at a time, and Wren saw him rub his thumb, without seeming to notice, across the palm of his right hand. “Good evening, Wren Ashby,” he said. “You have led me a long way. Across the Waste. Through the mothwings. Down a hole in the world.” He looked round at the ledge, at the crowding Delvers, at the swaying bridge, with polite interest. “And here you are, holding the door for the very people who meant to drop you down a well. I confess I find that hard to understand.” “Nobody asked you to understand it,” said Wren. “Quite right.” He inclined his head. “Let me be plain, as I was before. I can’t take your lamp. You know that. It must be given. I am not here to take anything. I am here to make an offer.” “I’ve heard your offers.” “Not this one.” He nodded towards the bridge, and the Delvers feeling their way across it, and the dark mouth of the Stair beyond. “A thousand steps. In the dark. The old ones. The little ones. And my Hollows, I should tell you, do not tire, and do not make a sound. These people find their way by echoes. They will never hear them coming.” He let that sit a moment. “Or. You could give me the lamp. And I will take my Knights back up the way I came, and my Hollows with them, and not one more voice in Deepholm will stop. You have my word.” He smiled at her, quite kindly. “Give me the lamp, child, and I leave them their songs.” The ledge was silent. Even the crying child had stopped. Wren felt every blind face on the ledge turn towards her, listening. She felt Mira’s hand find her sleeve and hold on. And the worst of it — I must tell you this, because it is true — was that a part of her wanted to. Not for herself. For Tavi, lying on the stones. For the old woman who had held out her hands and said warm. Just hand it over, said a voice in her that sounded almost kind. Just once, give it up, and let it be over, and let them sing. Then there was a scraping sound behind her. Old Ash was getting up. He did it the slow, dreadful way, with his pole planted on the stones and both hands on it, hauling himself up off the sledge onto his one good leg. His face was the colour of ash. Tobin started forward to help, and Ash waved him off without looking. He stood, at last, swaying, leaning on the brass-hooked pole, very tall in the gold light, his singed white beard on his chest. He looked across the ledge at Captain Varrick. “Lad,” he said. Only that. And Varrick went still. It lasted one heartbeat. Wren saw it, and she was always sure afterwards that she had seen it, just as she had on the top of the Beacon. His left hand had closed over his right palm, over the old scar, and was holding it. And his grey eyes, looking at the old man leaning on his pole, were not quite grey. “You used to sing the night-song on the wall,” said Old Ash, low. “Louder than any of us. Out of tune, every time.” He drew a breath. “Do you remember the words, lad? Because I do.” Varrick’s hand fell from his palm. “That was somebody else, old man,” he said. His voice was as smooth as ever, but it had come a moment late. “You buried him a long time ago.” “No,” said Old Ash. “I never did. I’ve been waiting.” For an instant something moved in Varrick’s face, and was gone. Then he turned his back on the old man, as if he had not spoken, and looked at Wren again, and his voice was oiled iron. “I am a patient man,” he said. “I will wait, as well. My Knights will hold this ledge. Your bridge is narrow and your Stair is long, and the old man cannot climb a single step of it. Think it over, Wren Ashby. When you are ready to be sensible, I shall be here.” He stepped back into the mouth of the Galleries. The Knights closed in front of him, shoulder to shoulder, grey and silent. And beyond them, at the very edge of the light, the cold came creeping, and waited. Wren stood on the ledge with the lamp in her hands. She looked at the bridge, swaying, with its long, slow line of blind Delvers feeling their way across. She looked at the Black Stair beyond it — a thousand steps in total dark, where the Hollows would come without a sound, and nobody who climbed it would ever hear them. Whoever went up those stairs would need the light. And whoever stayed on this ledge, with the Knights at the tunnel-mouth and Old Ash who could not climb, would need it too. There was only one lamp. And there was only one of her. Slowly, without wanting to, she turned her head; and she looked at Tobin.

fields.title: The Black Stair
fields.body_html:
The Delvers had a name for the place at the bottom of the Stair, and Mira had told it to Wren as they ran back and forth through the Galleries. In the old Delver tongue it was one long humming word, and it meant where the songs stop.

Wren had thought that a horrible name. Now, standing on the ledge with Varrick’s Knights at her back, she understood it.

It was a cavern so tall that the lamplight never found the roof, and across the middle of it ran a crack in the world. The floor simply ended in a ragged lip of stone, and beyond the lip there was nothing — no bottom, no sound, only a cold breath coming up out of the deep as if something very large were asleep down there. Over the crack hung a Delver bridge of plaited rope as thick as Wren’s arm, with slats of pale stone threaded on it like beads. It was so narrow that two people could not have passed on it without one climbing over the other. On the far side, cut into the rock, was a doorway. And through the doorway, going up and round into a blackness so complete that the lamplight seemed to stop at the edge of it, was the first of a thousand steps.

Behind them, Deepholm was going quiet.

That was the worst thing, worse than the cold. Wren had never once heard the city of the Delvers silent. Now, far back along the tunnels, the sounds were going out one by one, the way lamps go out along a wall. A song would be running, and then it would stop in the middle. A child would be crying, and then it would not be.

“They are all still there,” said Mira. She had her head tipped towards the Galleries, her pale face perfectly still. “Hollows at the back. Then men in iron. Then him.” She did not say Varrick’s name. None of the Delvers would.

The ledge was still crowded with Delvers, hundreds upon hundreds of them, pale and frightened, carrying their children and their old people and their bundles, and all of them clicking at once, so that the vast cave rattled like rain on a slate roof. Those who had crossed had stopped at the foot of the Stair, and those still waiting had stopped at the lip of the crack.

None of them would go up.

“Why won’t they go?” said Wren. “It’s right there!”

“It is not the bridge they fear,” said a deep, slow voice behind her. “It is what is at the end of it.”

Speaker Gorrim stood at the edge of the crowd. Only that morning he had called them liars in the Hall of Answers. Now his fine grey robe was torn at the hem, and in his arms, wrapped in a blanket, he held his son. Tavi’s eyes were open. He was looking at nothing. His round face was the colour of old candle-wax.

“No Delver has climbed the Black Stair in three hundred years,” said Gorrim. “The stone of it is broken. There are gaps where the steps have fallen, and holes in the wall that go nowhere, and in the stair the echoes lie. Listen to my people. When one Delver clicks, he hears the world. When four hundred click at once, they hear only each other. On that stair we would be blinder than you.”

“A thousand clicks is no clicks at all,” said Mira quietly. “It’s a Delver saying. I always thought it was a silly one.”

Wren looked up at the black doorway. Then she looked down at the lamp in her hands, and she knew — the way you know you are going to be sick a moment before you are — exactly what was going to have to happen. And she did not want to know it at all.

Four Delver stone-carriers had lifted Old Ash off the sledge into a sling-chair made of rope and a door, and they had set him down on a flat rock near the bridge. His bad leg was splinted from ankle to hip. He could not have climbed ten steps on it, let alone a thousand, and he was more cross about it than Wren had ever seen him.

“Hm,” he said, when she knelt beside him. He did not ask what she was thinking. He never needed to.

“The stair needs a light at the front,” said Wren, in a rush. “Somebody who can see the gaps and shout back. The Delvers can’t see the lamp, but Mira says they can feel the warm on their faces. So if the warm goes up first, they’ll follow it.”

“Yes,” said Ash.

“And somebody has to stop the Knights crossing the bridge behind them, or they’ll catch everybody halfway, on the broken bits. And whoever stops them has to be somebody who doesn’t mind the dark, because there won’t be any light down here once the lamp’s gone up.” She swallowed. “I’ve been in the dark all my life. Chimneys are dark. I’m good in the dark. Mira’s better. And Cinder doesn’t care about anything.”

At her feet, Cinder sneezed a small shower of sparks, as if to agree.

“So it’s us down here,” said Wren. She did not look round, but she knew where Tobin was. He was standing three paces behind her, and she could hear his breathing. “And the lamp goes up. With him.”

“Me,” said Tobin. His voice cracked straight down the middle.

“It’s simple arithmetic,” said Wren. “You said that once, on the Beacon stair. You’re no good in the dark. I am. So I hold the bridge, and you carry the light. It’s the only sum that comes out.”

“Wren, I froze,” said Tobin. “In the stream-bed. You saw me. Ash got hurt because I stood there like a — like a hat-stand — and you said—“

“I know what I said.”

She had said a great many things in the stream-bed, with Ash lying on the stones and the Hollows drifting away into the dusk. She had called him a nob’s boy with a bag full of spanners, who should have stopped at home with his father. She had said it to hurt, and it had, and she had been glad. She was not glad now.

“You can carry it for me,” she said. “Just up the stair. Just till I get there. Then you give it back, and—“

“Child,” said Old Ash.

Wren stopped.

He laid one long cold hand over hers, over the lamp. His eyes, under their white brows, were very kind and very sorry.

“You know its law,” he said. “It will not burn for a borrower. It is not a coat, to be lent for an evening and asked back at the door. If the lad carries it for you, he carries a cold lump of brass up a black stair. If you want it to burn for him, you must give it to him. Truly. With nothing held back and nothing asked.”

“And then it’s his,” said Wren.

“And then it’s his.”

“And it doesn’t come back to me. Not unless he wants to give it.”

“Hm,” said Ash, very gently. “No. It does not.”

This is the part of the story, I think, that Wren found hardest to tell afterwards. Not the bridge, and not the dark, and not the Knights. This.

You may think it ought to have been easy. After all, she had given the Flame away once before, at the top of the Great Beacon, and it had cost her nothing. But that had been the Flame. She had poured it into a bowl and kept the lamp. This was the lamp itself — the dented brass, the little hook on top, the crack in the chimney she knew better than the lines on her own palm. It was the first thing in her life that had ever been given to her. It had come back to her out of the canal and out of the tannery mud. It had lit Nettle’s freckles back into her face. It was the only thing she had ever owned that nobody could take off her.

And nobody was taking it off her. That was the whole trouble. She had to hand it over, freely, to a boy who had frozen in a stream-bed — and then go and stand on a bridge in the pitch dark without it, and trust him to climb all the way and not drop it, and not run, and not decide at the top that it was his now and he would rather keep it. Which was what anybody would decide. Which was what she would have decided, once.

Everybody always takes everything in the end. The old feeling came up in her, the oldest one she had.

And then, right behind it, another feeling, quieter, that she had not had for very long at all. What is given, grows.

From the tunnels, close now, came a long sigh of cold air, and somewhere a singing-stone stopped humming in the middle of its note.

Wren stood up and turned round.

Tobin was as white as paper.

“I’ll drop it,” he said. “I really might. I’ll get halfway and freeze again, with four hundred people behind me in the dark, and—“

“Hold out your hands, you great lump,” said Wren.

He held them out.

She put the lamp into them. Then — because it was not done yet, because she could feel her own fingers still curled round the brass as if they had a mind of their own — she made herself let go. One finger. Then the next. Then all of them.

“It’s yours,” she said hoarsely. “Not lent. Not for me. Yours. I’m not asking for it back.” And she said the words that she had said to Nettle and Mrs Fenn and Gristle Mott. “Here. It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

For one dreadful moment the flame shrank down to a little blue bead, as if it were thinking about going out. Wren’s heart stopped. It’s not enough, she thought. I’m still holding on, inside, and it knows.

Then the lamp blazed.

It went up in Tobin’s hands like a struck match, white-gold and roaring-bright, brighter than Wren had ever seen it in her own. The light leapt across the cavern and found, far overhead, a roof of hanging stone like a forest upside down. It washed over the crowd on the cliff-edge, and four hundred pale faces turned towards it at once — not because they could see it, but because they could feel it, warm on their cheeks, like the breath of an oven door. A soft, astonished murmur went through them, all the way to the back.

Tobin stared down at the lamp, with the light in his spectacles and his mouth open.

“It’s warm,” he whispered. “Wren. It’s warm.”

“Course it is,” said Wren roughly. “It’s yours.” She turned away fast, before anyone could see her face. “Now go on. Before I change my mind.”

They did it the Delver way, because there was no other.

The longest rope in Deepholm was a hand-line for lowering stone into the deep quarries, so long that six men had to carry the coil. They paid it out over the bridge and up into the doorway, and every Delver who could walk took hold of it with one hand. Tobin went first, with the end of the rope knotted round his waist and the lamp held up before him. Behind him came Speaker Gorrim with Tavi tied on his back in the blanket, the boy’s grey head lolling on his father’s shoulder. Then the stone-carriers with Old Ash in his sling-chair, and Mother Hessa scolding them to mind his leg. And behind them, the whole of Deepholm, a long pale river of people flowing over the bridge one at a time and up into the dark.

Wren stood at the far end of the bridge, beside the doorway, with Mira and Cinder, and watched the light go.

She saw it through the doorway, swinging and climbing round the first curve of the wall above her. Then she saw only the glow of it on the stone. Then the glow faded, and the Delvers on the bridge became shadows, and then only sounds.

And then there was no light at all.

Wren looked down at her wrist, out of habit. She could not see her ribbon. She could not see her hand. She knew without seeing it that her mother’s ribbon was grey again, the colour of dishwater and dust.

“You are breathing like someone who has run a long way,” said Mira softly, out of the dark.

“I’m fine.”

“You are not fine.” A hand found her sleeve, cool and very sure. “That was the bravest thing I have ever heard. I could hear your heart doing it.”

“Shut up,” said Wren. But she did not pull her sleeve away.

Tobin was counting.

“Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen.”

The Black Stair felt as if it had been built by someone who wanted to be left alone. It wound round a central pillar of rough black rock, and the steps were narrow and uneven, some as high as his knee and some so shallow he stumbled on them. The lamp made a little golden room around him, six steps up and six steps down, and beyond that the dark simply stood there, waiting, like water outside the glass of a diving-bell.

He felt the rope at his waist tighten and slacken. Every pull was a person.

“You are shaking, boy,” said Speaker Gorrim, just below him. “The rope tells me.”

“Yes. Sorry. Technically it’s an involuntary response of the—“ Tobin stopped. “Yes. I’m shaking.”

“So am I,” said Gorrim, after a moment. “Climb anyway.”

At the forty-first step there was a gap. Three steps had broken away into the black, and on the far side the stair went on as if nothing had happened.

“Gap!” called Tobin, and the shaft threw his voice back at him from every direction at once. “A long step! Keep to the wall side!”

The message went down the rope behind him in a ripple of soft clicks and murmurs, passed from mouth to mouth into the dark. Then Gorrim’s hand closed on his shoulder. “Show me with the warm,” he said. “Hold it where I must put my foot.”

Tobin held the lamp low over the far side. He felt Gorrim lean, and stretch, and step — the big man and the grey boy on his back — and land. Then he stood holding the light out over the hole for what felt like an hour, while the Delvers came across one by one, following the warmth on their faces to the place where the stone was. And not one of them fell.

By two hundred his legs were burning. By two hundred and fifty his voice was a croak from calling gap and loose step back down the line.

It was at two hundred and ninety-four that the draught came.

He felt it first on the back of his neck — a breath of cold coming up the shaft from far below. Not the ordinary cold of stone. The other cold. The cold that came with Hollows. It flowed up the stair, and Tobin heard the Delvers gasp, one after another, all the way up the line, and then it reached him.

And the lamp dipped.

Only a little. It leaned over in the draught, and shrank, and spat — and for one terrible moment Tobin was not on the Black Stair at all. He was on the thirtieth step under his father’s Hall, with his mother’s night-lamp hissing out in his hand and the whole world going black.

He stopped dead. His feet would not go up. The golden room around him seemed to shrink to three steps, and then two, and the dark leaned in.

It’s going to go out, said the frightened voice inside him, and it was not small any more; it was enormous. It was never meant for you. It was Wren’s. You’ll freeze, just like the stream-bed, just like always, and they’ll all—

“I can’t,” Tobin whispered. “I’m sorry. Somebody else should — I should give it to somebody else—“

“There is nobody else,” said Gorrim. His voice was not unkind. It was only very tired, and very certain. “There is a girl on the bridge in the dark, who gave you the warm. There is my son on my back. There are four hundred people holding a rope that is tied to you. You are the one with the warm, boy.”

Tobin shut his eyes. It made no difference to the dark. It never did.

And into his head, without his asking, came the Greywaste: the first night out of Emberwick, with the grey grass hissing and Old Ash saying the Lamplighters’ Psalm into the fire in his slow dry voice — and underneath Ash’s voice, years and years away, his mother’s, saying the very same words at his bedside. That night he had only been able to remember the first line. He had whispered it over and over to his little night-lamp until his hands stopped shaking.

He opened his mouth. His voice came out a croak.

“Though I walk through the gloaming,” said Tobin Harrowgate, “I will fear no dark—“

He put his foot on the next step.

“for the Flame is with me. It goes before me on the road; it keeps the watch while I am sleeping.”

And the next.

The rest came back to him then, all of it, as if someone had put it into his hand. “The night is long, but it is not for ever. My light was lit by another’s hand, and no dark can take it from me. So I will walk in the Flame’s keeping, all my days, until morning comes.”

There was a pause. Then Gorrim’s deep slow voice said the words back to him, stumbling, the way you say words in a language not your own. And behind Gorrim, Mother Hessa said them, and behind Hessa the stone-carriers, and the words went down the rope just as the clicks had done, down and down the Black Stair into the dark, until the whole shaft was full of four hundred voices murmuring, like the sea heard from a long way off.

I will fear no dark, for the Flame is with me.

The lamp stood up straight in the draught. It stopped spitting. It burned.

Tobin climbed.

And there was something else, though he never told anyone about it but Wren, much later, and he went red when he did. A little way above the gap in the wall, he became aware that he was not cold any more. Not the front of him, where the lamp was — that was always warm. The back of him: his shoulders, and the back of his neck, where the Hollow-draught had touched. It was as if someone were climbing just behind him, between him and Gorrim, close enough to touch. Someone very tall, who was not in the least out of breath. Someone warm.

He did not look round. He knew that if he looked there would be nobody there.

But his hands, he noticed, had stopped shaking.

“Two hundred and ninety-nine,” he said aloud, and his voice was steadier. “Three hundred. Three hundred and one.”

And from far, far below — so far that it came up the shaft as the ghost of a sound — he heard the groan of thick rope taking a heavy weight, and a clang of iron on stone, and a girl’s voice, in a dark with no light in it at all, shouting.

Then — because it was not done yet, because she could feel her own fingers still curled round the brass as if they had a mind of their own — she made herself let go. One finger. Then the next. Then all of them. “It’s yours,” she said hoarsely. “Not lent. Not for me. Yours. I’m not asking for it back.” And she said the words that she had said to Nettle and Mrs Fenn and Gristle Mott. “Here. It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.” For one dreadful moment the flame shrank down to a little blue bead, as if it were thinking about going out. Wren’s heart stopped. It’s not enough, she thought. I’m still holding on, inside, and it knows. Then the lamp blazed. It went up in Tobin’s hands like a struck match, white-gold and roaring-bright, brighter than Wren had ever seen it in her own. The light leapt across the cavern and found, far overhead, a roof of hanging stone like a forest upside down. It washed over the crowd on the cliff-edge, and four hundred pale faces turned towards it at once — not because they could see it, but because they could feel it, warm on their cheeks, like the breath of an oven door. A soft, astonished murmur went through them, all the way to the back. Tobin stared down at the lamp, with the light in his spectacles and his mouth open. “It’s warm,” he whispered. “Wren. It’s warm.” “Course it is,” said Wren roughly. “It’s yours.” She turned away fast, before anyone could see her face. “Now go on. Before I change my mind.” They did it the Delver way, because there was no other. The longest rope in Deepholm was a hand-line for lowering stone into the deep quarries, so long that six men had to carry the coil. They paid it out over the bridge and up into the doorway, and every Delver who could walk took hold of it with one hand. Tobin went first, with the end of the rope knotted round his waist and the lamp held up before him. Behind him came Speaker Gorrim with Tavi tied on his back in the blanket, the boy’s grey head lolling on his father’s shoulder. Then the stone-carriers with Old Ash in his sling-chair, and Mother Hessa scolding them to mind his leg. And behind them, the whole of Deepholm, a long pale river of people flowing over the bridge one at a time and up into the dark. Wren stood at the far end of the bridge, beside the doorway, with Mira and Cinder, and watched the light go. She saw it through the doorway, swinging and climbing round the first curve of the wall above her. Then she saw only the glow of it on the stone. Then the glow faded, and the Delvers on the bridge became shadows, and then only sounds. And then there was no light at all. Wren looked down at her wrist, out of habit. She could not see her ribbon. She could not see her hand. She knew without seeing it that her mother’s ribbon was grey again, the colour of dishwater and dust. “You are breathing like someone who has run a long way,” said Mira softly, out of the dark. “I’m fine.” “You are not fine.” A hand found her sleeve, cool and very sure. “That was the bravest thing I have ever heard. I could hear your heart doing it.” “Shut up,” said Wren. But she did not pull her sleeve away. Tobin was counting. “Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen.” The Black Stair felt as if it had been built by someone who wanted to be left alone. It wound round a central pillar of rough black rock, and the steps were narrow and uneven, some as high as his knee and some so shallow he stumbled on them. The lamp made a little golden room around him, six steps up and six steps down, and beyond that the dark simply stood there, waiting, like water outside the glass of a diving-bell. He felt the rope at his waist tighten and slacken. Every pull was a person. “You are shaking, boy,” said Speaker Gorrim, just below him. “The rope tells me.” “Yes. Sorry. Technically it’s an involuntary response of the—“ Tobin stopped. “Yes. I’m shaking.” “So am I,” said Gorrim, after a moment. “Climb anyway.” At the forty-first step there was a gap. Three steps had broken away into the black, and on the far side the stair went on as if nothing had happened. “Gap!” called Tobin, and the shaft threw his voice back at him from every direction at once. “A long step! Keep to the wall side!” The message went down the rope behind him in a ripple of soft clicks and murmurs, passed from mouth to mouth into the dark. Then Gorrim’s hand closed on his shoulder. “Show me with the warm,” he said. “Hold it where I must put my foot.” Tobin held the lamp low over the far side. He felt Gorrim lean, and stretch, and step — the big man and the grey boy on his back — and land. Then he stood holding the light out over the hole for what felt like an hour, while the Delvers came across one by one, following the warmth on their faces to the place where the stone was. And not one of them fell. By two hundred his legs were burning. By two hundred and fifty his voice was a croak from calling gap and loose step back down the line. It was at two hundred and ninety-four that the draught came. He felt it first on the back of his neck — a breath of cold coming up the shaft from far below. Not the ordinary cold of stone. The other cold. The cold that came with Hollows. It flowed up the stair, and Tobin heard the Delvers gasp, one after another, all the way up the line, and then it reached him. And the lamp dipped. Only a little. It leaned over in the draught, and shrank, and spat — and for one terrible moment Tobin was not on the Black Stair at all. He was on the thirtieth step under his father’s Hall, with his mother’s night-lamp hissing out in his hand and the whole world going black. He stopped dead. His feet would not go up. The golden room around him seemed to shrink to three steps, and then two, and the dark leaned in. It’s going to go out, said the frightened voice inside him, and it was not small any more; it was enormous. It was never meant for you. It was Wren’s. You’ll freeze, just like the stream-bed, just like always, and they’ll all— “I can’t,” Tobin whispered. “I’m sorry. Somebody else should — I should give it to somebody else—“ “There is nobody else,” said Gorrim. His voice was not unkind. It was only very tired, and very certain. “There is a girl on the bridge in the dark, who gave you the warm. There is my son on my back. There are four hundred people holding a rope that is tied to you. You are the one with the warm, boy.” Tobin shut his eyes. It made no difference to the dark. It never did. And into his head, without his asking, came the Greywaste: the first night out of Emberwick, with the grey grass hissing and Old Ash saying the Lamplighters’ Psalm into the fire in his slow dry voice — and underneath Ash’s voice, years and years away, his mother’s, saying the very same words at his bedside. That night he had only been able to remember the first line. He had whispered it over and over to his little night-lamp until his hands stopped shaking. He opened his mouth. His voice came out a croak. “Though I walk through the gloaming,” said Tobin Harrowgate, “I will fear no dark—“ He put his foot on the next step. “for the Flame is with me. It goes before me on the road; it keeps the watch while I am sleeping.” And the next. The rest came back to him then, all of it, as if someone had put it into his hand. “The night is long, but it is not for ever. My light was lit by another’s hand, and no dark can take it from me. So I will walk in the Flame’s keeping, all my days, until morning comes.” There was a pause. Then Gorrim’s deep slow voice said the words back to him, stumbling, the way you say words in a language not your own. And behind Gorrim, Mother Hessa said them, and behind Hessa the stone-carriers, and the words went down the rope just as the clicks had done, down and down the Black Stair into the dark, until the whole shaft was full of four hundred voices murmuring, like the sea heard from a long way off. I will fear no dark, for the Flame is with me. The lamp stood up straight in the draught. It stopped spitting. It burned. “Though I walk through the gloaming,” said Tobin Harrowgate, “I will fear no dark—” Tobin climbed. And there was something else, though he never told anyone about it but Wren, much later, and he went red when he did. A little way above the gap in the wall, he became aware that he was not cold any more. Not the front of him, where the lamp was — that was always warm. The back of him: his shoulders, and the back of his neck, where the Hollow-draught had touched. It was as if someone were climbing just behind him, between him and Gorrim, close enough to touch. Someone very tall, who was not in the least out of breath. Someone warm. He did not look round. He knew that if he looked there would be nobody there. But his hands, he noticed, had stopped shaking. “Two hundred and ninety-nine,” he said aloud, and his voice was steadier. “Three hundred. Three hundred and one.” And from far, far below — so far that it came up the shaft as the ghost of a sound — he heard the groan of thick rope taking a heavy weight, and a clang of iron on stone, and a girl’s voice, in a dark with no light in it at all, shouting.

fields.title: Light in the Low Places
fields.body_html:
In all the world there was only one light left at the bottom of the Black Stair, and it was on the end of a fox’s tail.

Cinder stood in the doorway with her legs braced and her ears flat, and the spark at the tip of her tail burned so fiercely that it lit her own grey muzzle and her bared white teeth and nothing else at all. Beyond her, out in the cavern, the cold was gathering. Wren could not see the Hollows. She did not need to. She could feel them the way you feel the sea when you stand at the edge of it at night — a great grey weight of nothing, leaning in.

They did not come past the fox. Not yet.

“The last of my people have gone up,” said Mira, close beside her. “I counted their feet. There were four hundred and twelve, and old Bettle with his stick, which I counted as one and a half.” Then her voice changed. “And now there are others on the bridge.”

Wren gripped the pole in her hands. It was a Delver bridge-pole, long and smooth, with a hook of worn bronze on the end for catching loose ropes, and it was not so very different from a sweep’s brush. She had been poking things with long sticks since she was five years old.

“Where?” she whispered.

Mira clicked. It was a tiny sound, no louder than a fingernail on a cup, and it went out across the chasm and came back to her changed.

“Two men in iron. The first is eleven slats out, coming slowly, holding both hand-ropes. The second is four behind him. They cannot see either, Wren. They are feeling their way, like you.”

“Not like me,” said Wren. “I’m a sweep.”

She crept out onto the first slat of the bridge and crouched there. The whole thing swayed under her like a hammock. Below was a black so deep it had a smell. She heard it now herself — the creak of the ropes, the slow chink of armour, the scrape of an iron boot on stone.

“Seven slats,” breathed Mira. “Five. He is reaching forward with his right hand. Now, Wren — low, by the left rope—“

Wren swung.

The bronze hook struck something that rang like a pot-lid, and a hand let go of a rope. The bridge lurched wildly. In the dark a man grunted — the first sound she had ever heard a Hollow Knight make — and there was a long scrabbling as he caught hold again.

“Back three slats,” said Mira. “He is holding on with both hands now, and not moving. He does not like this bridge.”

“Nobody likes this bridge,” said Wren. Her heart was hammering. She was grinning in the dark like a lunatic.

I should say here, in case you are worried, that nobody fell into the chasm that night. Wren saw to that. She had made up her mind about it before the first Knight ever set foot on the slats, and I think it was one of the best things she ever decided.

What followed was the strangest fight she was ever in. She never once saw her enemy. She crouched on the swaying slats with her pole, and Mira knelt at the bridge-post behind her with one hand on Wren’s ankle, clicking, and told her everything. Left rope. Low. He is lifting his foot. Two of them now, close together. Leave the first; the second is the one reaching. And Wren poked, and hooked, and rapped iron knuckles, and set the bridge swinging under them until the Knights clung to the ropes and could not go forward. And behind her in the doorway Cinder blazed and snarled, and the great grey cold leaned in and leaned in, and did not come past.

They could not have held it alone, any of them. Wren could not see. Mira could not fight. Cinder could not do both. But all three together, in the dark, at the bottom of the world, they held the bridge.

Then, across the chasm, someone began clapping. Slowly.

“Very good,” said a voice. Smooth as oiled iron. “Very good indeed, Wren Ashby.”

Wren’s mouth went dry.

“You gave it away,” said Captain Varrick. He was on the far lip, she thought, by the sound. He was not shouting. He had no need to; the cavern carried his voice to her as if he were standing at her shoulder. “I felt it go up the stair. Do you know, I almost did not believe it. The only thing you ever had. Given to a boy who freezes. And here you are, in the pitch dark, with a blind girl and a fox, holding a bridge for people who were going to throw you into a pit.” He paused. “I wonder what you think you will get for it.”

“Nothing,” said Wren. “That’s the point, you great lump.”

“Hm,” said Varrick — and for one horrible instant he sounded exactly like Old Ash, as if he had caught the habit long ago and never quite shaken it. “My men do not tire, child. You do. In an hour, or two, your arms will give out. And then I will come across, and you will be very cold, and very far down, and nobody will be coming back for you. They never do. You know that better than anyone.”

Wren said nothing. Her arms were already aching. She hated that he knew it.

Mira’s fingers tightened on her ankle. Then Mira leaned close, and her breath was warm on Wren’s ear.

“Every Delver bridge,” she whispered, “has a warden’s knot. On this side. On the post by my hand. It is for floods — if the river comes down the cleft, the wardens pull the pin and let the bridge go, so it does not pull the posts out of the rock. My grandmother showed me when I was little. I can feel it now. One pull, Wren. And then there is no bridge.”

Wren’s heart jumped. “And no way back,” she whispered.

“There is no back,” said Mira simply. “There is only up.”

“There’s Knights on it.”

“Yes.”

“Then we don’t pull it.” Wren set her jaw. “Not with anyone on it. I don’t care who they are. I’m not doing that.”

Mira was quiet for a heartbeat. Then her hand found Wren’s in the dark and squeezed it, very hard, and Wren understood that she had said the right thing.

“Then we must make them go back,” said Mira. “All of them. And I will listen for the last foot.”

Wren looked at the only light there was. “Cinder,” she said. “Can you run a rope?”

The ember-fox looked round at her, and the spark on her tail flared like a coal under a bellows.

She went out along the hand-rope like a squirrel along a washing line, and as she ran her spark blazed brighter and brighter, until for a moment Wren could actually see: the long bridge sagging across the black, the pale stone slats, and three grey figures in grey armour clinging to the ropes with grey, empty faces turned towards a little burning fox. Cinder sneezed. A shower of sparks went over the first Knight’s helmet.

The Hollow Knights could stand the dark. They could stand the cold. I do not think, in all the years since they had been hollowed, that any of them had had a fox sneeze fire on them. They went backwards along the bridge in a clattering hurry, all three of them, and Cinder came trotting back along the rope with her tail held high, looking very pleased with herself.

“Listening,” whispered Mira. Her head was tipped to one side. “Three on the slats. Two. One. He is stepping off. He is off.” Her voice went tight. “The bridge is empty, Wren.”

Wren put both hands round the pin. It was cold bronze, as long as her forearm.

“Varrick!” she shouted. “Keep your men back! I’m letting it go!”

There was a silence on the far side of the chasm. Then, very quietly, Varrick said, “Stand back from the ropes.” And iron feet shuffled away from the edge.

Wren pulled.

The pin came out with a squeal. Something went crack inside the post, and the hand-ropes leapt out of her reach like living things, and the whole bridge — every rope and every pale stone slat — swung away from her into the dark. She heard it go. It hissed down the face of the far cliff, a long, long whispering, and then the whispering went on, fainter and fainter, and then there was nothing. No crash. No splash. Only the cold breath coming up, the same as before.

Nobody said anything for a long time.

“Well,” said Varrick at last, from the far side. His voice had changed. It sounded, for the first time, a little tired. “There is more than one road to the top of the world, Wren Ashby. I will finish this somewhere else.”

His footsteps went away, back into the silent tunnels of Deepholm. And as they went, the great grey cold went with them, slowly, like a tide going out, until the air at the bottom of the Black Stair was only the ordinary cold of stone.

Wren sat down on the floor, very suddenly, because her legs had stopped working.

Up above, the lamp was getting brighter.

Tobin noticed it first at about the four-hundredth step, and thought he was imagining it. By the five-hundredth he was sure. It was no longer a little golden room around him, six steps up and six steps down. It was ten steps. Then twelve. By the six-hundredth he could see the curve of the wall going up ahead of him, and the curve going down behind, and Gorrim’s face — wet with sweat, set like stone — and the grey head on his shoulder.

He did not know why. He was only holding it. He had not done anything. He had climbed, that was all, one step and then the next, holding it up so that four hundred people could feel it on their faces. He had held it low over every gap. He had held it out to an old Delver woman who had sat down on the four hundred and twentieth step and said she could go no further, and she had felt the warm on her cheeks and got up again.

What is given, grows. He had written that in his notebook too. He had thought he understood it.

At some point, the cold draught from below stopped. It did not fade; it simply was not there, as if a door had been shut far underneath them. Tobin did not know what it meant. He hoped very much that he knew.

“Nine hundred and ninety-eight,” he croaked. “Nine hundred and ninety-nine.”

There was no thousandth step. There was a slab of stone overhead, flat and heavy, with a crack round its edge, and through the crack came a breath of air so different from the air of the stair that Tobin nearly sat down. It was cold — but it was a clean cold, a moving cold. It smelled of grass.

It took Gorrim and two of the stone-carriers, braced on the top steps with their shoulders under the slab, to move it. It went over with a great grinding thud. And above them there was no roof at all.

Tobin climbed out onto a rough hilltop among tumbled stones, with the grey grass of the Greywaste hissing all around, and he looked up.

There was a moon. It was pale, as the moon in Gloamhaven always was — a thin white coin behind thin cloud. But after a thousand steps in the dark, it was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen in his life. He stared at it while the Delvers came up out of the ground behind him, still holding the rope.

They did not look at the moon. They could not. But as each one came out into the open, they stopped, and lifted their faces, and clicked — and nothing came back. No roof. No walls. Only the wind, going on and on for ever. Some of them sat down and held on to the grass. One small girl began to cry, and her mother picked her up, and then began to cry as well, and then — this was the odd part — began to laugh.

Speaker Gorrim did not lift his face to the sky at all. He knelt down on the grass and untied the blanket from his shoulders, and laid his son in it, very gently, as if he were made of glass.

Tavi lay there, grey and still, staring at nothing.

Tobin knelt down on the other side of him. And then he did not know what to do.

He had seen Wren do this. He had seen her kneel on a bakery step in Soot Lane, and outside the sweep yard, and in a hundred doorways. But that had been Wren, with Wren’s lamp. He looked down at the little dented brass thing in his hands, burning white-gold, brighter now than he had ever seen it, and he heard her voice in his head: It’s yours. Not lent. Yours.

It was his. So it was his to give.

“Here,” said Tobin. His voice shook, so he started again. “Here. It’s for you, Tavi. You don’t have to do anything.”

He held out the lamp.

The flame leaned out of it towards the grey boy, the way a flower leans towards a window, and warmth spread over the grass. And the colour came back into Tavi as the dawn comes up over a hill — slowly, then all at once: the pale pink in his cheeks, the soft brown of his hair, a flush along his ears. He blinked. His hand moved on the blanket. His head turned — towards the warmth, not towards any light, for he had never seen a light in his life — and his face screwed up in deep puzzlement.

“Father?” he said. “Why is it warm? Where is the roof?”

Speaker Gorrim made a sound that Tobin had never heard a grown man make.

He gathered his son up off the grass, blanket and all, and held him against his chest and bowed his great grey head over him. His shoulders shook. He did not make any more sound, and he did not need to. The proud Speaker of the Delvers, who had called the lamp a lie and sent strangers to the Silent Pit, knelt on the hilltop under the pale moon with his boy in his arms and wept, and did not care who heard.

When at last he lifted his head, his wet face was turned towards Tobin — or towards the warmth in Tobin’s hands.

“The Delvers have a word for everything,” he said, in his deep slow voice, and it broke. “Nine words for the sound of water. Four for the quiet before a song. And I have no word for this.” He bent his head over his son again. “None at all.”

Tobin had no idea what to say to that, so he pushed his spectacles up his nose, and said, “There are some more. Greyed ones. Further down the line. I’d better—“ and went, before anyone could see that he was crying too.

Wren and Mira climbed the Black Stair together in the dark, and Cinder went in front.

With four hundred Delvers clicking, Mira had said, the stair was a din. With one, it was a map. Mira went first, with Wren’s hand on her shoulder, and every few steps she clicked once, softly, and listened, and said, “Gap. Long step. Wall side,” or “Loose stone. Step over,” exactly as if she could see it. Behind them, Cinder’s little spark bobbed, lighting nothing but itself.

“You’re showing off,” said Wren, at about the two-hundredth step.

“A little,” said Mira. She clicked. “Step.”

Somewhere about the six-hundredth step, Mira stopped.

“Wren,” she said. “May I ask you something?”

“You’re going to anyway.”

“Are you afraid he will keep it?”

Wren opened her mouth to say no, quickly, the way she said most things. Then she shut it again, and thought, because Mira would hear if she lied. She thought of Tobin in the stream-bed, frozen like a hat-stand. She thought of Tobin on the thirtieth step under his father’s Hall, all alone in the dark, saying It’s not mine. I’m taking it back to her. She thought of a compass needle in a cell lock, and a letter left for a father who could not look at him.

“No,” she said at last, and was surprised to find it was true. “He won’t keep it. He’s not the keeping sort. He’s a great swot and he talks too much and he’s frightened of his own shadow. But he’s not the keeping sort.”

“Good,” said Mira. She clicked. “Step.”

They climbed on. And Wren found that the dark of the Black Stair, which should have been the worst dark she had ever been in, with no lamp and no ribbon and no end to it, was not so very bad after all. It was only dark. She had a hand on a friend’s shoulder, and a fox at her heels, and somewhere up above her, in the hands of someone she trusted, the light was going on ahead.

At the top of the Black Stair there was light.

Wren saw it from far below, a faint gold glow on the curve of the wall, and she began to climb faster and faster until Mira said, “Wren, I can hear you not looking where you’re going.” And then they came up the last steps and out through the hole into the wind, and there was the pale moon, and the grey grass, and four hundred Delvers sitting about on a hilltop with their faces turned to the sky. And there was Tobin, sitting on a stone by the hole, waiting, with the lamp in his lap.

He stood up when he saw her. He looked dreadful. His spectacles were cracked across one lens, his knees were through his trousers, and his face was streaked with soot and something else. He was smiling.

He held out the lamp.

“Here,” he said. “It’s yours. Not lent. I’m not asking for it back.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “You don’t have to do anything.”

Wren looked at it for a moment.

Then she took it. And the lamp did not dip, or flicker, or go small. It blazed up in her hands exactly as bright as it had blazed in his — brighter, if anything — and the ribbon on her wrist flushed red as a rose in the moonlight, and it was not one bit the less for having been given away.

“You didn’t drop it,” she said.

“I very nearly did,” said Tobin. “Twice.”

“Yes, well,” said Wren. “I very nearly didn’t give it you.” And she shoved him, quite gently, with her shoulder, which was the nearest she had ever come to a hug.

Behind them, Mira came up out of the hole into the open air. She stood quite still. She lifted her face, and clicked once, upwards, at the sky — and waited — and nothing came back.

“Oh,” said Mira, very quietly. “Oh. It goes on for ever.”

And here you are, in the pitch dark, with a blind girl and a fox, holding a bridge for people who were going to throw you into a pit.” He paused. “I wonder what you think you will get for it.” “Nothing,” said Wren. “That’s the point, you great lump.” “Hm,” said Varrick — and for one horrible instant he sounded exactly like Old Ash, as if he had caught the habit long ago and never quite shaken it. “My men do not tire, child. You do. In an hour, or two, your arms will give out. And then I will come across, and you will be very cold, and very far down, and nobody will be coming back for you. They never do. You know that better than anyone.” Wren said nothing. Her arms were already aching. She hated that he knew it. Mira’s fingers tightened on her ankle. Then Mira leaned close, and her breath was warm on Wren’s ear. “Every Delver bridge,” she whispered, “has a warden’s knot. On this side. On the post by my hand. It is for floods — if the river comes down the cleft, the wardens pull the pin and let the bridge go, so it does not pull the posts out of the rock. My grandmother showed me when I was little. I can feel it now. One pull, Wren. And then there is no bridge.” Wren’s heart jumped. “And no way back,” she whispered. “There is no back,” said Mira simply. “There is only up.” “There’s Knights on it.” “Yes.” “Then we don’t pull it.” Wren set her jaw. “Not with anyone on it. I don’t care who they are. I’m not doing that.” Mira was quiet for a heartbeat. Then her hand found Wren’s in the dark and squeezed it, very hard, and Wren understood that she had said the right thing. “Then we must make them go back,” said Mira. “All of them. And I will listen for the last foot.” Wren looked at the only light there was. “Cinder,” she said. “Can you run a rope?” The ember-fox looked round at her, and the spark on her tail flared like a coal under a bellows. She went out along the hand-rope like a squirrel along a washing line, and as she ran her spark blazed brighter and brighter, until for a moment Wren could actually see: the long bridge sagging across the black, the pale stone slats, and three grey figures in grey armour clinging to the ropes with grey, empty faces turned towards a little burning fox. Cinder sneezed. A shower of sparks went over the first Knight’s helmet. The Hollow Knights could stand the dark. They could stand the cold. I do not think, in all the years since they had been hollowed, that any of them had had a fox sneeze fire on them. They went backwards along the bridge in a clattering hurry, all three of them, and Cinder came trotting back along the rope with her tail held high, looking very pleased with herself. “Listening,” whispered Mira. Her head was tipped to one side. “Three on the slats. Two. One. He is stepping off. He is off.” Her voice went tight. “The bridge is empty, Wren.” Wren put both hands round the pin. It was cold bronze, as long as her forearm. “Varrick!” she shouted. “Keep your men back! I’m letting it go!” There was a silence on the far side of the chasm. Then, very quietly, Varrick said, “Stand back from the ropes.” And iron feet shuffled away from the edge. Wren pulled. The pin came out with a squeal. Something went crack inside the post, and the hand-ropes leapt out of her reach like living things, and the whole bridge — every rope and every pale stone slat — swung away from her into the dark. She heard it go. It hissed down the face of the far cliff, a long, long whispering, and then the whispering went on, fainter and fainter, and then there was nothing. No crash. No splash. Only the cold breath coming up, the same as before. Nobody said anything for a long time. “Well,” said Varrick at last, from the far side. His voice had changed. It sounded, for the first time, a little tired. “There is more than one road to the top of the world, Wren Ashby. I will finish this somewhere else.” His footsteps went away, back into the silent tunnels of Deepholm. And as they went, the great grey cold went with them, slowly, like a tide going out, until the air at the bottom of the Black Stair was only the ordinary cold of stone. Wren sat down on the floor, very suddenly, because her legs had stopped working. Up above, the lamp was getting brighter. Tobin noticed it first at about the four-hundredth step, and thought he was imagining it. By the five-hundredth he was sure. It was no longer a little golden room around him, six steps up and six steps down. It was ten steps. Then twelve. By the six-hundredth he could see the curve of the wall going up ahead of him, and the curve going down behind, and Gorrim’s face — wet with sweat, set like stone — and the grey head on his shoulder. He did not know why. He was only holding it. He had not done anything. He had climbed, that was all, one step and then the next, holding it up so that four hundred people could feel it on their faces. He had held it low over every gap. He had held it out to an old Delver woman who had sat down on the four hundred and twentieth step and said she could go no further, and she had felt the warm on her cheeks and got up again. What is given, grows. He had written that in his notebook too. He had thought he understood it. At some point, the cold draught from below stopped. It did not fade; it simply was not there, as if a door had been shut far underneath them. Tobin did not know what it meant. He hoped very much that he knew. “Nine hundred and ninety-eight,” he croaked. “Nine hundred and ninety-nine.” There was no thousandth step. There was a slab of stone overhead, flat and heavy, with a crack round its edge, and through the crack came a breath of air so different from the air of the stair that Tobin nearly sat down. It was cold — but it was a clean cold, a moving cold. It smelled of grass. It took Gorrim and two of the stone-carriers, braced on the top steps with their shoulders under the slab, to move it. It went over with a great grinding thud. And above them there was no roof at all. Tobin climbed out onto a rough hilltop among tumbled stones, with the grey grass of the Greywaste hissing all around, and he looked up. There was a moon. It was pale, as the moon in Gloamhaven always was — a thin white coin behind thin cloud. But after a thousand steps in the dark, it was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen in his life. He stared at it while the Delvers came up out of the ground behind him, still holding the rope. They did not look at the moon. They could not. But as each one came out into the open, they stopped, and lifted their faces, and clicked — and nothing came back. No roof. No walls. Only the wind, going on and on for ever. Some of them sat down and held on to the grass. One small girl began to cry, and her mother picked her up, and then began to cry as well, and then — this was the odd part — began to laugh. Speaker Gorrim did not lift his face to the sky at all. He knelt down on the grass and untied the blanket from his shoulders, and laid his son in it, very gently, as if he were made of glass. Tavi lay there, grey and still, staring at nothing. Tobin knelt down on the other side of him. And then he did not know what to do. He had seen Wren do this. He had seen her kneel on a bakery step in Soot Lane, and outside the sweep yard, and in a hundred doorways. But that had been Wren, with Wren’s lamp. He looked down at the little dented brass thing in his hands, burning white-gold, brighter now than he had ever seen it, and he heard her voice in his head: It’s yours. Not lent. Yours. It was his. So it was his to give. “Here,” said Tobin. His voice shook, so he started again. “Here. It’s for you, Tavi. You don’t have to do anything.” He held out the lamp. The flame leaned out of it towards the grey boy, the way a flower leans towards a window, and warmth spread over the grass. And the colour came back into Tavi as the dawn comes up over a hill — slowly, then all at once: the pale pink in his cheeks, the soft brown of his hair, a flush along his ears. He blinked. His hand moved on the blanket. His head turned — towards the warmth, not towards any light, for he had never seen a light in his life — and his face screwed up in deep puzzlement. “Father?” he said. “Why is it warm? Where is the roof?” Speaker Gorrim made a sound that Tobin had never heard a grown man make. He gathered his son up off the grass, blanket and all, and held him against his chest and bowed his great grey head over him. His shoulders shook. He did not make any more sound, and he did not need to. The proud Speaker of the Delvers, who had called the lamp a lie and sent strangers to the Silent Pit, knelt on the hilltop under the pale moon with his boy in his arms and wept, and did not care who heard. “Why is it warm? Where is the roof?” When at last he lifted his head, his wet face was turned towards Tobin — or towards the warmth in Tobin’s hands. “The Delvers have a word for everything,” he said, in his deep slow voice, and it broke. “Nine words for the sound of water. Four for the quiet before a song. And I have no word for this.” He bent his head over his son again. “None at all.” Tobin had no idea what to say to that, so he pushed his spectacles up his nose, and said, “There are some more. Greyed ones. Further down the line. I’d better—“ and went, before anyone could see that he was crying too. Wren and Mira climbed the Black Stair together in the dark, and Cinder went in front. With four hundred Delvers clicking, Mira had said, the stair was a din. With one, it was a map. Mira went first, with Wren’s hand on her shoulder, and every few steps she clicked once, softly, and listened, and said, “Gap. Long step. Wall side,” or “Loose stone. Step over,” exactly as if she could see it. Behind them, Cinder’s little spark bobbed, lighting nothing but itself. “You’re showing off,” said Wren, at about the two-hundredth step. “A little,” said Mira. She clicked. “Step.” Somewhere about the six-hundredth step, Mira stopped. “Wren,” she said. “May I ask you something?” “You’re going to anyway.” “Are you afraid he will keep it?” Wren opened her mouth to say no, quickly, the way she said most things. Then she shut it again, and thought, because Mira would hear if she lied. She thought of Tobin in the stream-bed, frozen like a hat-stand. She thought of Tobin on the thirtieth step under his father’s Hall, all alone in the dark, saying It’s not mine. I’m taking it back to her. She thought of a compass needle in a cell lock, and a letter left for a father who could not look at him. “No,” she said at last, and was surprised to find it was true. “He won’t keep it. He’s not the keeping sort. He’s a great swot and he talks too much and he’s frightened of his own shadow. But he’s not the keeping sort.” “Good,” said Mira. She clicked. “Step.” They climbed on. And Wren found that the dark of the Black Stair, which should have been the worst dark she had ever been in, with no lamp and no ribbon and no end to it, was not so very bad after all. It was only dark. She had a hand on a friend’s shoulder, and a fox at her heels, and somewhere up above her, in the hands of someone she trusted, the light was going on ahead. At the top of the Black Stair there was light. Wren saw it from far below, a faint gold glow on the curve of the wall, and she began to climb faster and faster until Mira said, “Wren, I can hear you not looking where you’re going.” And then they came up the last steps and out through the hole into the wind, and there was the pale moon, and the grey grass, and four hundred Delvers sitting about on a hilltop with their faces turned to the sky. And there was Tobin, sitting on a stone by the hole, waiting, with the lamp in his lap. He stood up when he saw her. He looked dreadful. His spectacles were cracked across one lens, his knees were through his trousers, and his face was streaked with soot and something else. He was smiling. He held out the lamp. “Here,” he said. “It’s yours. Not lent. I’m not asking for it back.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “You don’t have to do anything.” Wren looked at it for a moment. Then she took it. And the lamp did not dip, or flicker, or go small. It blazed up in her hands exactly as bright as it had blazed in his — brighter, if anything — and the ribbon on her wrist flushed red as a rose in the moonlight, and it was not one bit the less for having been given away. “You didn’t drop it,” she said. “I very nearly did,” said Tobin. “Twice.” “Yes, well,” said Wren. “I very nearly didn’t give it you.” And she shoved him, quite gently, with her shoulder, which was the nearest she had ever come to a hug. Behind them, Mira came up out of the hole into the open air. She stood quite still. She lifted her face, and clicked once, upwards, at the sky — and waited — and nothing came back. “Oh,” said Mira, very quietly. “Oh. It goes on for ever.”

fields.title: The Ferryman of the Gloam River
fields.body_html:
The Delvers did not like the morning.

It came up grey and pale over the Greywaste, the way mornings always did in Gloamhaven, and the wind came with it, and four hundred people who had lived their whole lives under a roof of stone sat huddled among the tumbled rocks at the top of the Black Stair and held on to the grass. They could feel the open all around them. It frightened them, Mira said, the way a cliff-edge frightens you even when you are standing well back from it.

“They will get used to it,” she said. “I am getting used to it. Listen.” She clicked, upwards, and nothing came back, and she laughed out loud, the way a small child laughs at a game it does not want to stop. “Nothing! Nothing at all! Wren, it is the best thing I ever heard.”

Wren was sitting on a stone with the lamp in her lap, eating a cold Delver cake that tasted mostly of mushrooms. She did not say anything. But she had been watching Mira click at the sky for some time, and she was smiling.

Old Ash was not smiling. Mother Hessa was re-binding his leg, and she was humming as she did it, and pulling the bandages tight in a way that made him say “Hm,” every few seconds in a rising note, like a cart-wheel wanting grease.

“You will not walk on it for a week,” said Hessa briskly. “You will not walk far on it for a month. You will not climb any more stairs at all, ever, if you have any sense, which I am beginning to doubt.”

“Madam,” said Ash, “I have been climbing stairs for seventy years.”

“Then you have had a good long go,” said Hessa, “and can stop.”

In the end he walked with the Delver bridge-pole that Wren had carried up the Black Stair, its bronze hook worn smooth, and his own brass-hooked lamplighter’s pole in his other hand, so that he went along between them like a very tall, very cross insect. Tobin, who had been looking at his compass, said that this was actually a very sound arrangement from the point of view of weight distribution. Ash told him to hush.

The compass still pointed north and a bit east. But between the hilltop and the pale tooth of the Bright Mountain, Ash said, lay the Gloam River, and the Gloam River had no bridge.

“There used to be a ferry,” he said. “In my master’s day. A Lamplighter’s ferry. It went over twice a day, morning and evening, and charged nothing.” He shook his head slowly. “Hm. That was a long time ago.”

Speaker Gorrim came to see them off. He had Tavi on his hip, though Tavi was far too big to be carried and kept trying to get down, and Tavi was asking questions so fast that his father could not answer any of them. What is the wind for? Where does it go? Why is the warm thing warm? Is the sky very high? Higher than the Great Hall? Higher than the Pit is deep?

“My people will rest here,” said Gorrim. “A day. Perhaps two. We cannot go back, and we do not yet know how to go forward.” He was quiet for a moment, as if the words cost him something. “I would know what lies across that river. Whether there is a road for us there. Will you let one of my people walk with you to the water, and listen to it, and come back and tell me?”

“I’ll go,” said Mira at once.

Gorrim turned his face towards her. Only the day before, in the Hall of Answers, he had silenced her before everyone. Wren remembered it, and Mira certainly did. But he did not silence her now.

“Yes,” he said slowly. “You will. You have the best ears in Deepholm, and you have been right about more than I have.” He bowed his great head to her — a small bow, but a real one. “Go, Mira. Listen well.”

It took them until the middle of the afternoon to reach the Gloam River, and they heard it long before they saw it.

At least, Mira heard it. “There is something ahead,” she said, an hour out from the hilltop, “breathing. Something very big and very slow, breathing in its sleep.” Wren could hear nothing but the wind in the grass. Another hour, and she could hear it too — a deep soft sound like wind in a chimney. And then the grey grass sloped down, and the ground grew damp and soft, and there was the river.

It was the widest thing Wren had ever seen. It was wider than the Soot Canal, wider than Beacon Square, wider than the whole of Soot Lane laid end to end. It went slowly past them, grey as pewter, with a cold white mist lying on it so that they could not see the far side at all. There were reeds along the edge, dry and rattling. There was no bridge. There was no boat. There was nothing on the bank but a single old post, leaning, with an iron ring rusted to it and an empty lamp-niche in its top, like the waystones on the Greywaste road.

“The ferry-post,” said Ash quietly. “Hm. So it was here.”

Tobin stood at the water’s edge and looked at the river with his head on one side, and Wren could see him working out sums.

“Allowing for the current,” he said, “and assuming the far bank is roughly as far off as the near one — which it would be, of course, by definition — and allowing for Ash’s leg, and the fact that I can’t swim very well, and Wren can’t swim at all—“

“I can so swim.”

“You can drown in an energetic manner,” said Tobin. “I’ve seen you in the canal. It isn’t the same thing.”

“Hush,” said Mira suddenly.

They hushed.

She was standing very still, with her face turned towards the mist. She clicked once, out over the water. Then again.

“There is a boat,” she said. “Out there. Someone is rowing. Slowly. One of the oars creaks.” She listened. “He is coming this way.”

Wren could see nothing but white. But after a moment she heard it too: a soft creak and splash, creak and splash, getting nearer. Cinder, at her feet, sat up very straight with her ears pricked — but she did not growl. Her tail-spark, Wren noticed, had begun to glow.

Then out of the mist came the prow of a boat.

It was a long flat ferry-boat, old and grey and weathered, with a bench across the middle and a lantern-hook at the bow with no lantern on it. Standing in the stern, rowing with one long oar, was an old man. He was tall, and he wore a hooded coat the colour of the river, and his beard was short and grey, and when the boat bumped gently against the bank among the reeds, he shipped the oar and looked up at them.

He had kind eyes. That was the first thing Wren thought, and afterwards it was the thing she remembered best. Not the colour of them. Only that they were kind, the way a fire is warm — not because it is trying to be, but because that is what it is.

“Going over?” he said.

“Yes, please,” said Tobin, before anyone else could speak. “That is — if it isn’t too much trouble. There are five of us. Four and a fox. And one of us has a bad leg, so we would need to — and, I’m sorry, but what do you charge? Because we haven’t very much. Actually we haven’t anything. I’ve a penknife, and a notebook, and—“

“No charge,” said the ferryman.

Wren went very still.

She did not know why. It was only two words. People said them sometimes. But something about the way he said them went into her like a splinter of warmth, and stuck, and she found that she was holding the lamp very tightly.

“Nothing’s free,” she heard herself say. It came out sharper than she meant. “Everything costs. There’s always a catch.”

The old man looked at her. He did not seem offended. If anything, he looked as if she had said something he had heard before, a long time ago, and was glad to hear again.

“Not this,” he said. “This is given.” He held out his hand to help her into the boat. “Come along, child. The mist won’t wait for ever.”

She took his hand. It was warm — as warm as the lamp — and rough with old work, and across the palm of it ran a scar, white and old, the kind of scar you get from holding something very hot for a very long time.

Wren looked at it. Something tugged in her memory — a market, a smell of new bread, a warm loaf put into her hands. But before she could catch hold of it she was in the boat, and Tobin was helping Ash down, and Ash was saying Hm in a strange, soft voice, and the moment went by.

Last of all, Mira stood on the bank alone.

“And me?” she said, a little uncertainly. “I am only meant to listen to the river. I am meant to go back.”

“There’s room for you,” said the ferryman. “There is always room.” And he held out his hand to her too, and she took it, and stepped down into the boat as lightly as if she had been doing it all her life.

The ferryman pushed off, and the bank slid away behind them, and in a dozen strokes it was gone in the mist.

I do not know if you have ever been out on wide water in a fog. It is a very quiet thing. There is no up and down, no near and far; there is only the boat, and the people in it, and the creak of the oar, and white on every side. Even Tobin stopped talking. Cinder lay curled in the bottom of the boat with her chin on Wren’s boot. Ash sat in the bow with his bad leg stretched out and his eyes on the ferryman, and his face was very strange — not grieved, the way it went when he spoke of Varrick, but the opposite of grieved, if there is such a thing. As if he were holding something in, very carefully, so that it would not spill.

Mira sat on the bench beside Wren, trailing one hand in the river.

“It is cold,” she said. “And soft. And it goes all the way, doesn’t it? Over to the other side, and down to the sea, and nobody ever has to carry it.” She tipped her head. “Ferryman. Your oar creaks on the left.”

“So it does,” said the ferryman. “It always has.”

“I can hear the other bank,” said Mira. “A long way off. Reeds, like these. And a bird.” She smiled. “I have never heard a bird before. Not a real one. Only singing-stones made to sound like them.”

The ferryman rested on his oar. The boat drifted, turning a little on the slow grey water, in the middle of the mist, in the middle of the river.

“You were born in the dark,” he said. It was not a question.

“Yes,” said Mira. And then, quickly, with her chin up, in the way she had: “But I am not broken. I want you to know that. People from up here always think we must be broken, and we’re not. I hear the whole world. I hear more than Wren does, and Wren hears more than anyone.” She paused. “Wren could not see on the bridge. I could. I held the bridge. Us. We held it.”

“I know,” said the ferryman gently. “I heard.”

Wren looked up sharply. But the old man’s face was only kind.

“No,” he said to Mira, “you are not broken, child. You never were. This is not a mending.” He shipped the oar, and leaned forward on the bench, and his voice was very quiet. “It is a gift. That is all. You may have it, if you like. You do not have to do anything.”

Mira was silent for a long moment. Her face had gone very still, the way it did when she was listening hard.

“What gift?” she whispered.

The ferryman did not answer. He dipped his two thumbs in the grey water of the Gloam River. Then he reached out, slowly, so that she could hear him coming, and laid them very lightly on her closed eyes.

Nobody in the boat breathed.

Wren could not have said how long it lasted. A heartbeat. A minute. The mist stood round them. The water lapped at the boat. And the warmth — she felt it, sitting beside Mira; she felt it the way she had felt the lamp blaze up in Tobin’s hands at the foot of the Black Stair — the warmth came out of the old man’s hands like the first warmth of the sun on your face, if you can imagine such a thing, in a land where the sun had not been warm for three hundred years.

“Your hands are warm,” whispered Mira. “Like Wren’s lamp. Exactly like it.”

He took his hands away.

“Open your eyes, child,” he said.

This is the part of the story that Mira always told best, and she told it all her life, so I will let you hear it, as nearly as I can, the way she told it.

She said that at first there was nothing. Then there was a greyness, which she did not know was greyness, because she had no name for it. It was not a sound and not a touch and not a smell, and it was everywhere at once, and it frightened her. She said it was like being shouted at by the whole world without anyone making a noise.

And then, in the middle of the greyness, there was something else.

It was small. It was close to her. It was in Wren’s lap. It was golden-white, and it moved — it danced — and it was the same as the warmth. That was how she knew. It was the warmth, made into something she could — she did not have the word yet. See. It was the warmth, and the warmth had a shape, and the shape was beautiful, and it was the first thing that Mira of Deepholm ever saw in her life.

“Wren,” she whispered. She was shaking. “Wren. What is that?”

Wren’s throat was so tight she could hardly get the words out.

“That’s the lamp,” she said. “That’s — that’s the light, Mira. That’s what light is.”

Mira stared at it. She did not blink. Tears were running down her face and she did not seem to notice them.

“It’s true,” she said. “It’s true. The Warm Man said. On the Wall. He said one day we would see, and I never — I believed it, but I never—“ She put out one shaking hand towards the flame, not touching, the way you would reach towards something very precious. “Oh, it’s beautiful. Oh, Wren. Nobody ever told me it would be beautiful. They only ever said it was bright.”

And then she laughed, and clicked her tongue — out of sheer habit, at the flame, as if to make sure of it — and the click came back to her off Wren and Tobin and the boat and the water, exactly as it always had.

“I can still hear,” she said, astonished. “I can hear and see. Both at once. Is that allowed?”

“I think,” said the ferryman, and there was a smile in his voice, “you will find it is.”

Wren looked down at her wrist. Her ribbon was red. It was the reddest she had ever seen it, as red as it had been at the top of the Beacon. And she turned to look at the old man in the stern — to say something, she did not know what; she thought, perhaps, thank you, which was not a thing she was good at saying — and he had already taken up his oar, and was rowing, slow and steady, creak and splash, as if nothing at all had happened.

The boat bumped against the far bank among the reeds.

They climbed out. Tobin helped Ash, who leaned on both his poles and said nothing at all. Cinder jumped ashore and shook herself. Wren gave Mira her hand, and Mira stepped onto the bank and stood there in the grey grass, turning her head this way and that, looking at everything — at the reeds and the mist and her own hands, which she held up in front of her face and turned over, and over, and over again.

Then Wren turned back to the boat to say thank you.

The boat was not there.

The mist lay on the river, thick and white and still. There was no ferry. There was no old man. There was no creak of an oar going away, no splash, no ripple spreading on the grey water where a boat had been pushed off. There was only the river, going slowly past, breathing in its sleep, as it had been when they came.

“But—“ said Tobin. He stared at the mist. “But he can’t have — he’d have had to turn the boat, and that takes at least — and we’d have heard — the left oar creaked, Mira heard it, so we’d have—“ He stopped. He pushed his spectacles up his nose. He opened his mouth again, and shut it, and for once in his life, Tobin Harrowgate had nothing whatever to say.

“He didn’t charge,” said Wren, to nobody. She was holding the lamp against her chest. “He didn’t charge us anything.”

She looked round at Old Ash.

The old man was standing on the bank, leaning on his two poles, looking out at the mist where the boat had been. He did not say Hm. He did not say anything at all. But his old face, under the singed white beard, was full of light — and he was smiling, the way Wren had never once seen him smile, as if he had been waiting a very long time for something, and it had come.

Nobody asked him what he knew. Somehow, none of them wanted to.

And Mira, who had been looking at everything, stopped looking at everything. She turned round in the grey grass and looked, very carefully, at Wren — at her face, for a long, long moment, the way you might look at a map of a country you had only ever heard described.

“So that,” she said softly, “is what you look like.”
