Listen.” She clicked, upwards, and nothing came back, and she laughed out loud, the way a small child laughs at a game it does not want to stop. “Nothing! Nothing at all! Wren, it is the best thing I ever heard.” Wren was sitting on a stone with the lamp in her lap, eating a cold Delver cake that tasted mostly of mushrooms. She did not say anything. But she had been watching Mira click at the sky for some time, and she was smiling. Old Ash was not smiling. Mother Hessa was re-binding his leg, and she was humming as she did it, and pulling the bandages tight in a way that made him say “Hm,” every few seconds in a rising note, like a cart-wheel wanting grease. “You will not walk on it for a week,” said Hessa briskly. “You will not walk far on it for a month. You will not climb any more stairs at all, ever, if you have any sense, which I am beginning to doubt.” “Madam,” said Ash, “I have been climbing stairs for seventy years.” “Then you have had a good long go,” said Hessa, “and can stop.” In the end he walked with the Delver bridge-pole that Wren had carried up the Black Stair, its bronze hook worn smooth, and his own brass-hooked lamplighter’s pole in his other hand, so that he went along between them like a very tall, very cross insect. Tobin, who had been looking at his compass, said that this was actually a very sound arrangement from the point of view of weight distribution. Ash told him to hush. The compass still pointed north and a bit east. But between the hilltop and the pale tooth of the Bright Mountain, Ash said, lay the Gloam River, and the Gloam River had no bridge. “There used to be a ferry,” he said. “In my master’s day. A Lamplighter’s ferry. It went over twice a day, morning and evening, and charged nothing.” He shook his head slowly. “Hm. That was a long time ago.” Speaker Gorrim came to see them off. He had Tavi on his hip, though Tavi was far too big to be carried and kept trying to get down, and Tavi was asking questions so fast that his father could not answer any of them. What is the wind for? Where does it go? Why is the warm thing warm? Is the sky very high? Higher than the Great Hall? Higher than the Pit is deep? “My people will rest here,” said Gorrim. “A day. Perhaps two. We cannot go back, and we do not yet know how to go forward.” He was quiet for a moment, as if the words cost him something. “I would know what lies across that river. Whether there is a road for us there. Will you let one of my people walk with you to the water, and listen to it, and come back and tell me?” “I’ll go,” said Mira at once. Gorrim turned his face towards her. Only the day before, in the Hall of Answers, he had silenced her before everyone. Wren remembered it, and Mira certainly did. But he did not silence her now. “Yes,” he said slowly. “You will. You have the best ears in Deepholm, and you have been right about more than I have.” He bowed his great head to her — a small bow, but a real one. “Go, Mira. Listen well.” It took them until the middle of the afternoon to reach the Gloam River, and they heard it long before they saw it. At least, Mira heard it. “There is something ahead,” she said, an hour out from the hilltop, “breathing. Something very big and very slow, breathing in its sleep.” Wren could hear nothing but the wind in the grass. Another hour, and she could hear it too — a deep soft sound like wind in a chimney. And then the grey grass sloped down, and the ground grew damp and soft, and there was the river. It was the widest thing Wren had ever seen. It was wider than the Soot Canal, wider than Beacon Square, wider than the whole of Soot Lane laid end to end. It went slowly past them, grey as pewter, with a cold white mist lying on it so that they could not see the far side at all. There were reeds along the edge, dry and rattling. There was no bridge. There was no boat. There was nothing on the bank but a single old post, leaning, with an iron ring rusted to it and an empty lamp-niche in its top, like the waystones on the Greywaste road. “The ferry-post,” said Ash quietly. “Hm. So it was here.” Tobin stood at the water’s edge and looked at the river with his head on one side, and Wren could see him working out sums. “Allowing for the current,” he said, “and assuming the far bank is roughly as far off as the near one — which it would be, of course, by definition — and allowing for Ash’s leg, and the fact that I can’t swim very well, and Wren can’t swim at all—“ “I can so swim.” “You can drown in an energetic manner,” said Tobin. “I’ve seen you in the canal. It isn’t the same thing.” “Hush,” said Mira suddenly. They hushed. She was standing very still, with her face turned towards the mist. She clicked once, out over the water. Then again. “There is a boat,” she said. “Out there. Someone is rowing. Slowly. One of the oars creaks.” She listened. “He is coming this way.” Wren could see nothing but white. But after a moment she heard it too: a soft creak and splash, creak and splash, getting nearer. Cinder, at her feet, sat up very straight with her ears pricked — but she did not growl. Her tail-spark, Wren noticed, had begun to glow. Then out of the mist came the prow of a boat. It was a long flat ferry-boat, old and grey and weathered, with a bench across the middle and a lantern-hook at the bow with no lantern on it. Standing in the stern, rowing with one long oar, was an old man. He was tall, and he wore a hooded coat the colour of the river, and his beard was short and grey, and when the boat bumped gently against the bank among the reeds, he shipped the oar and looked up at them. He had kind eyes. That was the first thing Wren thought, and afterwards it was the thing she remembered best. Not the colour of them. Only that they were kind, the way a fire is warm — not because it is trying to be, but because that is what it is. “Going over?” he said. “Yes, please,” said Tobin, before anyone else could speak. “That is — if it isn’t too much trouble. There are five of us. Four and a fox. And one of us has a bad leg, so we would need to — and, I’m sorry, but what do you charge? Because we haven’t very much. Actually we haven’t anything. I’ve a penknife, and a notebook, and—“ “No charge,” said the ferryman. Wren went very still. She did not know why. It was only two words. People said them sometimes. But something about the way he said them went into her like a splinter of warmth, and stuck, and she found that she was holding the lamp very tightly. “Nothing’s free,” she heard herself say. It came out sharper than she meant. “Everything costs. There’s always a catch.” The old man looked at her. He did not seem offended. If anything, he looked as if she had said something he had heard before, a long time ago, and was glad to hear again. “Not this,” he said. “This is given.” He held out his hand to help her into the boat. “Come along, child. The mist won’t wait for ever.” She took his hand. It was warm — as warm as the lamp — and rough with old work, and across the palm of it ran a scar, white and old, the kind of scar you get from holding something very hot for a very long time. Wren looked at it. Something tugged in her memory — a market, a smell of new bread, a warm loaf put into her hands. But before she could catch hold of it she was in the boat, and Tobin was helping Ash down, and Ash was saying Hm in a strange, soft voice, and the moment went by. Last of all, Mira stood on the bank alone. “And me?” she said, a little uncertainly. “I am only meant to listen to the river. I am meant to go back.” “There’s room for you,” said the ferryman. “There is always room.” And he held out his hand to her too, and she took it, and stepped down into the boat as lightly as if she had been doing it all her life. The ferryman pushed off, and the bank slid away behind them, and in a dozen strokes it was gone in the mist. I do not know if you have ever been out on wide water in a fog. It is a very quiet thing. There is no up and down, no near and far; there is only the boat, and the people in it, and the creak of the oar, and white on every side. Even Tobin stopped talking. Cinder lay curled in the bottom of the boat with her chin on Wren’s boot. Ash sat in the bow with his bad leg stretched out and his eyes on the ferryman, and his face was very strange — not grieved, the way it went when he spoke of Varrick, but the opposite of grieved, if there is such a thing. As if he were holding something in, very carefully, so that it would not spill. Mira sat on the bench beside Wren, trailing one hand in the river. “It is cold,” she said. “And soft. And it goes all the way, doesn’t it? Over to the other side, and down to the sea, and nobody ever has to carry it.” She tipped her head. “Ferryman. Your oar creaks on the left.” “So it does,” said the ferryman. “It always has.” “I can hear the other bank,” said Mira. “A long way off. Reeds, like these. And a bird.” She smiled. “I have never heard a bird before. Not a real one. Only singing-stones made to sound like them.” The ferryman rested on his oar. The boat drifted, turning a little on the slow grey water, in the middle of the mist, in the middle of the river. “You were born in the dark,” he said. It was not a question. “Yes,” said Mira. And then, quickly, with her chin up, in the way she had: “But I am not broken. I want you to know that. People from up here always think we must be broken, and we’re not. I hear the whole world. I hear more than Wren does, and Wren hears more than anyone.” She paused. “Wren could not see on the bridge. I could. I held the bridge. Us. We held it.” “I know,” said the ferryman gently. “I heard.” Wren looked up sharply. But the old man’s face was only kind. “No,” he said to Mira, “you are not broken, child. You never were. This is not a mending.” He shipped the oar, and leaned forward on the bench, and his voice was very quiet. “It is a gift. That is all. You may have it, if you like. You do not have to do anything.” Mira was silent for a long moment. Her face had gone very still, the way it did when she was listening hard. “What gift?” she whispered. The ferryman did not answer. He dipped his two thumbs in the grey water of the Gloam River. Then he reached out, slowly, so that she could hear him coming, and laid them very lightly on her closed eyes. “It is a gift. That is all.” Nobody in the boat breathed. Wren could not have said how long it lasted. A heartbeat. A minute. The mist stood round them. The water lapped at the boat. And the warmth — she felt it, sitting beside Mira; she felt it the way she had felt the lamp blaze up in Tobin’s hands at the foot of the Black Stair — the warmth came out of the old man’s hands like the first warmth of the sun on your face, if you can imagine such a thing, in a land where the sun had not been warm for three hundred years. “Your hands are warm,” whispered Mira. “Like Wren’s lamp. Exactly like it.” He took his hands away. “Open your eyes, child,” he said. This is the part of the story that Mira always told best, and she told it all her life, so I will let you hear it, as nearly as I can, the way she told it. She said that at first there was nothing. Then there was a greyness, which she did not know was greyness, because she had no name for it. It was not a sound and not a touch and not a smell, and it was everywhere at once, and it frightened her. She said it was like being shouted at by the whole world without anyone making a noise. And then, in the middle of the greyness, there was something else. It was small. It was close to her. It was in Wren’s lap. It was golden-white, and it moved — it danced — and it was the same as the warmth. That was how she knew. It was the warmth, made into something she could — she did not have the word yet. See. It was the warmth, and the warmth had a shape, and the shape was beautiful, and it was the first thing that Mira of Deepholm ever saw in her life. “Wren,” she whispered. She was shaking. “Wren. What is that?” Wren’s throat was so tight she could hardly get the words out. “That’s the lamp,” she said. “That’s — that’s the light, Mira. That’s what light is.” Mira stared at it. She did not blink. Tears were running down her face and she did not seem to notice them. “It’s true,” she said. “It’s true. The Warm Man said. On the Wall. He said one day we would see, and I never — I believed it, but I never—“ She put out one shaking hand towards the flame, not touching, the way you would reach towards something very precious. “Oh, it’s beautiful. Oh, Wren. Nobody ever told me it would be beautiful. They only ever said it was bright.” And then she laughed, and clicked her tongue — out of sheer habit, at the flame, as if to make sure of it — and the click came back to her off Wren and Tobin and the boat and the water, exactly as it always had. “I can still hear,” she said, astonished. “I can hear and see. Both at once. Is that allowed?” “I think,” said the ferryman, and there was a smile in his voice, “you will find it is.” Wren looked down at her wrist. Her ribbon was red. It was the reddest she had ever seen it, as red as it had been at the top of the Beacon. And she turned to look at the old man in the stern — to say something, she did not know what; she thought, perhaps, thank you, which was not a thing she was good at saying — and he had already taken up his oar, and was rowing, slow and steady, creak and splash, as if nothing at all had happened. The boat bumped against the far bank among the reeds. They climbed out. Tobin helped Ash, who leaned on both his poles and said nothing at all. Cinder jumped ashore and shook herself. Wren gave Mira her hand, and Mira stepped onto the bank and stood there in the grey grass, turning her head this way and that, looking at everything — at the reeds and the mist and her own hands, which she held up in front of her face and turned over, and over, and over again. Then Wren turned back to the boat to say thank you. The boat was not there. The mist lay on the river, thick and white and still. There was no ferry. There was no old man. There was no creak of an oar going away, no splash, no ripple spreading on the grey water where a boat had been pushed off. There was only the river, going slowly past, breathing in its sleep, as it had been when they came. “But—“ said Tobin. He stared at the mist. “But he can’t have — he’d have had to turn the boat, and that takes at least — and we’d have heard — the left oar creaked, Mira heard it, so we’d have—“ He stopped. He pushed his spectacles up his nose. He opened his mouth again, and shut it, and for once in his life, Tobin Harrowgate had nothing whatever to say. “He didn’t charge,” said Wren, to nobody. She was holding the lamp against her chest. “He didn’t charge us anything.” She looked round at Old Ash. The old man was standing on the bank, leaning on his two poles, looking out at the mist where the boat had been. He did not say Hm. He did not say anything at all. But his old face, under the singed white beard, was full of light — and he was smiling, the way Wren had never once seen him smile, as if he had been waiting a very long time for something, and it had come. Nobody asked him what he knew. Somehow, none of them wanted to. And Mira, who had been looking at everything, stopped looking at everything. She turned round in the grey grass and looked, very carefully, at Wren — at her face, for a long, long moment, the way you might look at a map of a country you had only ever heard described. “So that,” she said softly, “is what you look like.”

fields.title: Colours
fields.body_html:
Mira did not sleep that night. Nobody had really expected her to.

She sat on a flat rock at the edge of the Gloam River with the lamp on the stones in front of her, and she looked at it. She looked at it the way you might read a letter from someone you had given up hoping to hear from: over and over, from the beginning, in case you had missed a word. Now and then she put her face so close to the glass that her nose nearly touched it. Once she shut her eyes tight and clicked her tongue at it — tk, tk — and then opened them again, quickly, as if to check that it was still there.

It was still there. It always was.

Wren lay a little way off, pretending to be asleep, and watched her. Mira wore an expression Wren had never seen before. It was not quite happiness. It was bigger and quieter than that. It was the look of someone who has been told a story all their life, and has believed it, and has just found out that it was true.

“You can come and sit by me,” said Mira, without turning round. “I can hear you not sleeping. You do it very loudly.”

So Wren went and sat by her. Mira turned and looked at her, very seriously, for a long time. Being looked at is not a thing most of us notice much. But Wren had never been looked at like that, and she found she did not know where to put her hands.

“You are smaller than your voice,” said Mira at last.

“Thanks very much.”

“It was not a complaint. My clicks told me you were small. They did not tell me you would look it.” Mira reached out a finger and touched the tufts of Wren’s hair where they stuck out over her ears. “And this is how your hair looks. I knew how it felt. I did not know a thing could look the way it feels. Does everything?”

Wren thought about it. “Mostly,” she said. “Mott looked the way he felt. Like a sack of wet coal.”

Mira laughed, a short, delighted bark.

The sun came up over the Gloam River, and Mira saw her first morning.

It was not, I am sorry to say, much of a morning. The cursed sun rose through the mist like a coin seen through dirty water, and turned the black river grey, and that was more or less the end of what it could do.

Mira thought it was the most wonderful thing she had ever seen.

“It is coming in from everywhere at once,” she said, standing up on her rock. “Wren, there is no edge to it. Where is the lamp of it?”

“That’s the sun,” said Wren. “It’s not much of one.”

“It is enormous,” said Mira, and would not be told otherwise.

All that first morning she went about the river-bank like a bee in a garden, and everything astonished her. She picked up handfuls of shingle and said that she had always known stones were different, but not that they were different-looking, which seemed to her a great extravagance on the part of stones.

She was very bad at distances. Her echo-sense had not gone anywhere — the Ferryman had given her eyes, not taken her ears — and when she clicked she could still tell you to a finger’s breadth how far off the river was, or the tree, or Tobin. But her eyes did not yet know what her ears knew, and they kept telling her lies. She reached out to touch the far bank of the Gloam, a quarter of a mile away, and was very much put out when she couldn’t. She walked straight into Old Ash’s back because, she said, he had looked a long way off and then had suddenly not been.

“Shut your eyes and click, then,” said Wren, “if your eyes are no good.”

“My eyes are perfectly good,” said Mira with dignity. “They are only new. One does not blame a baby for falling over.” Then she shut them, clicked, walked neatly round Ash, and opened them on the other side. “There. They agree with each other now. That is a relief. I was not sure they could be trusted.”

Tobin, watching with great scientific interest, said that, technically speaking, it was a matter of the brain learning the signals, and had she noticed whether the lamp looked further away when she shut one eye—

“Tobin,” said Mira. “You have a very long nose.”

Tobin went pink. “I — have I?”

“It is a good nose,” said Mira kindly. “I heard that it was long. I did not know it would go on for quite so long as it does.” She tilted her head. “And there is colour on your face. That is new.”

“That,” said Wren, enjoying herself enormously, “is called going red.”

It was the colours that undid her in the end.

There were not many to see. Out here, far from any Ring, the world was the old Gloamhaven world: grey and brown and dun and that tired blue-ish that people called dull. But near the lamp, as you know, the colours came back; and so all morning Mira kept running back to it, the way you keep running back to the one warm room in a cold house.

Close to its light, the ribbon on Wren’s wrist was red — a true, glad, berry red. Mira held Wren’s wrist in both hands and looked at it for so long that Wren began to feel awkward and tried to take it back.

“What is its name?” said Mira. “Not ribbon. The — the loud part of it.”

“Red,” said Wren.

“Red,” said Mira softly, the way you would say the name of a friend. “It sounds like it looks. It sounds warm. And Tobin’s hair, near the lamp? And Cinder’s tail — that is something else again.”

Wren said Tobin’s hair was yellow, because Nettle had said so. About Cinder’s tail nobody could agree until Ash, sitting on a stone by the little fire he had built with his bad leg out in front of him, said “Hm,” and that it was gold at the tip and orange behind, and that it did not matter very much what you called a thing so long as you saw it. Cinder, who knew perfectly well she was being talked about, let the spark at the end of her tail brighten until it glowed like a coal in a breeze. She was, I am afraid, showing off.

Then Mira went and knelt by the fire.

In the Deeps she had only ever felt fire, as a warmth with no shape to it. Now she saw the flames climbing over the sticks and falling back and climbing again, and she knelt there with her hands spread to it and her mouth a little open, and did not say anything at all.

“Tea,” said Old Ash, and handed her a tin cup.

Now, you will remember Old Ash’s tea. The Greywaste had not improved it. He made it from whatever leaves he could find, and on this particular morning, I am almost sure, he had forgotten it on the fire for a very long time indeed. Now she looked into the cup.

She tilted it towards the lamp. She looked at the grey-brown scum going round on the top, and at the bits of leaf, and at something small and dark at the bottom which might have been a leaf and might not. Then she looked up at Old Ash, her face perfectly serious and full of wonder.

“Oh,” she said. “It is the colour of what it tastes like.”

And Wren laughed.

I want to be careful how I tell this, because it matters. Wren had laughed before. She had laughed at Mott behind his back, and at Gutterlings, and at Tobin when he fell over. But all those laughs had been short and sharp — the kind you do with your mouth while the rest of you stays watchful, the way a sweep keeps one hand on the chimney-wall while she reaches with the other. Wren had never in her life laughed with all of herself at once. She had never had the time. There had always been a debt to pay or a meal to find or something coming up the lane behind her.

This was not that kind of laugh.

It came up from somewhere near her boots and took hold of her and would not let go. She laughed until she had to sit down on the shingle. She laughed until her eyes ran. She tried to stop, and looked at Mira’s grave face, and started again, worse. Cinder came and put her paws on her knee in some concern, and sneezed a spark, which set her off again.

Tobin stared. He had never heard Wren laugh like that. Nobody had. Then he began to laugh too, because it is very difficult not to; and then Mira, who did not quite understand what was funny but could see that it was something good, laughed as well, a bright, surprised sound that rang off the water.

Old Ash looked from one to the other of them.

“Hm,” he said. Then the corner of his beard twitched, and he took the cup back and tipped it, very slowly and with great dignity, into the Gloam River.

When it was over, and they lay back on the shingle with their stomachs aching, Wren felt lighter than she could remember — as if something tight inside her that she had not known was there had come undone.

The Delvers came down to the river that afternoon.

Mira heard them first, of course. She had been sent to listen to the river and come back, and she had not come back; so they had come to find her. Out of the mist on the far bank rose a sound like a hive: hundreds of voices, low and anxious, calling her name the long Delver way, Mi-i-ira, so that it rolled out over the water and came back off the reeds.

Mira cupped her hands and called back. A great rustling cheer went up on the other side. And within the hour, by the knock of stone on wood and the creak of good grey Delver rope, they had lashed a raft together from the dead black trees along the shore and were poling it across: two rafters, and Mother Hessa, and Tavi, and Speaker Gorrim.

Mira stood on the shingle and watched them come.

She had known them all her life by their voices and their footsteps. Now she saw them, which is a strange thing to do with people you love. “Ollan, your beard!” she cried, before the raft had even grounded. “Gran, you are so small!” And Mother Hessa, who was indeed very small, put both hands on Mira’s face and felt it all over, the old Delver way, and understood. Then she held Mira tight and hummed into her hair for a long time.

Tavi came off the raft at a run, found Cinder by the warmth of her tail, and picked her up. Cinder allowed it for exactly three seconds and then sneezed in his ear.

Last off the raft came Speaker Gorrim.

He was a great slow mountain of a man, with a white beard plaited past his belt, and he had sat in the Hall of Answers and condemned them all to the Silent Pit. Now he walked up the shingle towards the warmth of the lamp and stopped in front of Wren, and was silent for so long that she began to wonder whether he had come to condemn her all over again.

Then Speaker Gorrim knelt down on the stones.

He did it slowly, because he was not young and the stones were hard. Behind him the rafters went quiet. Even Tavi stopped fidgeting.

“I said there was no light,” said Gorrim, very low. “I said it was a story to frighten children, and I would have put you in the Pit for saying otherwise.” He turned his pale blind eyes towards the warmth. “And when the dark came for my boy, it was your light that went down after him. Not mine. Mine was never there. I was proud, and I was wrong, and I am sorry.”

Wren did not know what to do with a grown man kneeling in front of her. She looked at Ash, who only waited.

“Get up,” said Wren at last. “Please. It wasn’t mine anyway, the light. It was given me. Same as it was given Tavi.” She shifted her feet. “And I’d have thought I was a liar too, if I’d been you. I did think it was a trick, the first time I saw it.”

Something moved at the corner of Gorrim’s mouth — not quite a smile, but the place where a smile might one day go.

“Then we are a pair,” he said, and got up, and took something from inside his robe.

It was a stone, smooth and pale and the size of a hen’s egg, with a thin dark line running round its middle like a seam.

“A singing-stone,” said Gorrim. “Not one of the Hour-Stones. Older. Cut from the heart-wall of Deepholm, where the old songs were first sung, and cut to hear one thing only. It hears the cold.” He put it into Wren’s palm. It was cool and heavy, and it fitted her hand as if it had been made to. “When anything comes near that drinks songs — the grey things, the cold riders — it will hum. Low at first. Louder as they come. It was silent all my life, until the night Varrick came. Then it sang so that I could not sleep, and I did not listen.” He closed her fingers over it with his own. “Listen better than I did.”

Wren opened her mouth to say what she always said, which was what do you want for it?

She shut it again.

“Thank you,” she said instead. It was getting easier.

That night Gorrim and his party stayed on the near bank, round the company’s fire, and it was settled what the Delvers would do. They could not go home while the Hollows held the deep halls. But they had heard Wren and Tobin talk of Emberwick, away to the south, where the Ring burned white-gold along the wall, and they had made up their minds.

“We will go to your city,” said Gorrim. “We will learn to live where the warmth is. Slowly, perhaps. But we are stone-workers. We are patient.”

“Go to Soot Lane,” said Wren at once. “There’s a bakery. Mrs Fenn’s. Tell her Wren sent you. And tell Nettle—“ She stopped. She did not know what to tell Nettle. “Tell her I’ve still got the bread.”

Afterwards, when the fire had burned down to red, Wren lay with her head on her pack and the lamp in the crook of her arm, and without quite meaning to she began to hum.

It was the old tune. Morning comes, morning comes. The only part of her mother’s lullaby she had left.

Beside the fire, Mother Hessa sat up.

Then she began to hum too. Not a different song — the same one, note for note, rising and falling in the same places, only slower, the way Delvers did everything. Gorrim took it up, deep as a cellar. And then, from across the dark water, faint and far, the whole camp of the Delvers on the other bank took it up as well, hundreds of soft voices together, until the river itself seemed to be humming, low and warm, like a bell long after it has been struck.

Wren sat up. Her heart was going very fast.

“That’s mine,” she said. “That’s my mum’s song.” She had known since the Story-Wall that it was theirs too; but she had never heard it sung by so many.

“It is the Waking Song,” said Mira, beside her. “The oldest song in Deepholm. We sing it to babies, and when someone has been ill and gets better.” She hesitated. “Most of the words are gone. They wore away, Gran says, the way steps wear away when too many feet go up and down them. We only have the tune. And the one line on the Wall.”

“Sing it,” said Wren. She had hold of Mira’s sleeve, and had not noticed. “The line from the Wall. Sing it again.”

Mira took a breath and sang it. Her voice was small and clear and not very tuneful, and it went through Wren like warmth through a cold hand.

“…and the dark shall not keep us.”

That was all. The humming went on a while across the water, and faded, the way the fire was fading, and the river went on talking to itself in the dark.

Wren lay back down and held the line inside her carefully, like a full cup. Morning comes, morning comes … and the dark shall not keep us. There was still a great gap where the rest of it ought to be. But it was more than she had had a week ago, and she had not bought it, or stolen it, or earned it. It had simply been given to her: once by a blind girl in the dark, and now again by the same girl, who could see, beside a river at night.

She went to sleep with it.

In the morning, while the rafters were readying the raft to go back, Mira came and stood in front of Old Ash with her hands behind her back and her chin up. She looked, Wren thought, exactly the way Wren herself looked when she had made up her mind to ask for something and was ready to be told no.

“I wish to come with you,” said Mira. “To the Bright Mountain.”

“It’s a long road, child,” said Ash.

“I know. You say so often.”

“Hm. And a dangerous one. And dark, a good deal of it.”

“The dark,” said Mira, “is where I am best. In the light I am a baby who falls over things. But when the light goes, you will all be stumbling about like Delvers who have had too much mushroom-ale, and I will not. You need someone who can see in the dark. Now you have one who can see in both.” Her voice wobbled, very slightly, and steadied. “I have asked the Speaker. He has said yes. Gran cried, but she said yes. And I have never seen a mountain. I would like to see a great many things. I would like to see them with you.”

Ash looked at Wren.

It was her lamp; that was what the look meant. And Wren thought of the night in Deepholm when she had asked Mira for help — she, who never asked anybody for anything — and of how Mira had not asked for a single thing back.

“Course she’s coming,” said Wren. “Somebody’s got to tell me what colour things are.”

Mira’s face broke open like a morning.

It stayed silent for four days.
fields.body_text: Mira did not sleep that night. Nobody had really expected her to. She sat on a flat rock at the edge of the Gloam River with the lamp on the stones in front of her, and she looked at it. She looked at it the way you might read a letter from someone you had given up hoping to hear from: over and over, from the beginning, in case you had missed a word. Now and then she put her face so close to the glass that her nose nearly touched it. Once she shut her eyes tight and clicked her tongue at it — tk, tk — and then opened them again, quickly, as if to check that it was still there. It was still there. It always was. Wren lay a little way off, pretending to be asleep, and watched her. Mira wore an expression Wren had never seen before. It was not quite happiness. It was bigger and quieter than that. It was the look of someone who has been told a story all their life, and has believed it, and has just found out that it was true. “You can come and sit by me,” said Mira, without turning round. “I can hear you not sleeping. You do it very loudly.” So Wren went and sat by her. Mira turned and looked at her, very seriously, for a long time. Being looked at is not a thing most of us notice much. But Wren had never been looked at like that, and she found she did not know where to put her hands. “You are smaller than your voice,” said Mira at last. “Thanks very much.” “It was not a complaint. My clicks told me you were small. They did not tell me you would look it.” Mira reached out a finger and touched the tufts of Wren’s hair where they stuck out over her ears. “And this is how your hair looks. I knew how it felt. I did not know a thing could look the way it feels. Does everything?” Wren thought about it. “Mostly,” she said. “Mott looked the way he felt. Like a sack of wet coal.” Mira laughed, a short, delighted bark. The sun came up over the Gloam River, and Mira saw her first morning. It was not, I am sorry to say, much of a morning. The cursed sun rose through the mist like a coin seen through dirty water, and turned the black river grey, and that was more or less the end of what it could do. Mira thought it was the most wonderful thing she had ever seen. “It is coming in from everywhere at once,” she said, standing up on her rock. “Wren, there is no edge to it. Where is the lamp of it?” “That’s the sun,” said Wren. “It’s not much of one.” “It is enormous,” said Mira, and would not be told otherwise. All that first morning she went about the river-bank like a bee in a garden, and everything astonished her. She picked up handfuls of shingle and said that she had always known stones were different, but not that they were different-looking, which seemed to her a great extravagance on the part of stones. She was very bad at distances. Her echo-sense had not gone anywhere — the Ferryman had given her eyes, not taken her ears — and when she clicked she could still tell you to a finger’s breadth how far off the river was, or the tree, or Tobin. But her eyes did not yet know what her ears knew, and they kept telling her lies. She reached out to touch the far bank of the Gloam, a quarter of a mile away, and was very much put out when she couldn’t. She walked straight into Old Ash’s back because, she said, he had looked a long way off and then had suddenly not been. “Shut your eyes and click, then,” said Wren, “if your eyes are no good.” “My eyes are perfectly good,” said Mira with dignity. “They are only new. One does not blame a baby for falling over.” Then she shut them, clicked, walked neatly round Ash, and opened them on the other side. “There. They agree with each other now. That is a relief. I was not sure they could be trusted.” Tobin, watching with great scientific interest, said that, technically speaking, it was a matter of the brain learning the signals, and had she noticed whether the lamp looked further away when she shut one eye— “Tobin,” said Mira. “You have a very long nose.” Tobin went pink. “I — have I?” “It is a good nose,” said Mira kindly. “I heard that it was long. I did not know it would go on for quite so long as it does.” She tilted her head. “And there is colour on your face. That is new.” “That,” said Wren, enjoying herself enormously, “is called going red.” It was the colours that undid her in the end. There were not many to see. Out here, far from any Ring, the world was the old Gloamhaven world: grey and brown and dun and that tired blue-ish that people called dull. But near the lamp, as you know, the colours came back; and so all morning Mira kept running back to it, the way you keep running back to the one warm room in a cold house. Close to its light, the ribbon on Wren’s wrist was red — a true, glad, berry red. Mira held Wren’s wrist in both hands and looked at it for so long that Wren began to feel awkward and tried to take it back. “What is its name?” said Mira. “Not ribbon. The — the loud part of it.” “Red,” said Wren. “Red,” said Mira softly, the way you would say the name of a friend. “It sounds like it looks. It sounds warm. And Tobin’s hair, near the lamp? And Cinder’s tail — that is something else again.” Wren said Tobin’s hair was yellow, because Nettle had said so. About Cinder’s tail nobody could agree until Ash, sitting on a stone by the little fire he had built with his bad leg out in front of him, said “Hm,” and that it was gold at the tip and orange behind, and that it did not matter very much what you called a thing so long as you saw it. Cinder, who knew perfectly well she was being talked about, let the spark at the end of her tail brighten until it glowed like a coal in a breeze. She was, I am afraid, showing off. Then Mira went and knelt by the fire. In the Deeps she had only ever felt fire, as a warmth with no shape to it. Now she saw the flames climbing over the sticks and falling back and climbing again, and she knelt there with her hands spread to it and her mouth a little open, and did not say anything at all. “Tea,” said Old Ash, and handed her a tin cup. Now, you will remember Old Ash’s tea. The Greywaste had not improved it. He made it from whatever leaves he could find, and on this particular morning, I am almost sure, he had forgotten it on the fire for a very long time indeed. Now she looked into the cup. She tilted it towards the lamp. She looked at the grey-brown scum going round on the top, and at the bits of leaf, and at something small and dark at the bottom which might have been a leaf and might not. Then she looked up at Old Ash, her face perfectly serious and full of wonder. “Oh,” she said. “It is the colour of what it tastes like.” And Wren laughed. “It is the colour of what it tastes like.” I want to be careful how I tell this, because it matters. Wren had laughed before. She had laughed at Mott behind his back, and at Gutterlings, and at Tobin when he fell over. But all those laughs had been short and sharp — the kind you do with your mouth while the rest of you stays watchful, the way a sweep keeps one hand on the chimney-wall while she reaches with the other. Wren had never in her life laughed with all of herself at once. She had never had the time. There had always been a debt to pay or a meal to find or something coming up the lane behind her. This was not that kind of laugh. It came up from somewhere near her boots and took hold of her and would not let go. She laughed until she had to sit down on the shingle. She laughed until her eyes ran. She tried to stop, and looked at Mira’s grave face, and started again, worse. Cinder came and put her paws on her knee in some concern, and sneezed a spark, which set her off again. Tobin stared. He had never heard Wren laugh like that. Nobody had. Then he began to laugh too, because it is very difficult not to; and then Mira, who did not quite understand what was funny but could see that it was something good, laughed as well, a bright, surprised sound that rang off the water. Old Ash looked from one to the other of them. “Hm,” he said. Then the corner of his beard twitched, and he took the cup back and tipped it, very slowly and with great dignity, into the Gloam River. When it was over, and they lay back on the shingle with their stomachs aching, Wren felt lighter than she could remember — as if something tight inside her that she had not known was there had come undone. The Delvers came down to the river that afternoon. Mira heard them first, of course. She had been sent to listen to the river and come back, and she had not come back; so they had come to find her. Out of the mist on the far bank rose a sound like a hive: hundreds of voices, low and anxious, calling her name the long Delver way, Mi-i-ira, so that it rolled out over the water and came back off the reeds. Mira cupped her hands and called back. A great rustling cheer went up on the other side. And within the hour, by the knock of stone on wood and the creak of good grey Delver rope, they had lashed a raft together from the dead black trees along the shore and were poling it across: two rafters, and Mother Hessa, and Tavi, and Speaker Gorrim. Mira stood on the shingle and watched them come. She had known them all her life by their voices and their footsteps. Now she saw them, which is a strange thing to do with people you love. “Ollan, your beard!” she cried, before the raft had even grounded. “Gran, you are so small!” And Mother Hessa, who was indeed very small, put both hands on Mira’s face and felt it all over, the old Delver way, and understood. Then she held Mira tight and hummed into her hair for a long time. Tavi came off the raft at a run, found Cinder by the warmth of her tail, and picked her up. Cinder allowed it for exactly three seconds and then sneezed in his ear. Last off the raft came Speaker Gorrim. He was a great slow mountain of a man, with a white beard plaited past his belt, and he had sat in the Hall of Answers and condemned them all to the Silent Pit. Now he walked up the shingle towards the warmth of the lamp and stopped in front of Wren, and was silent for so long that she began to wonder whether he had come to condemn her all over again. Then Speaker Gorrim knelt down on the stones. He did it slowly, because he was not young and the stones were hard. Behind him the rafters went quiet. Even Tavi stopped fidgeting. “I said there was no light,” said Gorrim, very low. “I said it was a story to frighten children, and I would have put you in the Pit for saying otherwise.” He turned his pale blind eyes towards the warmth. “And when the dark came for my boy, it was your light that went down after him. Not mine. Mine was never there. I was proud, and I was wrong, and I am sorry.” Wren did not know what to do with a grown man kneeling in front of her. She looked at Ash, who only waited. “Get up,” said Wren at last. “Please. It wasn’t mine anyway, the light. It was given me. Same as it was given Tavi.” She shifted her feet. “And I’d have thought I was a liar too, if I’d been you. I did think it was a trick, the first time I saw it.” Something moved at the corner of Gorrim’s mouth — not quite a smile, but the place where a smile might one day go. “Then we are a pair,” he said, and got up, and took something from inside his robe. It was a stone, smooth and pale and the size of a hen’s egg, with a thin dark line running round its middle like a seam. “A singing-stone,” said Gorrim. “Not one of the Hour-Stones. Older. Cut from the heart-wall of Deepholm, where the old songs were first sung, and cut to hear one thing only. It hears the cold.” He put it into Wren’s palm. It was cool and heavy, and it fitted her hand as if it had been made to. “When anything comes near that drinks songs — the grey things, the cold riders — it will hum. Low at first. Louder as they come. It was silent all my life, until the night Varrick came. Then it sang so that I could not sleep, and I did not listen.” He closed her fingers over it with his own. “Listen better than I did.” Wren opened her mouth to say what she always said, which was what do you want for it? She shut it again. “Thank you,” she said instead. It was getting easier. That night Gorrim and his party stayed on the near bank, round the company’s fire, and it was settled what the Delvers would do. They could not go home while the Hollows held the deep halls. But they had heard Wren and Tobin talk of Emberwick, away to the south, where the Ring burned white-gold along the wall, and they had made up their minds. “We will go to your city,” said Gorrim. “We will learn to live where the warmth is. Slowly, perhaps. But we are stone-workers. We are patient.” “Go to Soot Lane,” said Wren at once. “There’s a bakery. Mrs Fenn’s. Tell her Wren sent you. And tell Nettle—“ She stopped. She did not know what to tell Nettle. “Tell her I’ve still got the bread.” Afterwards, when the fire had burned down to red, Wren lay with her head on her pack and the lamp in the crook of her arm, and without quite meaning to she began to hum. It was the old tune. Morning comes, morning comes. The only part of her mother’s lullaby she had left. Beside the fire, Mother Hessa sat up. Then she began to hum too. Not a different song — the same one, note for note, rising and falling in the same places, only slower, the way Delvers did everything. Gorrim took it up, deep as a cellar. And then, from across the dark water, faint and far, the whole camp of the Delvers on the other bank took it up as well, hundreds of soft voices together, until the river itself seemed to be humming, low and warm, like a bell long after it has been struck. Wren sat up. Her heart was going very fast. “That’s mine,” she said. “That’s my mum’s song.” She had known since the Story-Wall that it was theirs too; but she had never heard it sung by so many. “It is the Waking Song,” said Mira, beside her. “The oldest song in Deepholm. We sing it to babies, and when someone has been ill and gets better.” She hesitated. “Most of the words are gone. They wore away, Gran says, the way steps wear away when too many feet go up and down them. We only have the tune. And the one line on the Wall.” “Sing it,” said Wren. She had hold of Mira’s sleeve, and had not noticed. “The line from the Wall. Sing it again.” Mira took a breath and sang it. Her voice was small and clear and not very tuneful, and it went through Wren like warmth through a cold hand. “…and the dark shall not keep us.” That was all. The humming went on a while across the water, and faded, the way the fire was fading, and the river went on talking to itself in the dark. Wren lay back down and held the line inside her carefully, like a full cup. Morning comes, morning comes … and the dark shall not keep us. There was still a great gap where the rest of it ought to be. But it was more than she had had a week ago, and she had not bought it, or stolen it, or earned it. It had simply been given to her: once by a blind girl in the dark, and now again by the same girl, who could see, beside a river at night. She went to sleep with it. fields.title: A Letter Sealed in Grey
fields.body_html:
On the far side of the Gloam River the land began to change.

None of the changes were for the better, as far as Wren could see. The flat grey plain rose into long low hills of grey heather, which scratched your ankles, and dun bracken, which soaked your knees. The old Lamplighters’ road wound between them, very faint now, marked here and there by a waystone with its empty niche. Every time they came to one, Wren let the flame lean into the niche, and it caught and burned gold behind them as they walked on. By the fourth day there was a thin line of lit waystones running back across the hills, like the beads on a necklace.

Mira thought the hills were very fine. She thought most things were very fine. She had seen her first rain, and stood in it with her face turned up until she was soaked; she had seen her first rabbit, and chased it, and said that it was rude of things to be faster with their legs than she was with her eyes. She walked into things less each day, and in the evenings, when the light went and the others began to stumble, she clicked her way round the camp fetching sticks for the fire and laughed at them.

“How do you bear it?” she said, after Tobin had fallen over the same tree-root twice. “Your eyes stopping just because the sun has. It seems very badly made.”

“It’s worked well enough for most people,” said Tobin, from the ground.

“Most people,” said Mira, “have not met me.”

The food was running low. That was the real trouble. The Delvers had given them what they could spare: dried mushroom, and a hard grey biscuit that Ash said would keep for a hundred years and that Wren said tasted as if it already had. On the fourth day Ash opened the last packet and divided it by five, and then looked at it, and divided his own share again between Cinder and Mira, and said he was not hungry. Nobody believed him.

It was about the middle of that afternoon, on the long slope of a grey hill, that Wren’s pocket hummed.

She thought, at first, that it was her stomach. It had been making noises all day. She put her hand on her middle and frowned at it.

“Was that you?” said Tobin.

“Course it was me. I’m starving.”

“No,” said Mira. She had stopped dead in the road with her head on one side. “That was not a stomach. Stomachs do not hum in tune. Wren — your pocket.”

Wren put her hand in her coat pocket, and her fingers closed on the singing-stone.

It was cold — colder than the wind — and trembling faintly under her fingers, the way a glass trembles when someone sings near it. The hum was one long low note, so quiet that you felt it more in your teeth than heard it.

They all stood still.

Cinder’s ears went flat. A growl began somewhere deep in her chest, so low it was almost the same note as the stone. She was looking back down the road the way they had come.

“Something cold,” said Old Ash quietly. “Gorrim said so. Mira?”

Mira shut her eyes and clicked — three sharp clicks, tk-tk-tk — and listened, and clicked again.

“A horse,” she said. “Shod. Coming fast along the road behind us. One rider. He is—“ She frowned. “He is very quiet. He sits on the horse like a sack. And there is a bag on his back, full of something thin. Paper, I think.”

“Varrick?” said Tobin. His voice had gone high.

“No,” said Ash. “Varrick’s horse is heavier, and he doesn’t sit like a sack. Hm. A rider in a hurry, on the Queen’s business, with a bag of paper. I think, children, that we have met the post.”

The stone hummed louder in Wren’s hand.

There was not much time to argue, and so for once nobody did. At the foot of the slope, where the road ran between two banks of heather, stood a waystone they had passed an hour before. Ash sent them down off the road into the ditch beside it — Tobin and Mira on one side, Cinder flat in the bracken on the other — and he himself stood behind the waystone with his long brass-hooked pole held low along the ground, like a fisherman waiting for a pike.

“And me?” said Wren.

“You,” said Ash, “stand in the road. With the lamp. And don’t move.”

Wren looked at him. “You want me to stand in front of a galloping horse.”

“I want you to stand in front of a galloping horse,” said Ash, “holding the one thing in all Gloamhaven that horse has not seen for a very long time. Trust me, child. It will stop.”

I should tell you that Wren did not much like being told to trust people. But she had given the lamp to Tobin at the foot of the Black Stair and got it back again; and she had asked Mira for help in Deepholm and got that too. It is a strange thing about trust: the more you do it, the less it feels like falling. So she went and stood in the middle of the road with the lamp in both hands, and set her feet, and waited.

She heard the hooves before she saw them. Then the horse came round the bend at the bottom of the hill.

It was a grey horse — not grey the way a horse is born grey, but grey with all the colour wrung out of it — and it was thin, and its eyes rolled. On its back, swaying like a sack, sat a man in a grey cloak with a great leather satchel slung across him. His face was the colour of putty. His eyes were open and saw nothing, and the cold came off him ahead of the horse like a draught from an open door.

The horse saw the lamp.

It stopped so hard that its hooves skidded in the dirt. It stood with its legs braced and its nostrils wide, staring at the light, trembling all over. The rider swayed forward in the saddle. Without a word, without any change in his empty face, he kicked at the horse’s sides to make it go on.

The horse would not go.

And Old Ash stepped out from behind the waystone, swung his long pole, caught the rider neatly under the arm with the brass hook, and lifted him out of the saddle and into the heather as easily as you might lift a coat off a peg.

The rider did not fight. That was the worst of it. He only tried to get up, slowly, like a toy that has been wound and set going, and reach for the horse again. Cinder stood on his chest and growled, and he did not even seem to see her.

Wren knelt down beside him.

“Here,” she said. “It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

She held out the lamp, and the flame leaned out towards him. Warmth spread over the heather. And the colour came back into the man the way it had come back into Mrs Fenn and Gristle Mott and Tavi — slowly at first, then all in a rush. His cheeks went brown and red with weather. His cloak turned out to be a faded green, with a little brass badge on the shoulder in the shape of a horn. He blinked. He took a great gasping breath, as if he had been under water for a long time, and burst into tears.

He was quite young, they found, when he had stopped crying — eighteen, perhaps, or nineteen. His name was Dunstan, and he had been a post-rider once, carrying letters between the Ring-towns. One night, he could not say how long ago, he had been caught on the open road after dark.

“It was cold,” he said. “That’s all I remember. Cold, and then a voice. Ever so kind, it was. It said I’d been riding so hard for so long, and wasn’t I tired, and why not let somebody else do the deciding.” He shuddered. “After that, nothing. Only riding. Somebody’d put a bag in my hands, and I’d ride till somebody took it off me, and then there’d be another.” He looked down at the satchel across his chest as if he had never seen it before. “Where am I? Whose is all this?”

“That,” said Ash, “is what we should like to know.”

He lifted the satchel off Dunstan’s shoulder and opened it.

It was full of letters. There were perhaps two dozen, every one sealed with a blob of grey wax. Wren touched one and snatched her finger back. The wax was cold — not cold like a stone in winter, but cold the way the stone in her pocket had been cold, the way a Hollow is cold. Most had no crest pressed into them; only a smooth grey thumbprint, like a fingertip dipped in ash.

“Reading other folk’s letters,” said Ash, taking out his knife, “is a poor habit. But these were going to a poorer place.”

He broke the seals one by one, and read, and his face grew longer and greyer with every letter. Wren read some over his elbow. They were from places she had never heard of: a guard-captain in some city by a lake, a lamp-keeper in a town in the hills, a man who signed himself only a friend. Some were grovelling and some were proud. But they were all, when you got to the bottom of them, the same kind of letter.

“They’re bargains,” said Wren slowly. “Every one of them. I’ll let your grey things in at the north gate, if you’ll leave my house alone. I’ll put out the lamps on the east wall, if you’ll make me rich.” She looked up. “They’re all selling something.”

“Hm,” said Ash heavily. “Yes. That’s how she does it, child. Not with armies, mostly. With a great many small, frightened people, each one asking her to make an exception for him.” He laid the letters down on the heather, one after another. “Varrick was the polite one. These are the people who answered him.”

Tobin had picked up the last letter in the bag.

He had not opened it. He was just holding it, turning it over in his ink-stained fingers, and he had gone very still.

This one was not like the others. The paper was thick and good, the kind you only find in grand houses. And pressed into the grey wax, quite clearly, was a seal: a tall tower with a little flame on top. Wren had seen that seal before. It was carved over the gate of the Warden’s Hall in Emberwick, and on the badges of the Warden’s guards, and on the buckle of Sergeant Bracken’s belt.

On the front, in a tall, careful, slanting hand, it said: To Her Majesty. By the Captain’s rider.

“That’s my father’s writing,” said Tobin.

Nobody said anything.

Tobin broke the seal himself. His hands were perfectly steady while he did it, which was somehow worse than if they had shaken. He unfolded the paper and pushed his spectacles up his nose and read it aloud, in a clear, flat, careful voice, as if it were a lesson he had been set.

Madam,

Your Captain once made me an offer, and I did not keep my part of it, and my city has turned its face from me for having made it at all. I write now to make another.

The lamp you seek has gone out of Emberwick. It is carried by a sweep-girl and the old madman Ash, and by my son. They go towards the Bright Mountain by the old Lamplighters’ road. I have this from my son’s own hand; he wrote to tell me so before he left. I can tell you more of their road, if you wish it. And the boy will come home, in time. When he does, the lamp will come with him. I will see that it is put into your hands.

In return I ask only what your Captain spoke of: that when the Rings fail, as they all will, I shall not fail with them. Give me a throne over all the Rings, and I will keep them in good order for you.

I ask one thing more. Let no harm come to the boy. He is foolish, but he is mine.

Edric Harrowgate, Warden of Emberwick.

Tobin stopped reading. He folded the letter up again, very neatly, along its old creases. Then he stood up and walked away down the road, and sat down on the waystone with his back to them all, and did not move.

It was getting dark. The waystone glowed gold behind him, and Tobin sat on it with his shoulders hunched, a long thin black shape against the light.

“His breathing has gone very small,” said Mira quietly. “I don’t like it.”

Ash was looking at Wren.

“No,” said Wren. “No. Not me. You go. You’re old. You’re good at — at saying things.”

“Very likely,” said Ash. “Go and say it anyway.”

Tobin made a small sound.

“Not really,” said Tobin. But he had turned his head a little towards her.

fields.body_text: On the far side of the Gloam River the land began to change. None of the changes were for the better, as far as Wren could see. The flat grey plain rose into long low hills of grey heather, which scratched your ankles, and dun bracken, which soaked your knees. The old Lamplighters’ road wound between them, very faint now, marked here and there by a waystone with its empty niche. fields.title: The Lights of Vaelport
fields.body_html:
Mira heard the sea hours before anyone saw it.

They had turned west after Dunstan rode away, following the Gloam River down towards the sea, as he had told them to; and the compass in Tobin’s pocket did not like it at all. Every time he took it out, the needle swung round and pointed back over his right shoulder — north and a bit east, towards the Bright Mountain, which had sunk out of sight behind the hills — and Tobin would look at it and sigh and put it away again.

“It’s only a little way round,” said Wren. “Isn’t it?”

“Technically,” said Tobin, “it’s a great deal of the way round. About forty miles of the way round, and forty back, if my map’s right, which it may not be, since the man who drew it had obviously never been anywhere.”

“The Mountain will wait,” said Old Ash. “It has waited three hundred years. We need bread, and we need to tell the Rings what was in that bag. Both of those are at the coast.” He did not say what else they all knew: that his bad leg was getting worse, not better, and that he leaned harder on his two poles with every mile.

So they went west, beside the slow grey river, over the last of the grey hills; and on the second morning Mira stopped in the road and put her head on one side.

“There is something ahead,” she said. “Breathing. Like the river did, before we found it — only the river was asleep, and this is not.” She clicked, and listened, and frowned. “I can’t find the edge of it. It doesn’t send anything back. Wren, the river is going into it. There is something ahead of us that is breathing, and it is bigger than Deepholm.”

Wren went cold all over. Cinder, however, only sniffed the wind and sneezed, and trotted on with her tail up.

It was late afternoon before they came over the last rise and saw it.

If you have seen the sea, you will remember the first time. If you have not, I hope you will one day, and I hope that somebody you like is standing next to you when you do.

It lay below them at the foot of tall grey cliffs, and it went on for ever. It did not stop at the edge of the sky; it simply turned into the sky, grey into grey, so that you could not tell where one ended and the other began. It moved all over, all the time, in long slow ridges that came in from nowhere and broke white on the rocks below with a noise like a great slow breath going in and out. The wind off it was cold and wet and tasted of salt. Grey birds hung in it without moving their wings, crying in thin, complaining voices.

Wren had thought the Soot Canal was a lot of water. She stood on the clifftop with her mouth open and her hair blown flat and did not say anything at all, which was so unusual that Tobin looked at her twice.

“It’s the sea,” said Tobin, in a voice of great satisfaction, as if he had arranged it. “The Western Sea. It’s on all the old maps. I never thought I’d — well. There it is.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose and stared and stared.

Mira had gone very quiet. She stood right at the edge of the cliff with Ash’s hand on her shoulder in case she stepped off it, which she had nearly done twice, and she looked at the sea, and then shut her eyes and listened to it, and then opened them again.

“It is the shape of what it sounds like,” she said at last, softly. “I didn’t think anything could be.”

They went down a steep path to the shore and stood at the edge of the water. Wren held the lamp out over the place where the waves ran up the sand and spread out thin and foaming and slid back again. And in the lamp’s light, just for a moment, at the very edge of the foam, the grey water was not grey. It was a colour none of them had ever seen — not blue, not quite green, but something clear and deep and cold between the two, like the inside of a piece of glass.

“What’s that one?” said Mira at once. “Ash. What is that called?”

Old Ash looked at it for a long time.

“Sea-green,” he said at last, and his voice was rough. “My grandmother had a shawl that colour, when I was very small. She used to say that the sea had been that colour every day, once.” He cleared his throat. “Hm. Wind’s getting up. Come along.”

They saw Vaelport that evening.

They had walked south along the clifftops all afternoon, with the sea booming on their right hand, and as the dusk came down they rounded a great dark headland — and stopped, all five of them, as if they had walked into a wall.

Across a wide bay, perhaps ten miles off, a city was burning with light.

I do not mean that it was on fire. I mean that it shone. It climbed up the hills above the far shore in tier after tier of towers and walls and domes, and every one of them was lit — not here and there, the way a town is lit at night, with a lamp in this window and that, but all over, all at once, as if the whole city had been carved out of light and set down on the hills. Long white beams swung out from its towers across the dark water. Its harbour glittered. Its walls glittered. Even the clouds above it were lit up from beneath, so that the sky over Vaelport was paler than the sky anywhere else, as if a white sun were about to rise there instead of in the east.

Emberwick’s Ring, at its very best, burning gold along the wall on the night they lit the Beacon, had been a beautiful thing. Beside this, it would have looked like a string of birthday candles.

For a while nobody said anything at all.

Mira was the first to move. She had put both hands up in front of her face, and she was looking through her fingers. “It is so loud,” she whispered. “It’s shouting. Everything in it is shouting at once.” She took her hands away, and squinted, and put them back again, laughing a little and gasping, the way you do when you jump into cold water. “Oh, but it’s — Wren, it’s beautiful. I didn’t know there could be so much light in the whole world. There must be a thousand lamps. There must be ten thousand. Where do they get them all?”

Wren did not answer. She was asking herself the same thing; only she was not asking it in the same way.

Tobin had taken a step forward, to the very edge of the headland, and his face in that far-off white light was eager and pale and hopeful all at once. Wren had seen him look like that before — over a broken clock, or a map, or a puzzle he thought he could solve.

“Look at it,” he said. “Just look at it. That’s not a Ring, that’s — that’s a whole city that doesn’t need a Ring. No Hollow could get within a mile of that. They wouldn’t need anybody’s oil. They wouldn’t need to bargain with anybody.” He swallowed. His hand had gone to his coat pocket, where the letter was. “If Emberwick had light like that, Father wouldn’t — he wouldn’t have needed to be so frightened. Would he? He wouldn’t have had to — to write to anyone.” He turned round to them, and his spectacles flashed white. “Perhaps they could help. Perhaps if we went to them and told them, they’d — they could send some of it back. To Emberwick. And then he wouldn’t need a throne, he’d only need—“

He stopped, because nobody was answering him.

Wren was looking at her wrist.

They were ten miles away; but the light of Vaelport was so strong that it reached them even here, faint and white, across the bay. It lay on the heather. It lay on Tobin’s face, and on Mira’s hands, and on Ash’s beard. And it lay on the ribbon round Wren’s wrist. In that light, her ribbon was not red. It was not even the faded grey-with-a-little-pink it had been in the old days in Soot Lane. It was white — a bleached, washed-out white, like a rag that has been left out in the frost for a winter.

She brought her wrist up close to the lamp. The ribbon went red again at once, deep and warm and glad.

She held it out again, into the white light. White.

“Nobody’s got that much light for nothing,” said Wren slowly. “Nobody. Somebody’s paying for that.” She looked across the water. “And I’d like to know who.”

Cinder was not looking at the city at all. She was sitting very upright at Ash’s feet with her back to it, and the spark at the end of her tail, which had glowed so bright beside the sea that afternoon, had gone down small and dim, like an ember left in yesterday’s hearth. When Mira bent to stroke her, she sneezed — not crossly, but in a small, unhappy sort of way — and pushed her nose into Ash’s boot.

Old Ash had not said a word. He stood leaning on his two poles with the wind tugging at his beard, and he looked at Vaelport for a long, long time, the way you look at the face of somebody you think you may have met before.

“That isn’t Flame,” he said.

He said it quietly. He did not say it like a man who is guessing.

“But—“ Tobin turned round. “How can you possibly tell? From all the way over here?”

“Look at it, lad.” Ash did not take his eyes off the city. “It doesn’t flicker. It doesn’t lean. Flame leans towards you; you’ve seen it. It gives.” He was silent a moment. “And it’s warm. Look at that light, all that light — and tell me. Does it look warm to you?”

Tobin looked. They all looked. And it is a strange thing, but once Ash had said it, none of them could see anything else. Vaelport blazed across the dark water, brighter than anything they had ever imagined; and it was cold. Cold the way frost is cold, and moonlight, and a knife left out on a step overnight. It was the coldest light Wren had ever seen.

“Then what is it?” said Mira, very small.

“Hm,” said Ash. And that, for that night, was all he would say.

They camped on the headland, out of the wind, in the lee of a fallen waystone that Wren lit before she slept. Nobody talked much. Tobin lay with his hand in his pocket and his eyes open. Mira lay with her back to the city, because she said it was too loud to sleep with, and then turned over three times to look at it again.

Once, very late, Wren saw Tobin sit up and take out his compass. He opened the lid and held it up to catch the far white glow, and she saw his face as he looked at it. The needle was not pointing at Vaelport. It had never once pointed at Vaelport. It pointed steadily the other way, back over the dark hills, north and a bit east, towards a mountain none of them could see. Tobin looked at it for a long time. Then he shut the lid, very gently, and lay down again with it in his fist.

Wren lay awake with the singing-stone in her hand.

It was silent. She had half expected it to hum, and it did not; it lay in her palm cool and smooth and still. She did not know whether that meant there was nothing in that city that drank songs — or only that the city was a long way off, across a great deal of water, and that some kinds of cold take longer to reach you than others.

She turned it over in her fingers for a long time. In the end she put it back in her pocket and curled up with her arm round the lamp, with her mother’s song going round and round in her head — Morning comes, morning comes … and the dark shall not keep us — until she slept.

In the morning they walked to Vaelport.

The sun came up over the grey hills to the east, exactly as pale as it always did; and ahead of them, all along the shore, the city still blazed. It had not dimmed for the morning. It did not seem to know that morning had come.

There was a road along the bay, and the nearer they came to the city the busier it grew. There were carts piled with fish and carts piled with furniture, and pedlars and pilgrims and whole families walking with their bundles on their backs. Some of them, Wren saw, had the tired, frightened look of people who have come a long way from a city whose Ring was failing, and have heard that somewhere, at the end of the road, there is a place where it never gets dark. “They say nobody in Vaelport has ever been greyed,” she told them. Her face was thin and tired, and lit up as she talked. “Not one, not ever. They say it’s never dark there, not even at midnight. And they say the light’s free.” She hitched the baby higher. “Free to all who come in. Can you imagine?”

Wren could imagine a good many things. She had been imagining them all her life, mostly about what things cost. The road was paved, as they came closer, with a smooth white stone that glittered. The walls rose up ahead of them, white and smooth and very high. And in the middle of the walls, standing wide open, were the gates of Vaelport.

They were enormous. They were made of something that was not quite glass and not quite crystal, cut into a thousand faces that caught the white light and threw it back, so that the whole gateway blazed like a frozen waterfall. It was so bright that Mira had to walk the last half-mile with her hand over her eyes, holding on to Wren’s sleeve and clicking. Even Tobin, who loved anything that was cleverly made, went quiet when he looked at it.

“Wren,” said Mira, peering between her fingers. “What colour is that? The gate. You promised you would tell me what colour things are.”

Wren looked at the gate for a long moment. It was white, and it was bright, and it shone back every scrap of light that fell on it a hundred times over. There was not a single thing in it that was red, or gold, or sea-green, or any of the colours she had only just learned the names of.

She tucked the little battered brass lamp inside her coat, against her ribs, and did up the coat over it, the way she had done on the very first day, in the chimneys of Thornbury House, when she had not known what it was or what it would cost her or who had put it in the wall.

It lay there warm and steady, like a hand.

Then he straightened his back as well as he could, and set his two poles on the shining road, and walked on.

So they went up to the gates of Vaelport together: a tall, stooped old man in a coat that had once been Lamplighter blue; a gangly boy with a compass in one pocket and a grey-sealed letter in the other; a pale girl with her hand over her new eyes; a small grey fox whose tail had gone almost dark; and a sweep with cropped black hair and a ribbon on her wrist that had turned, in all that dazzle, as white as frost.

The light of Vaelport poured over them, cold and white and endless, and made them very small.

They had turned west after Dunstan rode away, following the Gloam River down towards the sea, as he had told them to; and the compass in Tobin’s pocket did not like it at all. About forty miles of the way round, and forty back, if my map’s right, which it may not be, since the man who drew it had obviously never been anywhere.” “The Mountain will wait,” said Old Ash. “It has waited three hundred years. We need bread, and we need to tell the Rings what was in that bag. Both of those are at the coast.” He did not say what else they all knew: that his bad leg was getting worse, not better, and that he leaned harder on his two poles with every mile. So they went west, beside the slow grey river, over the last of the grey hills; and on the second morning Mira stopped in the road and put her head on one side. “There is something ahead,” she said. “Breathing. Like the river did, before we found it — only the river was asleep, and this is not.” She clicked, and listened, and frowned. “I can’t find the edge of it. It doesn’t send anything back. Wren, the river is going into it. There is something ahead of us that is breathing, and it is bigger than Deepholm.” Wren went cold all over. Cinder, however, only sniffed the wind and sneezed, and trotted on with her tail up. It was late afternoon before they came over the last rise and saw it. If you have seen the sea, you will remember the first time. If you have not, I hope you will one day, and I hope that somebody you like is standing next to you when you do. It lay below them at the foot of tall grey cliffs, and it went on for ever. It did not stop at the edge of the sky; it simply turned into the sky, grey into grey, so that you could not tell where one ended and the other began. It moved all over, all the time, in long slow ridges that came in from nowhere and broke white on the rocks below with a noise like a great slow breath going in and out. The wind off it was cold and wet and tasted of salt. Grey birds hung in it without moving their wings, crying in thin, complaining voices. Wren had thought the Soot Canal was a lot of water. She stood on the clifftop with her mouth open and her hair blown flat and did not say anything at all, which was so unusual that Tobin looked at her twice. “It’s the sea,” said Tobin, in a voice of great satisfaction, as if he had arranged it. “The Western Sea. It’s on all the old maps. I never thought I’d — well. There it is.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose and stared and stared. Mira had gone very quiet. She stood right at the edge of the cliff with Ash’s hand on her shoulder in case she stepped off it, which she had nearly done twice, and she looked at the sea, and then shut her eyes and listened to it, and then opened them again. “It is the shape of what it sounds like,” she said at last, softly. “I didn’t think anything could be.” They went down a steep path to the shore and stood at the edge of the water. Wren held the lamp out over the place where the waves ran up the sand and spread out thin and foaming and slid back again. And in the lamp’s light, just for a moment, at the very edge of the foam, the grey water was not grey. It was a colour none of them had ever seen — not blue, not quite green, but something clear and deep and cold between the two, like the inside of a piece of glass. “What’s that one?” said Mira at once. “Ash. Across a wide bay, perhaps ten miles off, a city was burning with light. I do not mean that it was on fire. I mean that it shone. It climbed up the hills above the far shore in tier after tier of towers and walls and domes, and every one of them was lit — not here and there, the way a town is lit at night, with a lamp in this window and that, but all over, all at once, as if the whole city had been carved out of light and set down on the hills. Long white beams swung out from its towers across the dark water. Its harbour glittered. Its walls glittered. Emberwick’s Ring, at its very best, burning gold along the wall on the night they lit the Beacon, had been a beautiful thing. Beside this, it would have looked like a string of birthday candles. For a while nobody said anything at all. Mira was the first to move. She had put both hands up in front of her face, and she was looking through her fingers. “It is so loud,” she whispered. “It’s shouting. Everything in it is shouting at once.” She took her hands away, and squinted, and put them back again, laughing a little and gasping, the way you do when you jump into cold water. “Oh, but it’s — Wren, it’s beautiful. Tobin had taken a step forward, to the very edge of the headland, and his face in that far-off white light was eager and pale and hopeful all at once.
